paragraphs: This paper proposes an artificial neural network model aimed at improving how cochlear implants support speech perception. Its motivation is the gap between detecting sound through electrical stimulation and recognizing speech. The abstract describes implants as stimulating the remaining peripheral auditory nervous system in people with profound sensorineural deafness.

The authors argue that effective interaction with natural speech perception requires reproducing temporal dispersion and other phenomena found in natural receptors. Temporal dispersion concerns how a response is spread over time. In their account, these aspects of natural processing are absent from the implants under discussion, making the timing of stimulation a central modeling concern.

The paper introduces a computational neural network model directed at those natural cochlear phenomena. Its contribution is a proposed way to represent receptor behavior that the authors consider important for useful speech coding. The claim that the discussed implants had not achieved useful speech recognition motivates this model; the stated work is a computational proposal, rather than a reported improvement in patients' speech perception.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes a neural model of natural cochlear timing phenomena to inform electrical coding for implant-based speech perception.

title: Using Neural Networks to Improve Cochlear Implant Speech Perception

paragraphs: The paper models how learning about a stimulus extends to other stimuli that may have similar consequences. Starting from Shepard's generalization theory, the authors derive a multilayer network whose units represent spherical regions with adjustable centers and radii. Learning can therefore change both where a region lies and how broadly it extends.

The model uses a Cauchy mass function and extends a configural-cue network in several ways. Combinations of cues can be learned without prewiring every possible combination, and consequential regions are continuous rather than discrete. The authors also show that the global extent of the Cauchy function increases competition among receptive fields.

They compare the approach with Gaussian mass functions and standard backpropagation networks using hyperplane or logistic hidden units. The abstract reports that those alternatives fare less well as models of human generalization and learning. The contribution connects a psychological theory to adjustable geometric representations, with the choice of mass function affecting how regions compete and how learning generalizes.
summary.tldr: Learnable spherical regions with a Cauchy mass function model human generalization while supporting learned cue combinations and stronger receptive-field competition.

title: Spherical Units as Dynamic Consequential Regions: Implications for Attention, Competition and Categorization

abstract: A recognition system is reported which recognizes names spelled over the telephone with brief pauses between letters. The system uses separate neural networks to locate segment boundaries and classify letters. The letter scores are then used to search a database of names to find the best scoring name. The speaker-independent classification rate for spoken let(cid:173) ters is 89%. The system retrieves the correct name, spelled with pauses between letters, 91 % of the time from a database of 50,000 names.

paragraphs: This paper describes a system that recognizes names spelled aloud over the telephone. Speakers leave brief pauses between letters, giving the recognizer a sequence of spoken letter names to process. The task combines identifying individual letters with deciding which complete name best matches the available speech evidence.

Separate neural networks locate segment boundaries and classify the letters within those segments. The resulting letter scores are then used to search a database of names. This preserves the role of letter-level evidence while using the name collection to make the final decision. Recognition therefore spans both the acoustic pieces and the complete item being requested.

The system achieves an 89% speaker-independent classification rate for spoken letters. It retrieves the correct name 91% of the time from a database containing 50,000 names when names are spelled with pauses. These are distinct measures: one assesses individual letters, while the other assesses the final database result. Together, they demonstrate the reported performance of the component recognizer and the complete name-retrieval system.
summary.tldr: Neural letter recognition and database scoring retrieve telephone-spelled names with 91% accuracy from a collection of 50,000 names.

title: English Alphabet Recognition with Telephone Speech

abstract: Biological retinas extract spatial and temporal features in an attempt to reduce the complexity of performing visual tasks. We have built and tested a silicon retina which encodes several useful temporal features found in ver(cid:173) tebrate retinas. The cells in our silicon retina are selective to direction, highly sensitive to positive contrast changes around an ambient light level, and tuned to a particular velocity. Inhibitory connections in the null di(cid:173) rection perform the direction selectivity we desire. This silicon retina is on a 4.6 x 6.8mm die and consists of a 47 x 41 array of photoreceptors.

paragraphs: This paper describes a built and tested silicon retina that extracts temporal features of visual input. Its motivation comes from biological retinas, which process spatial and temporal structure before later visual processing. The device implements cells whose responses carry information about motion direction, changes in brightness, and movement speed.

Direction selectivity is created through inhibitory connections in the null direction, meaning the direction whose response should be suppressed. Inhibiting that response allows the circuit to distinguish directions of movement. The cells are also highly sensitive to increases in contrast around the ambient light level and are tuned to a particular velocity.

The hardware contains a 47 by 41 photoreceptor array on a 4.6 by 6.8 millimeter die. The reported achievement is a physical sensor that combines several useful retinal response properties. Directional inhibition is central to that design, showing how interactions between sensor cells can make their outputs selective for temporal features of a visual scene.
summary.tldr: A tested silicon retina uses directional inhibition to detect motion direction while responding selectively to contrast increases and velocity.

title: Direction Selective Silicon Retina that uses Null Inhibition

abstract: The performance requirements in experimental research on arti(cid:173) ficial neural nets often exceed the capability of workstations and PCs by a great amount. But speed is not the only requirement. Flexibility and implementation time for new algorithms are usually of equal importance. This paper describes the simulation of neural nets on the MUSIC parallel supercomputer, a system that shows a good balance between the three issues and therefore made many research projects possible that were unthinkable before. (MUSIC stands for Multiprocessor System with Intelligent Communication) 1 Overview of the MUSIC System The goal of the MUSIC project was to build a fast parallel system and to use it in real-world applications like neural net simulations, image processing or simulations in chemistry and physics [1, 2]. The system should be flexible, simple to program and the realization time should be short enough to not have an obsolete system by the time it is finished. Therefore, the fastest available standard components were used. The key idea of the architecture is to support the collection and redistribution of complete data blocks by a simple, efficient and autonomously working commu(cid:173) nication network realized in hardware. Instead of considering where to send data and where from to receive data, each processing element determines which part of a (virtual) data block it has produced and which other part of the same data block it wants to receive for the continuation of the algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper describes neural-network simulation on MUSIC, a parallel computer designed to balance speed, flexibility, and implementation time. These priorities reflect the needs of experimental research: a machine must run demanding simulations while also allowing researchers to implement new algorithms without excessive effort. The system uses standard components to support relatively rapid construction.

Its central architectural feature is an autonomous hardware network that collects and redistributes complete blocks of data. Each processor identifies the portion of a virtual data block it has produced and the portion it needs next. This gives communication a data-block description, reducing the need to express the computation through individual sending and receiving relationships.

The authors report that this balance enabled research projects that had previously been impractical. The contribution lies in treating communication support and ease of programming as integral parts of performance. For neural-network simulation, the architecture connects parallel numerical work to a hardware mechanism that moves the data required for subsequent stages of an algorithm.
summary.tldr: MUSIC supports flexible parallel neural-network simulation through hardware that autonomously collects and redistributes data blocks.

title: High Performance Neural Net Simulation on a Multiprocessor System with "Intelligent" Communication

abstract: This paper describes the use of a convolutional neural network to perform address block location on machine-printed mail pieces. Locating the address block is a difficult object recognition problem because there is often a large amount of extraneous printing on a mail piece and because address blocks vary dramatically in size and shape. We used a convolutional locator network with four outputs, each trained to find a different corner of the address block. A simple set of rules was used to generate ABL candidates from the network output. The system performs very well: when allowed five guesses, the network will tightly bound the address delivery information in 98.2% of the cases.

paragraphs: This paper uses a convolutional neural network to locate the delivery-address block on machine-printed mail. The challenge is identifying the correct region amid unrelated printing, while handling address blocks that differ greatly in size and shape. The task concerns where the delivery information is located on the mail piece.

The locator network has four outputs, each trained to find a different corner of the address block. A simple rule set then converts the network output into candidate address locations. This divides the task into learned corner localization and rule-based construction of possible bounding regions, giving the final system several candidate answers to consider.

When allowed five guesses, the system tightly bounds the delivery-address information in 98.2% of cases. The five-guess condition is essential to interpreting this result: it measures success among a set of proposed regions. The finding shows that corner-based convolutional localization can generate highly successful address candidates despite distracting print and substantial variation in the target region’s geometry.
summary.tldr: A convolutional network locates address-block corners and tightly bounds delivery information in 98.2% of cases when given five guesses.

title: Postal Address Block Location Using a Convolutional Locator Network

abstract: The goal of this work was to investigate the role of primate MT neurons in solving the structure from motion (SFM) problem. Three types of receptive field (RF) surrounds found in area MT neurons (K.Tanaka et al.,1986; Allman et al.,1985) correspond, as our analysis suggests, to the oth, pt and 2nd order fuzzy space-differential operators. The large surround/center both differentiation of smooth velocity fields and discontinuity detection at boundaries of objects. The model is in agreement with recent psychophysical data on surface interpolation involvement in SFM. We suggest that area MT partially segregates information about object shape from information about spatial relations necessary for navigation and manipulation.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how neurons in primate visual area MT could contribute to recovering object structure from motion. The relevant input is a velocity field: the pattern of image motion across space. The authors focus on receptive-field surrounds, the regions surrounding a neuron's central receptive field, as components of this computation.

Their analysis associates three observed surround types with approximate spatial operators of zeroth, first, and second order. This gives the surround organization a computational interpretation tied to spatial variation in motion. The proposed mechanism supports both differentiation of smoothly varying velocity fields and detection of discontinuities at object boundaries.

The model agrees with psychophysical evidence linking surface interpolation to structure from motion. That connection suggests a role for integrating motion information into an account of surfaces, alongside detecting their boundaries. The authors further propose that MT partly separates information about object shape from information about spatial relationships needed for navigation and manipulation. This is a functional interpretation of the modeled circuitry, connecting receptive-field organization to different uses of visual motion.
summary.tldr: MT receptive-field surrounds may act as spatial operators that extract surface shape and object boundaries from motion.

title: The Role of MT Neuron Receptive Field Surrounds in Computing Object Shape from Velocity Fields

abstract: Conditioning experiments probe the ways that animals make pre(cid:173) dictions about rewards and punishments and use those predic(cid:173) tions to control their behavior. One standard model of condition(cid:173) ing paradigms which involve many conditioned stimuli suggests that individual predictions should be added together. Various key results show that this model fails in some circumstances, and mo(cid:173) tivate an alternative model, in which there is attentional selection between different available stimuli. The new model is a form of mixture of experts, has a close relationship with some other exist(cid:173) ing psychological suggestions, and is statistically well-founded.

paragraphs: This paper examines how animals combine information from several cues when predicting rewards or punishments. Such predictions are studied through conditioning experiments and help explain how animals control their behavior. A standard account treats the prediction associated with each conditioned stimulus as a contribution to an overall sum.

The authors point to key experimental findings that this additive account cannot explain in some circumstances. They propose an alternative in which attention selects between the available stimuli. The central change concerns how multiple sources of predictive information are combined: their influence depends on selection rather than simply accumulating all individual predictions.

The resulting model takes the form of a mixture of experts and has a statistical foundation. It is also closely related to existing psychological proposals, connecting a formal modeling approach with ideas about attention in conditioning. Its significance lies in offering a principled alternative for the circumstances where additive predictions fail, with attentional selection built into the account of learning and behavior.
summary.tldr: A statistically grounded mixture-of-experts model explains conditioning through attentional selection among cues.

title: Statistical Models of Conditioning

abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of active learning in trigonomet(cid:173) ric polynomial networks and give a necessary and sufficient condition of sample points to provide the optimal generalization capability. By ana(cid:173) lyzing the condition from the functional analytic point of view, we clarify the mechanism of achieving the optimal generalization capability. We also show that a set of training examples satisfying the condition does not only provide the optimal generalization but also reduces the compu(cid:173) tational complexity and memory required for the calculation of learning results. Finally, examples of sample points satisfying the condition are given and computer simulations are performed to demonstrate the effec(cid:173) tiveness of the proposed active learning method.

By ana(cid:173) lyzing the condition from the functional analytic point of view, we clarify the mechanism of achieving the optimal generalization capability. We also show that a set of training examples satisfying the condition does not only provide the optimal generalization but also reduces the compu(cid:173) tational complexity and memory required for the calculation of learning results. Finally, examples of sample points satisfying the condition are given and computer simulations are performed to demonstrate the effec(cid:173) tiveness of the proposed active learning method.

paragraphs: This paper studies active learning for trigonometric polynomial networks, focusing on where training samples should be taken. The objective is to select sample points that provide optimal generalization within this setting. It treats the arrangement of training data as a mathematical design problem, rather than simply accepting the available points.

The authors derive a condition on sample points that is both necessary and sufficient for the stated optimal generalization capability. They use functional analysis to explain why the condition works. Within the problem they study, the condition therefore characterizes the desired sample sets, rather than merely giving one sufficient recipe for finding them.

Training examples satisfying the condition also reduce the computation and memory needed to calculate the learned result. This connects generalization quality with the resources required for learning. The paper supplies examples of qualifying sample points and computer simulations demonstrating the method's effectiveness. The contribution is specific to trigonometric polynomial networks: it combines a precise sampling criterion, an explanation of its mechanism, and evidence for its practical use.
summary.tldr: A necessary and sufficient sampling condition gives optimal generalization for trigonometric polynomial networks while reducing computation and memory.

title: Training Data Selection for Optimal Generalization in Trigonometric Polynomial Networks

paragraphs: The paper examines datasets with more measured dimensions than examples. In this setting, the training examples do not fully span the signal space. The authors identify a resulting bias: variance measured along directions chosen from the training data is too large compared with the average variance of independent test examples projected onto those same directions.

This matters when singular value decomposition is used to summarize the data before fitting another statistical model. The training-derived directions come with estimates of how much variation they explain, and those estimates can be misleading for new examples. Generalizable Singular Value Decomposition, or GenSVD, addresses the problem by re-estimating the singular values obtained from conventional SVD.

The intended effect is to reduce this variance bias and allow a subsequent model to generalize better. The authors demonstrate successful bias correction on data from a functional PET study of human brain activation. The contribution is therefore a correction to the statistical quantities attached to an SVD representation, motivated by their behavior on independent data.
summary.tldr: GenSVD re-estimates singular values to reduce inflated training-variance estimates in datasets with more dimensions than examples.

title: Generalizable Singular Value Decomposition for Ill-posed Datasets

Reinterpreting this mistake bound as a margin dependent sparsity guarantee allows us to give a PAC-style generalisation er(cid:173) ror bound for the classifier learned by the perceptron learning algo(cid:173) rithm. The bound value crucially depends on the margin a support vector machine would achieve on the same data set using the same kernel. Ironically, the bound yields better guarantees than are cur(cid:173) rently available for the support vector solution itself.

paragraphs: This paper connects three properties of a learned classifier: how many mistakes a learning algorithm makes, how sparsely its result can be represented, and how well it may generalize. The starting point is an improvement to Novikoff's perceptron convergence theorem. The authors reinterpret the resulting mistake bound as a guarantee about sparsity that depends on the classification margin.

That reinterpretation supports a PAC-style bound on the generalization error of the classifier produced by the perceptron. A crucial feature is that the bound depends on the margin a support vector machine would obtain using the same dataset and kernel. The support vector solution thus supplies a reference quantity for analyzing the perceptron's classifier.

The authors report that this bound gives stronger guarantees than those then available for the support vector solution itself. This is a comparison of theoretical guarantees, rather than a claim that the perceptron always predicts more accurately. The contribution shows how a margin-based analysis can yield a sparsity-based route to generalization guarantees.
summary.tldr: An improved perceptron mistake bound becomes a margin-dependent sparsity guarantee and then a generalization-error bound.

title: From Margin to Sparsity

abstract: We present an extension to the Mixture of Experts (ME) model, where the individual experts are Gaussian Process (GP) regression models. Us- ing an input-dependent adaptation of the Dirichlet Process, we imple- ment a gating network for an inﬁnite number of Experts. Inference in this model may be done efﬁciently using a Markov Chain relying on Gibbs sampling. The model allows the effective covariance function to vary with the inputs, and may handle large datasets – thus potentially over- coming two of the biggest hurdles with GP models. Simulations show the viability of this approach.

Us- ing an input-dependent adaptation of the Dirichlet Process, we imple- ment a gating network for an inﬁnite number of Experts. paragraphs: The paper extends mixture-of-experts modeling by making each expert a Gaussian process regression model. A gating mechanism determines how experts participate as the input changes. This arrangement lets the overall predictor combine Gaussian process models through an input-dependent structure.

The gating network uses an input-dependent adaptation of the Dirichlet process to accommodate an infinite number of experts. The authors describe inference through a Markov chain based on Gibbs sampling and state that this can be done efficiently. The model therefore combines flexibility in the expert collection with a sampling-based procedure for working with it.

One consequence is that the effective covariance function can vary with the inputs, allowing the overall model’s statistical relationships to differ across input locations. The authors also suggest that the approach may handle large datasets, potentially addressing another major difficulty of Gaussian processes. Simulations demonstrate viability. The findings support the construction as a promising modeling approach, while its large-dataset capability is presented as a possibility rather than an established general guarantee.
summary.tldr: An input-dependent infinite mixture of Gaussian process experts enables varying covariance structure and may improve handling of large datasets.

title: Infinite Mixtures of Gaussian Process Experts

abstract: Attempting to model human categorization and similarity judgements is both a very interesting but also an exceedingly difficult challenge. Some of the difficulty arises because of conflicting evidence whether human categorization and similarity judgements should or should not be modelled as to operate on a mental representation that is essentially metric. Intuitively, this has a strong appeal as it would allow (dis)similarity to be represented geometrically as distance in some internal space. Here we show how a single stimulus, carefully constructed in a psychophysical experiment, introduces l2 violations in what used to be an internal similarity space that could be adequately modelled as Euclidean. We term this one influential data point a conflictual judgement. We present an algorithm of how to analyse such data and how to identify the crucial point. Thus there may not be a strict dichotomy between either a metric or a non-metric internal space but rather degrees to which potentially large subsets of stimuli are represented metrically with a small subset causing a global violation of metricity.

Evidence about whether such a metric representation is appropriate has been conflicting. This paper examines how a set of judgments that fits a Euclidean representation can become incompatible with that representation through the addition of a carefully constructed stimulus.

In a psychophysical experiment, the authors show that one influential judgment can introduce violations of Euclidean, or l2, geometry. They call this a conflictual judgment. Its importance lies in the contrast between its small share of the observations and its effect on whether the full collection admits the geometric description.

The paper also provides an algorithm for analyzing these data and identifying the crucial point. The findings suggest that metric and nonmetric representations need not form a strict either-or distinction. Large subsets of stimuli may still have a suitable metric representation even when a small subset makes the full set violate metricity. This offers a more localized way to interpret conflicting similarity evidence.
summary.tldr: A carefully constructed stimulus can disrupt Euclidean similarity judgments even when a large subset remains compatible with metric representation.

title: Inducing Metric Violations in Human Similarity Judgements

abstract: Neuronal connection weights exhibit short-term depression (STD). The present study investigates the impact of STD on the dynamics of a continuous attractor neural network (CANN) and its potential roles in neural information processing. We find that the network with STD can generate both static and traveling bumps, and STD enhances the performance of the network in tracking external inputs. In particular, we find that STD endows the network with slow-decaying plateau behaviors, namely, the network being initially stimulated to an active state will decay to silence very slowly in the time scale of STD rather than that of neural signaling. We argue that this provides a mechanism for neural systems to hold short-term memory easily and shut off persistent activities naturally.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how temporary weakening of neuronal connections changes the behavior of a continuous attractor neural network. This weakening, called short-term synaptic depression, introduces a changing connection strength into the network's dynamics. The central question is how that change affects sustained activity and the processing of external inputs.

The authors find that the network can support both stationary and traveling concentrations of activity, described as bumps. They also find improved tracking of external inputs when synaptic depression is present. These results connect a short-term change in neuronal coupling with both stable activity patterns and the ability to follow changing stimulation.

A further finding is a slowly fading plateau after the network has been stimulated into an active state. Activity declines toward silence on the timescale of synaptic depression rather than the faster timescale of neural signaling. The authors argue that this behavior offers a possible mechanism for retaining short-term memories while allowing persistent activity to terminate naturally.
summary.tldr: Short-term synaptic depression improves input tracking and produces slowly fading activity that could support temporary memory in an attractor network.

title: Attractor Dynamics with Synaptic Depression

abstract: We propose an online prediction version of submodular set cover with connections to ranking and repeated active learning. In each round, the learning algorithm chooses a sequence of items. The algorithm then receives a monotone submodular function and suffers loss equal to the cover time of the function: the number of items needed, when items are selected in order of the chosen sequence, to achieve a coverage constraint. We develop an online learning algorithm whose loss converges to approximately that of the best sequence in hindsight. Our proposed algorithm is readily extended to a setting where multiple functions are revealed at each round and to bandit and contextual bandit settings.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an online prediction problem in which an algorithm repeatedly chooses an ordering of items. After each choice, a monotone submodular function is revealed. The ordering incurs a loss equal to how far along the sequence the algorithm must go before satisfying the function's coverage requirement.

This formulation makes early coverage the objective: two sequences containing the same items can have different losses because useful items appear in different positions. The authors develop a learning algorithm whose loss converges approximately to that of the best single sequence chosen in hindsight. The comparison therefore asks how well repeated prediction can approach an ordering selected with knowledge of the observed tasks.

The framework connects submodular set cover with ranking and repeated active learning. The proposed algorithm also extends to rounds revealing multiple functions and to bandit and contextual bandit settings. These extensions broaden the kinds of feedback and task information the approach can accommodate. The stated guarantee is an approximate comparison with the hindsight sequence, rather than exact equality with that benchmark.
summary.tldr: An online algorithm learns item orderings whose coverage loss approaches that of the best hindsight ordering up to approximation.

title: Online Submodular Set Cover, Ranking, and Repeated Active Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of identifying a sparse set of relevant columns and rows in a large data matrix with highly corrupted entries. This problem of identifying groups from a collection of bipartite variables such as proteins and drugs, biological species and gene sequences, malware and signatures, etc is commonly referred to as biclustering or co-clustering. Despite its great practical relevance, and although several ad-hoc methods are available for biclustering, theoretical analysis of the problem is largely non-existent. The problem we consider is also closely related to structured multiple hypothesis testing, an area of statistics that has recently witnessed a flurry of activity. We make the following contributions: i) We prove lower bounds on the minimum signal strength needed for successful recovery of a bicluster as a function of the noise variance, size of the matrix and bicluster of interest. ii) We show that a combinatorial procedure based on the scan statistic achieves this optimal limit. iii) We characterize the SNR required by several computationally tractable procedures for biclustering including element-wise thresholding, column/row average thresholding and a convex relaxation approach to sparse singular vector decomposition.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to locate a small, relevant group of rows and columns inside a large matrix whose entries are heavily corrupted. The problem is known as biclustering or co-clustering. It arises when relationships between two kinds of entities contain a meaningful subgroup that noise makes difficult to identify.

The authors establish lower bounds on the signal strength needed to recover such a subgroup successfully. Those bounds depend on noise variance, matrix dimensions, and the size of the target bicluster. They also show that a combinatorial procedure using a scan statistic reaches the optimal limit, connecting an impossibility threshold with a procedure that attains it.

The paper separately characterizes the signal-to-noise requirements of computationally tractable methods: entrywise thresholding, thresholding row or column averages, and a convex relaxation of sparse singular vector decomposition. This distinction matters because statistical optimality and computational convenience are different considerations. The results provide a theoretical basis for comparing what these methods require from the data, beyond whether they work on particular examples.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes optimal signal thresholds for noisy bicluster recovery and analyzes the requirements of tractable alternatives.

title: Minimax Localization of Structural Information in Large Noisy Matrices

abstract: We consider a multi-armed bandit problem where there are two phases. The first phase is an experimentation phase where the decision maker is free to explore multiple options. In the second phase the decision maker has to commit to one of the arms and stick with it. Cost is incurred during both phases with a higher cost during the experimentation phase. We analyze the regret in this setup, and both propose algorithms and provide upper and lower bounds that depend on the ratio of the duration of the experimentation phase to the duration of the commitment phase. Our analysis reveals that if given the choice, it is optimal to experiment $\Theta(\ln T)$ steps and then commit, where $T$ is the time horizon.

In the second phase the decision maker has to commit to one of the arms and stick with it. Cost is incurred during both phases with a higher cost during the experimentation phase. We analyze the regret in this setup, and both propose algorithms and provide upper and lower bounds that depend on the ratio of the duration of the experimentation phase to the duration of the commitment phase. Our analysis reveals that if given the choice, it is optimal to experiment $\Theta(\ln T)$ steps and then commit, where $T$ is the time horizon.

paragraphs: The paper considers decisions with a distinct period for experimentation followed by a period of commitment. During experimentation, the decision maker can try different options. Once commitment begins, one option must be chosen and retained. Both phases incur costs, but experimentation is more expensive, making the duration of exploration part of the decision problem.

The authors analyze regret in this two-phase bandit setting and propose algorithms with upper and lower bounds. These bounds depend on the ratio between the lengths of the experimentation and commitment phases. This dependence captures why the value of gathering more information must be considered together with how long the eventual choice will remain in effect.

When the decision maker can choose the phase lengths, the analysis finds that the optimal experimentation duration scales logarithmically with the total time horizon. Thus, a longer horizon calls for more experimentation, but the optimal number of exploratory steps grows much more slowly than the horizon itself. This conclusion applies to the paper's setup, including its higher experimentation costs and subsequent fixed commitment.
summary.tldr: In a bandit model with costly experimentation followed by fixed commitment, the optimal experimentation duration grows logarithmically with the time horizon.

title: Committing Bandits

abstract: A key function of brains is undoubtedly the abstraction and maintenance of information from the environment for later use. Neurons in association cortex play an important role in this process: during learning these neurons become tuned to relevant features and represent the information that is required later as a persistent elevation of their activity. It is however not well known how these neurons acquire their task-relevant tuning. Here we introduce a biologically plausible learning scheme that explains how neurons become selective for relevant information when animals learn by trial and error. We propose that the action selection stage feeds back attentional signals to earlier processing levels. These feedback signals interact with feedforward signals to form synaptic tags at those connections that are responsible for the stimulus-response mapping. A globally released neuromodulatory signal interacts with these tagged synapses to determine the sign and strength of plasticity. The learning scheme is generic because it can train networks in different tasks, simply by varying inputs and rewards. It explains how neurons in association cortex learn to (1) temporarily store task-relevant information in non-linear stimulus-response mapping tasks and (2) learn to optimally integrate probabilistic evidence for perceptual decision making.

paragraphs: Working memory depends on neurons maintaining information that will be useful later. The paper asks how neurons acquire the task-relevant selectivity needed for that role through trial and error. It proposes a biologically plausible learning scheme linking action selection, attention, and changes in the strengths of neural connections.

In the scheme, the action-selection stage sends attentional feedback to earlier processing stages. Feedback and feedforward signals interact to mark the synapses responsible for the stimulus-response mapping. A globally released neuromodulatory signal then acts on those marked connections, determining both the direction and magnitude of their plasticity.

The mechanism connects a broadly available learning signal to the particular connections involved in behavior. The authors describe it as generic because different tasks can be learned by changing inputs and rewards. It explains how networks can temporarily retain relevant information for nonlinear stimulus-response mappings and learn to integrate probabilistic evidence optimally for perceptual decisions. These are capabilities of the proposed learning scheme and its account of association-cortex function.
summary.tldr: A biologically plausible learning scheme combines attentional synaptic tags with a global modulation signal to learn memory and decision tasks.

title: Neurally Plausible Reinforcement Learning of Working Memory Tasks

abstract: We show how binary classification methods developed to work on i.i.d. data can be used for solving statistical problems that are seemingly unrelated to classification and concern highly-dependent time series. Specifically, the problems of time-series clustering, homogeneity testing and the three-sample problem are addressed. The algorithms that we construct for solving these problems are based on a new metric between time-series distributions, which can be evaluated using binary classification methods. Universal consistency of the proposed algorithms is proven under most general assumptions. The theoretical results are illustrated with experiments on synthetic and real-world data.

The algorithms that we construct for solving these problems are based on a new metric between time-series distributions, which can be evaluated using binary classification methods. Universal consistency of the proposed algorithms is proven under most general assumptions. The theoretical results are illustrated with experiments on synthetic and real-world data.

paragraphs: Methods built for independent binary classification may seem unrelated to comparing highly dependent time series. This paper creates a connection through a new distance between time-series distributions. The distance can be evaluated with binary classification methods, allowing familiar learning tools to support different statistical tasks.

Using that construction, the authors develop algorithms for time-series clustering, homogeneity testing, and the three-sample problem. The classifier acts as a component of distribution comparison rather than simply assigning a conventional class label to each observation. This reduction separates the statistical question from the particular classifier used to help answer it.

Universal consistency is proved under very general assumptions, and synthetic and real-data experiments illustrate the approach. The contribution shows how dependence need not prevent reuse of classification machinery when it is embedded in an appropriate distributional framework. A carefully chosen reduction can transfer algorithms between problem types that initially appear to require entirely different tools.
summary.tldr: A classification-based distance between time-series distributions yields consistent methods for clustering and distribution-comparison tasks.

title: Reducing statistical time-series problems to binary classification

abstract: In many sequential decision-making problems we may want to manage risk by minimizing some measure of variability in rewards in addition to maximizing a standard criterion. Variance related risk measures are among the most common risk-sensitive criteria in finance and operations research. However, optimizing many such criteria is known to be a hard problem. In this paper, we consider both discounted and average reward Markov decision processes. For each formulation, we first define a measure of variability for a policy, which in turn gives us a set of risk-sensitive criteria to optimize. For each of these criteria, we derive a formula for computing its gradient. We then devise actor-critic algorithms for estimating the gradient and updating the policy parameters in the ascent direction. We establish the convergence of our algorithms to locally risk-sensitive optimal policies. Finally, we demonstrate the usefulness of our algorithms in a traffic signal control application.

paragraphs: A decision-making policy can achieve a desirable average reward while still producing highly variable outcomes. This paper studies how to account for that variability when learning policies in Markov decision processes. It considers both discounted rewards and average rewards, rather than restricting the treatment of risk to one formulation.

For each formulation, the authors define a policy variability measure and use it to construct risk-sensitive objectives. They then derive gradients for those objectives. These formulas support actor-critic algorithms that estimate the relevant gradient and adjust policy parameters in a direction that improves the chosen criterion. This gives the risk objective a direct role in how the policy learns.

The paper establishes convergence to policies that are locally optimal for the risk-sensitive criteria. That qualification matters: the result does not promise the best policy among all possible policies. A traffic signal control application demonstrates the algorithms’ usefulness. Together, the theory and application show a route to learning policies that consider reward variability alongside conventional performance.
summary.tldr: Actor-critic algorithms optimize reward-variability criteria in discounted and average-reward settings, with convergence guarantees to locally risk-sensitive optimal policies.

title: Actor-Critic Algorithms for Risk-Sensitive MDPs

abstract: We develop a biologically-plausible learning rule that provably converges to the class means of general mixture models. This rule generalizes the classical BCM neural rule within a tensor framework, substantially increasing the generality of the learning problem it solves. It achieves this by incorporating triplets of samples from the mixtures, which provides a novel information processing interpretation to spike-timing-dependent plasticity. We provide both proofs of convergence, and a close fit to experimental data on STDP.
originalAbstract: We develop a biologically-plausible learning rule that provably converges to the class means of general mixture models. It achieves this by incorporating triplets of samples from the mixtures, which provides a novel information processing interpretation to spike-timing-dependent plasticity. We provide both proofs of convergence, and a close fit to experimental data on STDP.

paragraphs: The paper develops a biologically plausible learning rule for recovering the class means of general mixture models. A mixture describes observations drawn from multiple underlying classes, each with its own mean. The stated mathematical goal is convergence to those means, giving the neural learning rule a precise statistical target.

The authors extend the classical BCM neural rule through a tensor framework. Their construction incorporates triplets of samples from the mixture, substantially broadening the learning problems addressed by the original rule. The use of triplets also provides an information-processing interpretation of spike-timing-dependent plasticity, connecting a neural plasticity phenomenon to the statistical task the rule performs.

The paper supplies both convergence proofs and a close fit to experimental data on spike-timing-dependent plasticity. These findings support different aspects of the proposal: the proofs establish the rule's convergence claim, while the data fit connects it to observed plasticity behavior. Together, they link a formal mixture-learning objective with a biologically motivated mechanism for changing neural responses.
summary.tldr: A tensor-based extension of the BCM neural rule provably learns mixture class means and closely fits spike-timing-dependent plasticity data.

title: Feedforward Learning of Mixture Models

abstract: Training of the neural autoregressive density estimator (NADE) can be viewed as doing one step of probabilistic inference on missing values in data. We propose a new model that extends this inference scheme to multiple steps, arguing that it is easier to learn to improve a reconstruction in $k$ steps rather than to learn to reconstruct in a single inference step. The proposed model is an unsupervised building block for deep learning that combines the desirable properties of NADE and multi-predictive training: (1) Its test likelihood can be computed analytically, (2) it is easy to generate independent samples from it, and (3) it uses an inference engine that is a superset of variational inference for Boltzmann machines. The proposed NADE-k is competitive with the state-of-the-art in density estimation on the two datasets tested.

paragraphs: The paper starts from an interpretation of neural autoregressive density estimation as inference about missing data values. Standard NADE training can be viewed as performing this inference in a single step. The proposed NADE-k extends the process to multiple steps, allowing a reconstruction to be improved repeatedly instead of requiring one step to produce the entire result.

The motivation is that learning a sequence of improvements may be easier than learning a complete reconstruction at once. The model combines this iterative approach with properties of NADE and multi-predictive training. Its test likelihood can still be calculated analytically, independent samples can be generated easily, and its inference engine includes variational inference for Boltzmann machines as a special case.

These properties make NADE-k an unsupervised building block that supports both density evaluation and sample generation while using a richer inference procedure. On the two datasets evaluated, its density-estimation performance is competitive with the state of the art. The reported findings support multi-step reconstruction as a viable design choice while keeping the empirical claim specific to those two evaluations.
summary.tldr: NADE-k refines missing-value reconstructions over multiple inference steps while retaining analytic likelihood evaluation and easy independent sampling.

title: Iterative Neural Autoregressive Distribution Estimator NADE-k

abstract: We study the early locust olfactory system in an attempt to explain its well-characterized structure and dynamics. We first propose its computational function as recovery of high-dimensional sparse olfactory signals from a small number of measurements. Detailed experimental knowledge about this system rules out standard algorithmic solutions to this problem. Instead, we show that solving a dual formulation of the corresponding optimisation problem yields structure and dynamics in good agreement with biological data. Further biological constraints lead us to a reduced form of this dual formulation in which the system uses independent component analysis to continuously adapt to its olfactory environment to allow accurate sparse recovery. Our work demonstrates the challenges and rewards of attempting detailed understanding of experimentally well-characterized systems.

Instead, we show that solving a dual formulation of the corresponding optimisation problem yields structure and dynamics in good agreement with biological data. Further biological constraints lead us to a reduced form of this dual formulation in which the system uses independent component analysis to continuously adapt to its olfactory environment to allow accurate sparse recovery. Our work demonstrates the challenges and rewards of attempting detailed understanding of experimentally well-characterized systems.

paragraphs: The paper asks what computation the early locust smell system might perform, and how that computation could explain its observed organization and activity. Its starting proposal is sparse recovery: reconstructing a large olfactory signal from relatively few measurements when only a small part of that signal is active.

The biological evidence matters because it constrains which mathematical solutions are plausible. The authors find that standard algorithms for the proposed recovery problem do not fit the experimentally established system. They instead solve a dual formulation, an alternative mathematical expression of the optimization problem. The resulting structure and dynamics agree well with biological observations.

Additional biological constraints lead to a reduced version of this formulation. In that model, independent component analysis continually adapts the system to its olfactory environment, supporting accurate sparse recovery. The contribution is a computational explanation shaped by detailed biological evidence: it connects a proposed sensory task, an optimization procedure, and observed neural behavior without establishing that the brain literally implements every element of the model.
summary.tldr: A dual sparse-recovery formulation offers an explanation of locust olfactory structure and dynamics that agrees with biological observations.

title: A Dual Algorithm for Olfactory Computation in the Locust Brain

abstract: The accuracy of information retrieval systems is often measured using average precision (AP). Given a set of positive (relevant) and negative (non-relevant) samples, the parameters of a retrieval system can be estimated using the AP-SVM framework, which minimizes a regularized convex upper bound on the empirical AP loss. However, the high computational complexity of loss-augmented inference, which is required for learning an AP-SVM, prohibits its use with large training datasets. To alleviate this deficiency, we propose three complementary approaches. The first approach guarantees an asymptotic decrease in the computational complexity of loss-augmented inference by exploiting the problem structure. The second approach takes advantage of the fact that we do not require a full ranking during loss-augmented inference. This helps us to avoid the expensive step of sorting the negative samples according to their individual scores. The third approach approximates the AP loss over all samples by the AP loss over difficult samples (for example, those that are incorrectly classified by a binary SVM), while ensuring the correct classification of the remaining samples. Using the PASCAL VOC action classification and object detection datasets, we show that our approaches provide significant speed-ups during training without degrading the test accuracy of AP-SVM.

paragraphs: Average precision measures how well a retrieval system ranks relevant items among irrelevant ones. AP-SVM trains a retrieval model by minimizing a regularized convex upper bound on empirical average-precision loss. Its computational obstacle is loss-augmented inference, a learning operation that becomes expensive on large training sets.

The paper proposes three complementary ways to reduce that expense. The first exploits the problem's structure to guarantee lower asymptotic inference complexity. The second uses the fact that inference does not need a complete ranking, avoiding the costly sorting of negative examples by score. The third approximates the loss using difficult examples while enforcing correct classification of the remaining examples.

These approaches address different sources of training work: the inference procedure itself, unnecessary ordering, and the number of examples used in the loss approximation. On PASCAL VOC action classification and object detection datasets, they produce significant training speedups without reducing AP-SVM test accuracy. The findings show that substantial computation can be removed from this training framework while preserving its observed predictive performance on the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Three complementary optimization techniques accelerate AP-SVM training without degrading test accuracy in the reported evaluations.

title: Efficient Optimization for Average Precision SVM

abstract: Causal structure learning from time series data is a major scientific challenge. Existing algorithms assume that measurements occur sufficiently quickly; more precisely, they assume that the system and measurement timescales are approximately equal. In many scientific domains, however, measurements occur at a significantly slower rate than the underlying system changes. Moreover, the size of the mismatch between timescales is often unknown. This paper provides three distinct causal structure learning algorithms, all of which discover all dynamic graphs that could explain the observed measurement data as arising from undersampling at some rate. That is, these algorithms all learn causal structure without assuming any particular relation between the measurement and system timescales; they are thus rate-agnostic. We apply these algorithms to data from simulations. The results provide insight into the challenge of undersampling.

Existing algorithms assume that measurements occur sufficiently quickly; more precisely, they assume that the system and measurement timescales are approximately equal. In many scientific domains, however, measurements occur at a significantly slower rate than the underlying system changes. Moreover, the size of the mismatch between timescales is often unknown. This paper provides three distinct causal structure learning algorithms, all of which discover all dynamic graphs that could explain the observed measurement data as arising from undersampling at some rate. That is, these algorithms all learn causal structure without assuming any particular relation between the measurement and system timescales; they are thus rate-agnostic. We apply these algorithms to data from simulations. The results provide insight into the challenge of undersampling.

paragraphs: Time-series measurements may arrive much more slowly than the system being measured changes. This complicates causal structure learning because relationships visible at the measurement timescale need not directly describe the underlying dynamics. The problem becomes harder when the size of the mismatch between the two timescales is unknown.

The paper introduces three algorithms that account for this unknown undersampling rate. Each discovers all dynamic graphs that could explain the observed measurement data through undersampling at some rate. Their goal is therefore to identify the compatible underlying structures without fixing a particular relationship between measurement frequency and system frequency.

This all-compatible-graphs perspective matters because the output can preserve ambiguity about the underlying system instead of selecting a timescale in advance. The authors apply the algorithms to simulated data and use the results to examine the difficulties caused by undersampling. The contribution is a rate-agnostic formulation and three learning procedures for it, rather than a claim that slowly sampled observations always determine one unique causal graph.
summary.tldr: Three causal-learning algorithms recover all dynamic graphs compatible with observations under an unknown undersampling rate.

title: Rate-Agnostic (Causal) Structure Learning

abstract: We capitalize on large amounts of unlabeled video in order to learn a model of scene dynamics for both video recognition tasks (e.g. action classification) and video generation tasks (e.g. future prediction). We propose a generative adversarial network for video with a spatio-temporal convolutional architecture that untangles the scene's foreground from the background. Experiments suggest this model can generate tiny videos up to a second at full frame rate better than simple baselines, and we show its utility at predicting plausible futures of static images. Moreover, experiments and visualizations show the model internally learns useful features for recognizing actions with minimal supervision, suggesting scene dynamics are a promising signal for representation learning. We believe generative video models can impact many applications in video understanding and simulation.

paragraphs: This paper uses unlabeled video to learn how scenes change over time. The goal covers both generating moving scenes and learning representations useful for recognizing actions. That connection makes temporal change a potential training signal even when videos lack detailed human-provided labels.

The proposed video generative adversarial network uses convolutions across space and time and separates the scene's foreground from its background. This organization provides a way to model scene dynamics within a video generator. The authors also use the model to predict plausible future motion from a static image.

Experiments suggest that the model produces tiny videos lasting up to one second at full frame rate better than simple baselines. Experiments and visualizations further show useful internal features for action recognition with minimal supervision. These findings support the possibility that learning to generate scene dynamics can also help representation learning. The stated generation result concerns short, tiny videos, while broader applications in video understanding and simulation are presented as potential impacts.
summary.tldr: A foreground-background video GAN learns from unlabeled videos, generates short plausible clips, and develops features useful for minimally supervised action recognition.

title: Generating Videos with Scene Dynamics

abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have become the state-of-the-art choice for extracting patterns from temporal sequences. Current RNN models are ill suited to process irregularly sampled data triggered by events generated in continuous time by sensors or other neurons. Such data can occur, for example, when the input comes from novel event-driven artificial sensors which generate sparse, asynchronous streams of events or from multiple conventional sensors with different update intervals. In this work, we introduce the Phased LSTM model, which extends the LSTM unit by adding a new time gate. This gate is controlled by a parametrized oscillation with a frequency range which require updates of the memory cell only during a small percentage of the cycle. Even with the sparse updates imposed by the oscillation, the Phased LSTM network achieves faster convergence than regular LSTMs on tasks which require learning of long sequences. The model naturally integrates inputs from sensors of arbitrary sampling rates, thereby opening new areas of investigation for processing asynchronous sensory events that carry timing information. It also greatly improves the performance of LSTMs in standard RNN applications, and does so with an order-of-magnitude fewer computes.

paragraphs: Sensor observations do not always arrive at regular intervals. Event-driven sensors can emit sparse, asynchronous signals, and different sensors may update at different rates. Phased LSTM adapts recurrent sequence modeling to this setting by making the timing of memory updates an explicit part of the network architecture.

The model extends an LSTM unit with a time gate controlled by a parameterized oscillation. Its memory cell updates during only a small portion of each cycle. This creates sparse updates while allowing the network to integrate inputs with arbitrary sampling rates and process asynchronous events whose timing carries useful information.

Despite updating memory less often, the paper reports faster convergence than regular LSTMs on tasks requiring learning over long sequences. It also reports improved performance in standard recurrent-network applications with an order of magnitude fewer computations. These findings suggest that selective updates can help both computational efficiency and sequence learning, while the time gate supplies a natural mechanism for handling irregularly timed observations.
summary.tldr: Phased LSTM adds an oscillating time gate that enables sparse memory updates, faster reported convergence, and natural handling of asynchronous inputs.

title: Phased LSTM: Accelerating Recurrent Network Training for Long or Event-based Sequences

abstract: Humans process visual scenes selectively and sequentially using attention. Central to models of human visual attention is the saliency map. We propose a hierarchical visual architecture that operates on a saliency map and uses a novel attention mechanism to sequentially focus on salient regions and take additional glimpses within those regions. The architecture is motivated by human visual attention, and is used for multi-label image classification on a novel multiset task, demonstrating that it achieves high precision and recall while localizing objects with its attention. Unlike conventional multi-label image classification models, the model supports multiset prediction due to a reinforcement-learning based training process that allows for arbitrary label permutation and multiple instances per label.

paragraphs: The paper develops an image recognition architecture inspired by how people direct their visual attention. It uses a saliency map, which represents which image regions stand out, to guide a sequence of observations. Its hierarchy lets the model select a salient region and then take additional glimpses within that region, combining region selection with closer inspection.

The prediction task goes beyond listing the categories present in an image. The model predicts a multiset: a collection that can contain repeated labels. For example, two instances of the same category can contribute two occurrences of that category’s label. This makes repeated objects part of the prediction target.

A reinforcement learning training process allows arbitrary label order and multiple occurrences of each label. That flexibility matters because a collection of objects does not inherently require one fixed ordering, even when the model examines the image sequentially.

On the proposed multiset task, the authors report high precision and recall, alongside object localization through attention. These findings indicate that the architecture can identify the requested labels while directing attention toward object locations, connecting recognition with selective visual inspection.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical attention model examines salient image regions sequentially and uses reinforcement learning to predict unordered labels that can include repeated object categories.

title: Saliency-based Sequential Image Attention with Multiset Prediction

abstract: We study online learning with the general notion of transductive regret, that is regret with modification rules applying to expert sequences (as opposed to single experts) that are representable by weighted finite-state transducers. We show how transductive regret generalizes existing notions of regret, including: (1) external regret; (2) internal regret; (3) swap regret; and (4) conditional swap regret. We present a general and efficient online learning algorithm for minimizing transductive regret. We further extend that to design efficient algorithms for the time-selection and sleeping expert settings. A by-product of our study is an algorithm for swap regret, which, under mild assumptions, is more efficient than existing ones, and a substantially more efficient algorithm for time selection swap regret.

paragraphs: Online learning evaluates decisions as information arrives over time. This paper broadens the notion of regret by allowing comparison rules to modify sequences of expert choices rather than only individual experts. The resulting measure, transductive regret, considers modifications that can be represented by weighted finite-state transducers.

This sequence-based formulation includes external, internal, swap, and conditional swap regret within one framework. Its value is that several established comparison criteria become instances of a more general problem. The authors give an efficient online learning algorithm for minimizing this broader regret, so the unification comes with an algorithmic method as well as a definition.

They extend the approach to time-selection and sleeping-expert settings, addressing additional structure in when comparisons or experts are relevant. The framework also produces a swap-regret algorithm that is more efficient than existing alternatives under mild assumptions, plus a substantially more efficient algorithm for time-selection swap regret. These results show how the general formulation can improve algorithms for familiar special cases.
summary.tldr: Transductive regret unifies several online-learning regret notions through sequence transformations and yields efficient algorithms for general and specialized settings.

title: Online Learning with Transductive Regret

abstract: Sparse pseudo-point approximations for Gaussian process (GP) models provide a suite of methods that support deployment of GPs in the large data regime and enable analytic intractabilities to be sidestepped. However, the field lacks a principled method to handle streaming data in which both the posterior distribution over function values and the hyperparameter estimates are updated in an online fashion. The small number of existing approaches either use suboptimal hand-crafted heuristics for hyperparameter learning, or suffer from catastrophic forgetting or slow updating when new data arrive. This paper develops a new principled framework for deploying Gaussian process probabilistic models in the streaming setting, providing methods for learning hyperparameters and optimising pseudo-input locations. The proposed framework is assessed using synthetic and real-world datasets.

The proposed framework is assessed using synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Sparse Gaussian process approximations use a limited collection of pseudo-points to make probabilistic modeling practical for larger datasets. Streaming data adds another requirement: as observations arrive, the model must update both its beliefs about function values and the hyperparameters governing its behavior.

The paper identifies shortcomings in existing streaming approaches, including hand-designed hyperparameter updates, catastrophic forgetting, and slow incorporation of new data. It develops a principled framework for streaming Gaussian process models that includes hyperparameter learning and optimization of pseudo-input locations. The approximation's support locations can therefore be adjusted alongside the model settings as learning proceeds.

This addresses more than updating predictions with an otherwise fixed model. The framework brings the posterior, hyperparameters, and pseudo-input choices into the streaming learning problem, connecting uncertainty updates with adaptation of the sparse representation. The authors assess the framework on synthetic and real-world datasets. The abstract establishes the scope of that evaluation but does not state a particular performance margin or a universal elimination of the earlier methods' difficulties.
summary.tldr: A streaming sparse Gaussian process framework supports online posterior updates, hyperparameter learning, and pseudo-input optimization.

title: Streaming Sparse Gaussian Process Approximations

abstract: Recent work used importance sampling ideas for better variational bounds on likelihoods. We clarify the applicability of these ideas to pure probabilistic inference, by showing the resulting Importance Weighted Variational Inference (IWVI) technique is an instance of augmented variational inference, thus identifying the looseness in previous work. Experiments confirm IWVI's practicality for probabilistic inference. As a second contribution, we investigate inference with elliptical distributions, which improves accuracy in low dimensions, and convergence in high dimensions.
originalAbstract: Recent work used importance sampling ideas for better variational bounds on likelihoods. We clarify the applicability of these ideas to pure probabilistic inference, by showing the resulting Importance Weighted Variational Inference (IWVI) technique is an instance of augmented variational inference, thus identifying the looseness in previous work. Experiments confirm IWVI's practicality for probabilistic inference. As a second contribution, we investigate inference with elliptical distributions, which improves accuracy in low dimensions, and convergence in high dimensions.

paragraphs: Importance sampling had been used to improve variational bounds on likelihoods, but that leaves a separate question: how should these ideas be understood when the goal is probabilistic inference itself? This paper clarifies that connection through Importance Weighted Variational Inference, or IWVI, linking the weighting technique to a broader variational formulation.

The central theoretical observation is that IWVI is an instance of augmented variational inference. Viewing it this way identifies looseness in earlier work and makes the relationship between the inference procedure and its variational interpretation more explicit. Experiments then support IWVI as a practical method for probabilistic inference, complementing the conceptual analysis with evidence of usability.

A second contribution examines inference using elliptical distributions. The authors report improved accuracy in low-dimensional settings and improved convergence in high-dimensional settings. These are distinct benefits associated with different dimensional regimes. Together, the contributions address both the formulation of importance-weighted inference and the choice of distributions used for inference, showing that each can affect the resulting procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper interprets IWVI as augmented variational inference and reports dimension-dependent benefits from using elliptical distributions.

title: Importance Weighting and Variational Inference

abstract: Motivated by Fisher divergence, in this paper we present a new set of information quantities which we refer to as gradient information. These measures serve as surrogates for classical information measures such as those based on logarithmic loss, Kullback-Leibler divergence, directed Shannon information, etc. in many data-processing scenarios of interest, and often provide significant computational advantage, improved stability and robustness. As an example, we apply these measures to the Chow-Liu tree algorithm, and demonstrate remarkable performance and significant computational reduction using both synthetic and real data.

As an example, we apply these measures to the Chow-Liu tree algorithm, and demonstrate remarkable performance and significant computational reduction using both synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a family of quantities called gradient information, motivated by Fisher divergence. These quantities serve as alternatives to familiar information measures in data-processing problems. The measures they can stand in for include ones based on logarithmic loss, Kullback-Leibler divergence, and directed Shannon information.

The motivation is practical as well as mathematical. A useful information measure must support the computations needed by a modeling procedure, and the authors report that gradient information often offers substantial computational advantages together with improved stability and robustness. The claim concerns many relevant data-processing settings; it does not assert that the new quantities are identical to classical measures in every use.

As a concrete application, the authors incorporate these quantities into the Chow-Liu tree algorithm. Experiments on synthetic and real data show strong performance and a substantial reduction in computation. This example illustrates the paper's central proposal: changing the information quantity used within an established modeling procedure can improve its computational behavior while still supporting effective representation and modeling.
summary.tldr: Gradient information provides computationally attractive surrogates for classical information measures, demonstrated through the Chow-Liu tree algorithm.

title: Gradient Information for Representation and Modeling

abstract: Although optimization is the longstanding, algorithmic backbone of machine learning new models still require the time-consuming implementation of new solvers. As a result, there are thousands of implementations of optimization algorithms for machine learning problems. A natural question is, if it is always necessary to implement a new solver, or is there one algorithm that is sufficient for most models. Common belief suggests that such a one-algorithm-fits-all approach cannot work, because this algorithm cannot exploit model specific structure. At least, a generic algorithm cannot be efficient and robust on a wide variety of problems. Here, we challenge this common belief. We have designed and implemented the optimization framework GENO (GENeric Optimization) that combines a modeling language with a generic solver. GENO takes the declaration of an optimization problem and generates a solver for the specified problem class. The framework is flexible enough to encompass most of the classical machine learning problems. We show on a wide variety of classical but also some recently suggested problems that the automatically generated solvers are (1) as efficient as well engineered, specialized solvers, (2) more efficient by a decent margin than recent state-of-the-art solvers, and (3) orders of magnitude more efficient than classical modeling language plus solver approaches.

paragraphs: Developing a machine learning model often also requires implementing an optimization solver. Repeating that engineering work across models has produced many specialized implementations. GENO investigates whether a broadly applicable optimization framework can reduce this burden while retaining the efficiency usually associated with carefully engineered, problem-specific solvers.

The framework combines a modeling language with a generic solver. Users declare an optimization problem, and GENO generates a solver for the corresponding problem class. The authors describe the framework as flexible enough to cover most classical machine learning problems. This makes the problem declaration the starting point for obtaining an executable solution method.

Across a wide variety of classical problems and some recently proposed ones, the generated solvers match well-engineered specialized solvers, exceed recent state-of-the-art solvers by a substantial margin, and outperform classical modeling-language-plus-solver approaches by orders of magnitude in the reported comparisons. These findings challenge the belief that generic optimization must sacrifice practical efficiency across diverse machine learning problems.
summary.tldr: GENO generates solvers from optimization declarations and reports efficiency competitive with or better than specialized approaches across varied machine learning problems.

title: GENO -- GENeric Optimization for Classical Machine Learning

abstract: The alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) has recently received tremendous interests for distributed large scale optimization in machine learning, statistics, multi-agent networks and related applications. In this paper, we propose a new parallel multi-block stochastic ADMM for distributed stochastic optimization, where each node is only required to perform simple stochastic gradient descent updates. The proposed ADMM is fully parallel, can solve problems with arbitrary block structures, and has a convergence rate comparable to or better than existing state-of-the-art ADMM methods for stochastic optimization. Existing stochastic (or deterministic) ADMMs require each node to exchange its updated primal variables across nodes at each iteration and hence cause significant amount of communication overhead. Existing ADMMs require roughly the same number of inter-node communication rounds as the number of in-node computation rounds. In contrast, the number of communication rounds required by our new ADMM is only the square root of the number of computation rounds.
