paragraphs: Distributed optimization divides a learning problem across multiple computing nodes. The difficulty is not just doing the calculations: nodes also need to exchange information to coordinate their updates. This paper develops a stochastic version of the alternating direction method of multipliers, or ADMM, that reduces how frequently that communication must happen.

The proposed method supports multiple blocks of variables and runs their updates fully in parallel. Each node only needs to perform simple stochastic gradient descent updates. The method also accommodates arbitrary block structures, making its organization flexible rather than tied to one particular partition of the optimization variables.

The central result concerns the relationship between computation and communication. Whereas the existing ADMM methods discussed in the abstract communicate roughly once per computation round, the proposed method requires communication rounds proportional to the square root of the computation rounds. Its convergence rate remains comparable to or better than existing stochastic ADMM methods. Together, these claims show that reducing coordination frequency need not sacrifice the stated optimization guarantees.
summary.tldr: A parallel stochastic ADMM method reduces communication rounds to the square root of computation rounds while retaining competitive convergence guarantees.

title: A Communication Efficient Stochastic Multi-Block Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers

abstract: We introduce a feature scattering-based adversarial training approach for improving model robustness against adversarial attacks. Conventional adversarial training approaches leverage a supervised scheme (either targeted or non-targeted) in generating attacks for training, which typically suffer from issues such as label leaking as noted in recent works. Differently, the proposed approach generates adversarial images for training through feature scattering in the latent space, which is unsupervised in nature and avoids label leaking. More importantly, this new approach generates perturbed images in a collaborative fashion, taking the inter-sample relationships into consideration. We conduct analysis on model robustness and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach through extensively experiments on different datasets compared with state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: Adversarial training aims to improve robustness by training a model on deliberately perturbed examples. Conventional approaches often use supervised objectives to create those perturbations. This paper highlights label leaking as a problem with such attack-generation schemes and proposes a different way to construct adversarial training images.

The method creates perturbations through feature scattering in the model’s latent representation space. Its attack-generation procedure is unsupervised, which the authors state avoids label leaking. It also constructs perturbed images collaboratively, taking relationships between samples into account. The generation process therefore uses information about how examples relate to one another, rather than treating each image solely as an isolated attack target.

The paper analyzes model robustness and reports extensive experiments on different datasets, including comparisons with state-of-the-art approaches. Those experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed training method. The contribution combines two ideas in adversarial example generation: working through latent features without supervision and using inter-sample relationships to guide the perturbations used during training.
summary.tldr: Feature scattering generates adversarial training images without supervision while accounting for relationships between samples, improving robustness in reported experiments.

title: Defense Against Adversarial Attacks Using Feature Scattering-based Adversarial Training

abstract: We build a theoretical framework for designing and understanding practical meta-learning methods that integrates sophisticated formalizations of task-similarity with the extensive literature on online convex optimization and sequential prediction algorithms. Our approach enables the task-similarity to be learned adaptively, provides sharper transfer-risk bounds in the setting of statistical learning-to-learn, and leads to straightforward derivations of average-case regret bounds for efficient algorithms in settings where the task-environment changes dynamically or the tasks share a certain geometric structure. We use our theory to modify several popular meta-learning algorithms and improve their training and meta-test-time performance on standard problems in few-shot and federated learning.

We use our theory to modify several popular meta-learning algorithms and improve their training and meta-test-time performance on standard problems in few-shot and federated learning.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to use experience across tasks to improve learning on other tasks. Its usefulness depends on what those tasks share. This paper develops a theoretical framework that connects formal descriptions of task similarity with online convex optimization and sequential prediction, giving practical meta-learning methods a common basis for analysis and design.

A central feature is that the framework allows task similarity itself to be learned adaptively. The theory provides sharper bounds on transfer risk in statistical learning-to-learn. It also supports derivations of average-case regret bounds for efficient algorithms when the task environment changes over time or when tasks have a shared geometric structure.

The authors use these theoretical results to modify several popular meta-learning algorithms. They report improvements during training and at meta-test time on standard few-shot and federated learning problems. The contribution thus connects guarantees about transferring knowledge across tasks to concrete algorithm changes, including settings where the relationship among tasks cannot simply be treated as fixed.
summary.tldr: An adaptive theory of task similarity guides changes to meta-learning algorithms that improve reported few-shot and federated learning performance.

title: Adaptive Gradient-Based Meta-Learning Methods

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been successful in learning representations from graphs. Many popular GNNs follow the pattern of *aggregate-transform*: they aggregate the neighbors' attributes and then transform the results of aggregation with a learnable function. Analyses of these GNNs explain which pairs of non-identical graphs have different representations. However, we still lack an understanding of how similar these representations will be. We adopt kernel distance and propose *transform-sum-cat* as an alternative to aggregate-transform to reflect the continuous similarity between the node neighborhoods in the neighborhood aggregation. The idea leads to a simple and efficient graph similarity, which we name Weisfeiler-Leman similarity (WLS). In contrast to existing graph kernels, WLS is easy to implement with common deep learning frameworks. In graph classification experiments, transform-sum-cat significantly outperforms other neighborhood aggregation methods from popular GNN models. We also develop a simple and fast GNN model based on transform-sum-cat, which obtains, in comparison with widely used GNN models, (1) a higher accuracy in node classification, (2) a lower absolute error in graph regression, and (3) greater stability in adversarial training of graph generation.

paragraphs: Graph neural network analysis often asks whether two different graphs receive distinguishable representations. This paper asks a more graded question: how similar should their representations be? It focuses on neighborhood aggregation, where many popular networks combine neighboring attributes before applying a learned transformation.

The authors propose transform-sum-cat as an alternative aggregation scheme, using kernel distance to reflect continuous similarities between node neighborhoods. This leads to Weisfeiler-Leman similarity, or WLS, a graph similarity measure described as simple and efficient. The authors also emphasize that WLS is easy to implement using common deep learning frameworks, connecting the similarity construction to practical neural network development.

In graph classification experiments, transform-sum-cat significantly outperforms aggregation methods from popular graph neural networks. A simple, fast network built around it also achieves higher node classification accuracy, lower graph regression error, and more stable adversarial training for graph generation than widely used models in the reported comparisons. The results support designing aggregation around degrees of neighborhood similarity, alongside the ability to distinguish structures.
summary.tldr: A kernel-inspired aggregation scheme captures graded graph similarity and improves several graph learning tasks in the reported experiments.

title: A graph similarity for deep learning

abstract: Much recent work has focused on biologically plausible variants of supervised learning algorithms. However, there is no teacher in the motor cortex that instructs the motor neurons and learning in the brain depends on reward and punishment. We demonstrate a biologically plausible reinforcement learning scheme for deep networks with an arbitrary number of layers. The network chooses an action by selecting a unit in the output layer and uses feedback connections to assign credit to the units in successively lower layers that are responsible for this action. After the choice, the network receives reinforcement and there is no teacher correcting the errors. We show how the new learning scheme – Attention-Gated Brain Propagation (BrainProp) – is mathematically equivalent to error backpropagation, for one output unit at a time. We demonstrate successful learning of deep fully connected, convolutional and locally connected networks on classical and hard image-classification benchmarks; MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and Tiny ImageNet. BrainProp achieves an accuracy that is equivalent to that of standard error-backpropagation, and better than state-of-the-art biologically inspired learning schemes. The trial-and-error nature of learning is associated with limited additional training time so that BrainProp is a factor of 1-3.5 times slower. Our results thereby provide new insights into how deep learning may be implemented in the brain.

Our results thereby provide new insights into how deep learning may be implemented in the brain.

paragraphs: Standard supervised learning receives information about the correct answer, whereas the learning situation considered here supplies reward or punishment after an action. The paper asks how a deep network could assign responsibility for that outcome in a biologically plausible way. Its proposed scheme, BrainProp, supports networks with an arbitrary number of layers.

The network selects an action through one output unit. Feedback connections then identify the units in progressively earlier layers that contributed to that choice. Reinforcement arrives after the action, without a teacher supplying a correction. The authors show that this procedure is mathematically equivalent to error backpropagation for one output unit at a time, connecting reward-based credit assignment to a familiar learning mechanism.

Experiments cover fully connected, convolutional, and locally connected networks on MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and Tiny ImageNet. BrainProp achieves accuracy equivalent to standard backpropagation and exceeds the biologically inspired methods compared, with training taking 1–3.5 times as long. These findings suggest a possible mechanism for deep learning in the brain rather than establishing that the brain uses it.
summary.tldr: BrainProp uses action-specific feedback and reinforcement to reproduce backpropagation for one output at a time, with comparable classification accuracy.

title: Attention-Gated Brain Propagation: How the brain can implement reward-based error backpropagation

abstract: Feedforward networks (FFN) are ubiquitous structures in neural systems and have been studied to understand mechanisms of reliable signal and information transmission. In many FFNs, neurons in one layer have intrinsic properties that are distinct from those in their pre-/postsynaptic layers, but how this affects network-level information processing remains unexplored. Here we show that layer-to-layer heterogeneity arising from lamina-specific cellular properties facilitates signal and information transmission in FFNs. Specifically, we found that signal transformations, made by each layer of neurons on an input-driven spike signal, demodulate signal distortions introduced by preceding layers. This mechanism boosts information transfer carried by a propagating spike signal, and thereby supports reliable spike signal and information transmission in a deep FFN. Our study suggests that distinct cell types in neural circuits, performing different computational functions, facilitate information processing on the whole.

paragraphs: Feedforward networks in neural systems pass signals through successive layers of neurons. The cells in one layer often have intrinsic properties different from those in neighboring layers. This paper investigates what those differences contribute to reliable signal transmission, focusing on how information carried by an input-driven spike signal changes as it moves through the network.

The authors find that variation in cellular properties between layers can support transmission. Each layer transforms the incoming spike signal, and the transformations can demodulate distortions introduced by earlier layers. In this mechanism, the effect of a layer depends on how it processes the altered signal it receives from the preceding layer.

This interaction increases the information conveyed by the propagating spike signal and supports reliable transmission through a deep feedforward network. The result assigns a functional role to differences among layer-specific cell types: their distinct computations can work together to improve processing across the whole network. The authors present this as evidence suggesting that cellular diversity helps neural circuits preserve and transmit information.
summary.tldr: Differences in neuronal properties across layers can counteract preceding signal distortions and improve information transmission through feedforward networks.

title: Lamina-specific neuronal properties promote robust, stable signal propagation in feedforward networks

abstract: The rapid proliferation of decentralized learning systems mandates the need for differentially-private cooperative learning. In this paper, we study this in context of the contextual linear bandit: we consider a collection of agents cooperating to solve a common contextual bandit, while ensuring that their communication remains private. For this problem, we devise FedUCB, a multiagent private algorithm for both centralized and decentralized (peer-to-peer) federated learning. We provide a rigorous technical analysis of its utility in terms of regret, improving several results in cooperative bandit learning, and provide rigorous privacy guarantees as well. Our algorithms provide competitive performance both in terms of pseudoregret bounds and empirical benchmark performance in various multi-agent settings.

Our algorithms provide competitive performance both in terms of pseudoregret bounds and empirical benchmark performance in various multi-agent settings.

paragraphs: The paper studies multiple agents learning to make decisions together while keeping their communications private. Its setting is a contextual linear bandit, where agents face choices informed by context and cooperate on a common learning problem. This combines the challenge of learning good decisions with the requirement that information shared during cooperation receive formal privacy protection.

The authors introduce FedUCB, a private multiagent algorithm that works in both centralized and decentralized federated settings. In the centralized case, cooperation uses a central coordinating structure; in the decentralized case, agents communicate peer to peer. Supporting both arrangements makes the approach applicable to different ways of organizing the same cooperative bandit problem.

The analysis provides rigorous differential privacy guarantees and evaluates decision quality through regret, which measures the cost of learning relative to better decisions. The authors improve several results in cooperative bandit learning and report competitive pseudoregret bounds alongside empirical benchmark performance. These findings support the feasibility of combining private communication with effective cooperative decision-making across the multiagent settings studied.
summary.tldr: FedUCB enables cooperative contextual linear-bandit learning with formal privacy guarantees in centralized and peer-to-peer systems.

title: Differentially-Private Federated Linear Bandits

abstract: We propose the use of hyperedge replacement graph grammars for factor graphs, or actor graph grammars (FGGs) for short. FGGs generate sets of factor graphs and can describe a more general class of models than plate notation, dynamic graphical models, case-factor diagrams, and sum-product networks can. Moreover, inference can be done on FGGs without enumerating all the generated factor graphs. For finite variable domains (but possibly infinite sets of graphs), a generalization of variable elimination to FGGs allows exact and tractable inference in many situations. For finite sets of graphs (but possibly infinite variable domains), a FGG can be converted to a single factor graph amenable to standard inference techniques.

paragraphs: A factor graph represents relationships among variables through factors. This paper introduces factor graph grammars, which use graph-replacement rules to describe whole sets of factor graphs. The representation can express a broader class of models than plate notation, dynamic graphical models, case-factor diagrams, and sum-product networks, according to the authors.

The main computational contribution is that inference can operate on the grammar without listing every graph it generates. When variable domains are finite, the authors extend variable elimination to the grammar setting. This supports exact, tractable inference in many situations, even when the grammar describes infinitely many graphs.

The paper also treats a different case: a finite collection of generated graphs whose variables may have infinite domains. Here, the grammar can be converted into one factor graph, making standard inference techniques applicable. These two results distinguish the size of the graph collection from the size of each variable's domain, and show how different finiteness conditions enable different inference strategies.
summary.tldr: Factor graph grammars represent families of graphical models and enable inference without enumerating every generated graph under the stated conditions.

title: Factor Graph Grammars

abstract: The local Lipschitz constant of a neural network is a useful metric with applications in robustness, generalization, and fairness evaluation. We provide novel analytic results relating the local Lipschitz constant of nonsmooth vector-valued functions to a maximization over the norm of the generalized Jacobian. We present a sufficient condition for which backpropagation always returns an element of the generalized Jacobian, and reframe the problem over this broad class of functions. We show strong inapproximability results for estimating Lipschitz constants of ReLU networks, and then formulate an algorithm to compute these quantities exactly. We leverage this algorithm to evaluate the tightness of competing Lipschitz estimators and the effects of regularized training on the Lipschitz constant.

paragraphs: A local Lipschitz constant measures how strongly a network's output can change relative to changes in its input within a region. This makes it useful when evaluating robustness, generalization, and fairness. The paper investigates how to compute this quantity exactly for ReLU networks, whose functions are not smooth everywhere.

The theoretical foundation connects the local Lipschitz constant of nonsmooth, vector-valued functions to maximizing the norm of a generalized Jacobian. This extends the role of derivatives to settings where an ordinary Jacobian is insufficient. The authors also establish a sufficient condition under which backpropagation always produces an element of that generalized Jacobian; the claim is conditional, rather than a statement about every possible use of backpropagation.

The paper proves strong difficulty results for approximating ReLU-network Lipschitz constants and develops an exact computation algorithm. Exact values then serve as a reference for assessing how tight competing estimators are. The authors also use the algorithm to investigate how regularized training affects the constant, connecting the mathematical analysis to evaluation of trained networks.
summary.tldr: The paper connects local sensitivity to generalized Jacobians and develops an exact algorithm for evaluating ReLU-network Lipschitz constants.

title: Exactly Computing the Local Lipschitz Constant of ReLU Networks

abstract: We address the problem of zero-order optimization of a strongly convex function. The goal is to find the minimizer of the function by a sequential exploration of its function values, under measurement noise. We study the impact of higher order smoothness properties of the function on the optimization error and on the online regret. To solve this problem we consider a randomized approximation of the projected gradient descent algorithm. The gradient is estimated by a randomized procedure involving two function evaluations and a smoothing kernel. We derive upper bounds for this algorithm both in the constrained and unconstrained settings and prove minimax lower bounds for any sequential search method. Our results imply that the zero-order algorithm is nearly optimal in terms of sample complexity and the problem parameters. Based on this algorithm, we also propose an estimator of the minimum value of the function achieving almost sharp oracle behavior. We compare our results with the state-of-the-art, highlighting a number of key improvements.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to minimize a strongly convex function when only noisy measurements of its values are available. The learner must choose evaluation points sequentially without observing derivatives. The authors investigate how higher-order smoothness changes both the final optimization error and the regret accumulated while searching.

Their algorithm approximates projected gradient descent using a randomized gradient estimate. Each estimate combines two function evaluations with a smoothing kernel. This turns value measurements into information suitable for a gradient-style update. The analysis covers both constrained problems, where the search must remain within an allowed set, and unconstrained problems.

The authors prove upper bounds for their algorithm and minimax lower bounds that apply to any sequential search method in the studied setting. Comparing the two establishes near-optimal dependence on sample complexity and problem parameters. They also use the algorithm to estimate the minimum function value, obtaining nearly sharp oracle behavior. The work therefore addresses both locating a good solution and estimating how low the objective can go, while quantifying the value of additional smoothness.
summary.tldr: A two-evaluation randomized gradient method exploits higher-order smoothness to achieve nearly optimal noisy derivative-free optimization guarantees.

title: Exploiting Higher Order Smoothness in Derivative-free Optimization and Continuous Bandits

abstract: Distilling knowledge from an ensemble of teacher models is expected to have a more promising performance than that from a single one. Current methods mainly adopt a vanilla average rule, i.e., to simply take the average of all teacher losses for training the student network. However, this approach treats teachers equally and ignores the diversity among them. When conflicts or competitions exist among teachers, which is common, the inner compromise might hurt the distillation performance. In this paper, we examine the diversity of teacher models in the gradient space and regard the ensemble knowledge distillation as a multi-objective optimization problem so that we can determine a better optimization direction for the training of student network. Besides, we also introduce a tolerance parameter to accommodate disagreement among teachers. In this way, our method can be seen as a dynamic weighting method for each teacher in the ensemble. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our method for both logits-based and feature-based cases.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student network using guidance from teacher models. An ensemble can offer diverse guidance, but simply averaging teacher losses gives every teacher equal influence. When their recommendations conflict, the resulting compromise can hurt the student. This paper examines how that disagreement appears in the directions teachers suggest for updating the student's parameters.

The authors formulate ensemble distillation as a problem with multiple objectives. They compare teachers in gradient space, where each teacher's loss indicates a direction for changing the student, and use this information to determine a better optimization direction. A tolerance parameter lets the procedure accommodate disagreement rather than requiring the teachers to agree completely.

The resulting method acts as a dynamic weighting scheme: teachers' contributions can change according to their optimization relationships. Experiments support its effectiveness both when teachers provide output logits and when they provide internal features. The approach matters because it makes teacher diversity part of the training decision, instead of treating equal averaging as sufficient.
summary.tldr: Adaptive ensemble distillation uses teacher gradients and a disagreement tolerance to choose how teachers guide a student.

title: Agree to Disagree: Adaptive Ensemble Knowledge Distillation in Gradient Space

abstract: Nonlinear dimensionality reduction of high-dimensional data is challenging as the low-dimensional embedding will necessarily contain distortions, and it can be hard to determine which distortions are the most important to avoid. When annotation of data into known relevant classes is available, it can be used to guide the embedding to avoid distortions that worsen class separation. The supervised mapping method introduced in the present paper, called ClassNeRV, proposes an original stress function that takes class annotation into account and evaluates embedding quality both in terms of false neighbors and missed neighbors. ClassNeRV shares the theoretical framework of a family of methods descended from Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (SNE). Our approach has a key advantage over previous ones: in the literature supervised methods often emphasize class separation at the price of distorting the data neighbors' structure; conversely, unsupervised methods provide better preservation of structure at the price of often mixing classes. Experiments show that ClassNeRV can preserve both neighbor structure and class separation, outperforming nine state of the art alternatives.

paragraphs: Compressing high-dimensional data into a low-dimensional map inevitably changes some relationships among points. The useful question is which changes to discourage. When relevant class labels are available, they can help guide that choice, but separating classes too aggressively may damage the neighborhood structure that makes the map informative.

ClassNeRV introduces an objective that uses class annotations while accounting for two kinds of error: false neighbors, which appear close in the map despite being separated in the original data, and missed neighbors, whose original proximity is lost. It belongs to the theoretical family descending from Stochastic Neighbor Embedding and evaluates both neighborhood preservation and class-related distortions.

The authors report experiments in which ClassNeRV preserves neighborhood structure and class separation together, outperforming nine alternatives. This addresses a tension identified in earlier approaches: supervised maps often sacrifice neighborhoods for class separation, while unsupervised maps may preserve structure but mix classes. The result supports using labels to steer unavoidable distortion while still explicitly valuing local relationships.
summary.tldr: ClassNeRV uses class labels and neighborhood errors together to produce low-dimensional maps that preserve both local structure and class separation.

title: Steering Distortions to Preserve Classes and Neighbors in Supervised Dimensionality Reduction

abstract: Normalization operations are widely used to train deep neural networks, and they can improve both convergence and generalization in most tasks. The theories for normalization's effectiveness and new forms of normalization have always been hot topics in research. To better understand normalization, one question can be whether normalization is indispensable for training deep neural network? In this paper, we study what would happen when normalization layers are removed from the network, and show how to train deep neural networks without normalization layers and without performance degradation. Our proposed method can achieve the same or even slightly better performance in a variety of tasks: image classification in ImageNet, object detection and segmentation in MS-COCO, video classification in Kinetics, and machine translation in WMT English-German, etc. Our study may help better understand the role of normalization layers and can be a competitive alternative to normalization layers. Codes are available.

paragraphs: Normalization layers are widely used because they often help deep networks train and generalize. Their success raises a separate question: whether good performance actually requires these layers. This paper investigates that question by studying networks with normalization removed and developing a method for training them without the performance degradation that removal might otherwise cause.

The contribution is a demonstrated alternative training approach for deep networks without normalization layers. Its significance lies in separating the benefits commonly associated with normalization from the claim that normalization itself is indispensable. Showing that another approach can achieve comparable results provides a way to reconsider the role these layers play in successful training.

The reported evaluations cover ImageNet classification, MS-COCO detection and segmentation, Kinetics video classification, and WMT English–German translation. Across a variety of tasks, the proposed method matches or slightly improves performance. These findings establish a competitive alternative in the tested settings and motivate further understanding of normalization; they do not establish that removing normalization will improve every network or task.
summary.tldr: The paper demonstrates training deep networks without normalization layers while matching or slightly improving performance across several tasks.

title: Is normalization indispensable for training deep neural network?

abstract: Humans have an inherent ability to learn novel concepts from only a few samples and generalize these concepts to different situations. Even though today's machine learning models excel with a plethora of training data on standard recognition tasks, a considerable gap exists between machine-level pattern recognition and human-level concept learning. To narrow this gap, the Bongard problems (BPs) were introduced as an inspirational challenge for visual cognition in intelligent systems. Despite new advances in representation learning and learning to learn, BPs remain a daunting challenge for modern AI. Inspired by the original one hundred BPs, we propose a new benchmark Bongard-LOGO for human-level concept learning and reasoning. We develop a program-guided generation technique to produce a large set of human-interpretable visual cognition problems in action-oriented LOGO language. Our benchmark captures three core properties of human cognition: 1) context-dependent perception, in which the same object may have disparate interpretations given different contexts; 2) analogy-making perception, in which some meaningful concepts are traded off for other meaningful concepts; and 3) perception with a few samples but infinite vocabulary. In experiments, we show that the state-of-the-art deep learning methods perform substantially worse than human subjects, implying that they fail to capture core human cognition properties. Finally, we discuss research directions towards a general architecture for visual reasoning to tackle this benchmark.

The authors interpret this gap as evidence that the tested methods do not capture the targeted properties of human cognition. The benchmark makes those shortcomings measurable and motivates research toward a more general architecture for visual reasoning.
summary.tldr: Bongard-LOGO exposes a substantial gap between tested deep learning methods and humans on visual concept learning from few examples.

title: Bongard-LOGO: A New Benchmark for Human-Level Concept Learning and Reasoning

abstract: Causal treatment effect estimation is a key problem that arises in a variety of real-world settings, from personalized medicine to governmental policy making. There has been a flurry of recent work in machine learning on estimating causal effects when one has access to an instrument. However, to achieve identifiability, they in general require one-size-fits-all assumptions such as an additive error model for the outcome. An alternative is partial identification, which provides bounds on the causal effect. Little exists in terms of bounding methods that can deal with the most general case, where the treatment itself can be continuous. Moreover, bounding methods generally do not allow for a continuum of assumptions on the shape of the causal effect that can smoothly trade off stronger background knowledge for more informative bounds. In this work, we provide a method for causal effect bounding in continuous distributions, leveraging recent advances in gradient-based methods for the optimization of computationally intractable objective functions. We demonstrate on a set of synthetic and real-world data that our bounds capture the causal effect when additive methods fail, providing a useful range of answers compatible with observation as opposed to relying on unwarranted structural assumptions.

paragraphs: Estimating a treatment’s causal effect often requires assumptions that go beyond the observed data. Methods using an instrumental variable commonly impose a particular outcome structure, such as an additive error model, to obtain a single identifiable answer. This paper instead pursues partial identification: finding a range of causal effects compatible with the observations and the assumptions being made.

The authors develop a method for bounding causal effects in continuous distributions, addressing settings where treatment itself can vary continuously. Their approach uses advances in gradient-based optimization to handle objectives that are otherwise computationally intractable. The motivation is also to accommodate varying amounts of knowledge about the shape of the causal effect, allowing stronger background assumptions to support more informative bounds.

On synthetic and real-world data, the reported bounds contain the causal effect in cases where additive methods fail. The contribution is therefore a way to obtain useful, qualified answers without forcing every problem into the same structural model. The output is a range of possibilities rather than an unjustifiably precise single estimate.
summary.tldr: The paper develops gradient-based methods for bounding causal effects with continuous treatments, avoiding reliance on a single additive outcome model.

title: A Class of Algorithms for General Instrumental Variable Models

abstract: Deep probabilistic generative models enable modeling the likelihoods of very high dimensional data. An important application of generative modeling should be the ability to detect out-of-distribution (OOD) samples by setting a threshold on the likelihood. However, a recent study shows that probabilistic generative models can, in some cases, assign higher likelihoods on certain types of OOD samples, making the OOD detection rules based on likelihood threshold problematic. To address this issue, several OOD detection methods have been proposed for deep generative models. In this paper, we make the observation that some of these methods fail when applied to generative models based on Variational Auto-encoders (VAE). As an alternative, we propose Likelihood Regret, an efficient OOD score for VAEs. We benchmark our proposed method over existing approaches, and empirical results suggest that our method obtains the best overall OOD detection performances compared with other OOD method applied on VAE.

paragraphs: A generative model assigns likelihoods to data, suggesting a straightforward way to flag unfamiliar inputs: reject examples with low likelihood. However, such models can sometimes assign higher likelihoods to out-of-distribution examples than to data resembling their training distribution. In those cases, a simple likelihood threshold can give misleading results.

This paper focuses on variational autoencoders, or VAEs. The authors observe that some detection methods proposed for deep generative models also fail when applied to VAEs. That observation motivates evaluating the detection score in the context of this particular model family, where existing approaches may not provide the intended separation between familiar and unfamiliar inputs.

The proposed alternative is Likelihood Regret, described as an efficient out-of-distribution score for VAEs. The authors benchmark it against existing approaches, and their empirical results suggest the best overall detection performance among the methods compared on VAEs. The stated contribution is therefore a VAE-focused detection score supported by comparative evidence, with the improvement expressed as an overall empirical finding.
summary.tldr: Likelihood Regret is an efficient VAE out-of-distribution score whose benchmark results suggest better overall detection than the compared alternatives.

title: Likelihood Regret: An Out-of-Distribution Detection Score For Variational Auto-encoder

abstract: This paper proposes a theoretical analysis of recommendation systems in an online setting, where items are sequentially recommended to users over time. In each round, a user, randomly picked from a population of $m$ users, arrives. The decision-maker observes the user and selects an item from a catalogue of $n$ items. Importantly, an item cannot be recommended twice to the same user. The probabilities that a user likes each item are unknown, and the performance of the recommendation algorithm is captured through its regret, considering as a reference an Oracle algorithm aware of these probabilities. We investigate various structural assumptions on these probabilities: we derive for each of them regret lower bounds, and devise algorithms achieving these limits. Interestingly, our analysis reveals the relative weights of the different components of regret: the component due to the constraint of not presenting the same item twice to the same user, that due to learning the chances users like items, and finally that arising when learning the underlying structure.

We investigate various structural assumptions on these probabilities: we derive for each of them regret lower bounds, and devise algorithms achieving these limits. Interestingly, our analysis reveals the relative weights of the different components of regret: the component due to the constraint of not presenting the same item twice to the same user, that due to learning the chances users like items, and finally that arising when learning the underlying structure.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes recommendation as a sequence of decisions made with incomplete knowledge. In each round, a randomly selected user arrives, and the system chooses an item for that user. An item cannot be recommended to the same user twice, so each choice affects which recommendations remain available later.

The system does not know the probabilities that users will like particular items. Its performance is measured through regret relative to an oracle that knows those probabilities. The authors examine several structural assumptions about user preferences, derive lower bounds on regret for each, and construct algorithms that attain those limits.

The analysis also separates the contributions of three difficulties: the prohibition on repeating items, uncertainty about preference probabilities, and uncertainty about the underlying preference structure. This separation clarifies why recommendation errors accumulate in the studied settings. Matching algorithms and lower bounds establish what performance is attainable under each structure, while the decomposition explains how much each source of difficulty contributes to that performance.
summary.tldr: The paper derives attainable regret limits for online recommendations and separates the costs of learning preferences, learning structure, and avoiding repeated items.

title: Regret in Online Recommendation Systems

abstract: We present and analyze an algorithm for optimizing smooth and convex or strongly convex objectives using minibatch stochastic gradient estimates. The algorithm is optimal with respect to its dependence on both the minibatch size and minimum expected loss simultaneously. This improves over the optimal method of Lan, which is insensitive to the minimum expected loss; over the optimistic acceleration of Cotter et al., which has suboptimal dependence on the minibatch size; and over the algorithm of Liu and Belkin, which is limited to least squares problems and is also similarly suboptimal. Applied to interpolation learning, the improvement over Cotter et al.~and Liu and Belkin translates to a linear, rather than square-root, parallelization speedup.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic optimization when each update uses a minibatch of gradient estimates. Its setting is smooth optimization with convex or strongly convex objectives. The central question is how convergence can benefit simultaneously from larger minibatches and a smaller minimum expected loss, rather than obtaining a favorable dependence on only one of these quantities.

The proposed algorithm is analyzed as optimal in its dependence on both quantities at once. The comparison with earlier methods identifies distinct shortcomings: one method does not adapt to the minimum expected loss, another has a weaker dependence on minibatch size, and a third both has that weaker dependence and applies only to least-squares problems.

For interpolation learning, the improved minibatch dependence yields a linear parallelization speedup where the compared methods yield a square-root speedup. This gives the theoretical improvement a concrete computational interpretation: increasing parallel work can translate more effectively into optimization progress in that setting. The claim is about the stated optimization regime and parameter dependence, rather than a guarantee of linear hardware speedups for arbitrary learning problems.
summary.tldr: A stochastic optimization algorithm achieves jointly optimal dependence on minibatch size and minimum expected loss, yielding linear parallelization speedups in interpolation learning.

title: An Even More Optimal Stochastic Optimization Algorithm: Minibatching and Interpolation Learning

abstract: This paper explores the generalization loss of linear regression in variably parameterized families of models, both under-parameterized and over-parameterized. We show that the generalization curve can have an arbitrary number of peaks, and moreover, the locations of those peaks can be explicitly controlled. Our results highlight the fact that both the classical U-shaped generalization curve and the recently observed double descent curve are not intrinsic properties of the model family. Instead, their emergence is due to the interaction between the properties of the data and the inductive biases of learning algorithms.

Instead, their emergence is due to the interaction between the properties of the data and the inductive biases of learning algorithms.

paragraphs: A generalization curve describes how prediction loss changes as a model's parameterization varies. Familiar accounts emphasize either a U-shaped curve or double descent. This paper investigates linear regression across model families that include both under-parameterized and over-parameterized cases, asking how restrictive those familiar shapes actually are.

The authors show that the curve can contain an arbitrary number of peaks. They also show that the locations of those peaks can be explicitly controlled. The result goes beyond exhibiting one additional rise and fall: it establishes that much more varied patterns are possible within the studied linear-regression setting.

This changes how such curves should be interpreted. Neither the classical U shape nor double descent is an intrinsic signature of the model family alone. Their appearance depends on the interaction between the data's properties and the learning algorithm's inductive biases. The finding establishes possible behavior under that interaction; it does not claim that every dataset or training procedure will naturally produce multiple peaks.
summary.tldr: Linear-regression generalization curves can have arbitrarily many controllable peaks, reflecting interactions between data and learning biases.

title: Multiple Descent: Design Your Own Generalization Curve

abstract: Recent empirical studies show that adversarial topic models (ATM) can successfully capture semantic patterns of the document by differentiating a document with another dissimilar sample. However, utilizing that discriminative-generative architecture has two important drawbacks: (1) the architecture does not relate similar documents, which has the same document-word distribution of salient words; (2) it restricts the ability to integrate external information, such as sentiments of the document, which has been shown to benefit the training of neural topic model. To address those issues, we revisit the adversarial topic architecture in the view point of mathematical analysis, propose a novel approach to re-formulate discriminative goal as an optimization problem, and design a novel sampling method which facilitates the integration of external variables. The reformulation encourages the model to incorporate the relations among similar samples and enforces the constraint on the similarity among dissimilar ones; while the sampling method, which is based on the internal input and reconstructed output, helps inform the model of salient words contributing to the main topic. Experimental results show that our framework outperforms other state-of-the-art neural topic models in three common benchmark datasets that belong to various domains, vocabulary sizes, and document lengths in terms of topic coherence.

The authors revisit the adversarial formulation mathematically and express its discriminative objective as a new optimization problem. This formulation encourages relationships among similar samples while constraining similarity among dissimilar ones. They also introduce a sampling method based on the input and its reconstructed output. That method helps identify salient words associated with the main topic and facilitates the inclusion of external variables.

Experiments on three common benchmark datasets report better topic coherence than other state-of-the-art neural topic models. The datasets vary in domain, vocabulary size, and document length, giving the empirical comparison several different text settings. The stated improvement concerns coherence of the learned topics. The broader methodological contribution is to make both similarity and dissimilarity useful training signals while opening the model to additional document information.
summary.tldr: A reformulated topic-model objective and sampling strategy incorporate document similarities and external information, improving topic coherence on three benchmarks.

title: Contrastive Learning for Neural Topic Model

abstract: Deep neural networks have provided state-of-the-art solutions for problems such as image denoising, which implicitly rely on a prior probability model of natural images. Two recent lines of work – Denoising Score Matching and Plug-and-Play – propose methodologies for drawing samples from this implicit prior and using it to solve inverse problems, respectively. Here, we develop a parsimonious and robust generalization of these ideas. We rely on a classic statistical result that shows the least-squares solution for removing additive Gaussian noise can be written directly in terms of the gradient of the log of the noisy signal density. We use this to derive a stochastic coarse-to-fine gradient ascent procedure for drawing high-probability samples from the implicit prior embedded within a CNN trained to perform blind denoising. A generalization of this algorithm to constrained sampling provides a method for using the implicit prior to solve any deterministic linear inverse problem, with no additional training, thus extending the power of supervised learning for denoising to a much broader set of problems. The algorithm relies on minimal assumptions and exhibits robust convergence over a wide range of parameter choices. To demonstrate the generality of our method, we use it to obtain state-of-the-art levels of unsupervised performance for deblurring, super-resolution, and compressive sensing.

This paper develops a way to use that information for sampling and reconstruction tasks beyond denoising. It builds on a statistical connection between least-squares removal of additive Gaussian noise and the gradient of a noisy signal's log probability density.

From that connection, the authors derive a stochastic procedure that moves from coarse to fine scales to draw high-probability samples. The procedure uses a convolutional network trained for blind denoising. summary.tldr: A stochastic sampler reuses a trained denoiser's implicit image prior to solve deterministic linear inverse problems without additional training.

title: Stochastic Solutions for Linear Inverse Problems using the Prior Implicit in a Denoiser

abstract: We revisit offline reinforcement learning on episodic time-homogeneous Markov Decision Processes (MDP). For tabular MDP with $S$ states and $A$ actions, or linear MDP with anchor points and feature dimension $d$, given the collected $K$ episodes data with minimum visiting probability of (anchor) state-action pairs $d_m$, we obtain nearly horizon $H$-free sample complexity bounds for offline reinforcement learning when the total reward is upper bounded by 1. Specifically:• For offline policy evaluation, we obtain an $\tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1}{Kd_m}} \right)$ error bound for the plug-in estimator, which matches the lower bound up to logarithmic factors and does not have additional dependency on $\mathrm{poly}(H, S, A, d)$ in higher-order term.• For offline policy optimization, we obtain an $\tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1}{Kd_m}} + \frac{\min(S, d)}{Kd_m}\right)$ sub-optimality gap for the empirical optimal policy, which approaches the lower bound up to logarithmic factors and a high-order term, improving upon the best known result by [Cui and Yang 2020] that has additional $\mathrm{poly} (H, S, d)$ factors in the main term.To the best of our knowledge, these are the first set of nearly horizon-free bounds for episodic time-homogeneous offline tabular MDP and linear MDP with anchor points. Central to our analysis is a simple yet effective recursion based method to bound a "total variance" term in the offline scenarios, which could be of individual interest.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must evaluate or improve policies using already collected episodes. This paper studies how the amount of data needed depends on episode length. It considers time-homogeneous episodic environments with either tabular structure or a linear representation with anchor points, and assumes total reward is bounded above by one.

For policy evaluation, the authors obtain an error bound scaling roughly as the inverse square root of the number of episodes times minimum state-action visiting probability. It matches a lower bound up to logarithmic factors, without extra polynomial dependence on horizon or model size in higher-order terms. Policy optimization receives a related bound with an additional higher-order term involving the smaller of the state count and feature dimension.

The main result is that strong offline guarantees can be nearly independent of horizon under these assumptions. Coverage still matters through the minimum visiting probability. A recursion that controls total variance is central to the analysis, explaining how the authors avoid horizon factors present in earlier bounds.
summary.tldr: Under bounded total reward and specified MDP structure, offline policy evaluation and optimization admit nearly horizon-free error guarantees.

title: Nearly Horizon-Free Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: A neural network model of a differential equation, namely neural ODE, has enabled the learning of continuous-time dynamical systems and probabilistic distributions with high accuracy. The neural ODE uses the same network repeatedly during a numerical integration. The memory consumption of the backpropagation algorithm is proportional to the number of uses times the network size. This is true even if a checkpointing scheme divides the computation graph into sub-graphs. Otherwise, the adjoint method obtains a gradient by a numerical integration backward in time. Although this method consumes memory only for a single network use, it requires high computational cost to suppress numerical errors. This study proposes the symplectic adjoint method, which is an adjoint method solved by a symplectic integrator. The symplectic adjoint method obtains the exact gradient (up to rounding error) with memory proportional to the number of uses plus the network size. The experimental results demonstrate that the symplectic adjoint method consumes much less memory than the naive backpropagation algorithm and checkpointing schemes, performs faster than the adjoint method, and is more robust to rounding errors.

paragraphs: A neural ODE repeatedly evaluates a neural network during numerical integration. Ordinary backpropagation consumes memory proportional to the number of evaluations multiplied by network size, including when checkpointing splits the computation into smaller pieces. An adjoint method reduces memory by integrating backward in time, but controlling its numerical errors can require substantial computation.

This paper proposes a symplectic adjoint method, using a symplectic integrator to compute the adjoint. The method obtains the exact gradient up to rounding error while using memory proportional to the number of network evaluations plus the network size. Replacing multiplicative memory dependence with additive dependence is central to its stated computational advantage.

The experiments report much lower memory use than naive backpropagation and checkpointing, faster execution than the compared adjoint method, and greater robustness to rounding errors. These findings connect the mathematical gradient property with practical training costs. The result addresses a specific tradeoff in neural ODE learning: preserving gradient accuracy while reducing the memory and computation needed to obtain it.
summary.tldr: The symplectic adjoint method computes neural ODE gradients exactly up to rounding error with additive memory scaling and reported efficiency gains.

title: Symplectic Adjoint Method for Exact Gradient of Neural ODE with Minimal Memory

abstract: Rules have a number of desirable properties. It is easy to understand, infer new knowledge, and communicate with other inference systems. One weakness of the previous rule induction systems is that they only find rules within a knowledge base (KB) and therefore cannot generalize to more open and complex real-world rules. Recently, the language model (LM)-based rule generation are proposed to enhance the expressive power of the rules.In this paper, we revisit the differences between KB-based rule induction and LM-based rule generation. We argue that, while KB-based methods inducted rules by discovering data commonalitiess, the current LM-based methods are ``learning rules from rules''. This limits these methods to only produce ``canned'' rules whose patterns are constrained by the annotated rules, while discarding the rich expressive power of LMs for free text.Therefore, in this paper, we propose the open rule induction problem, which aims to induce open rules utilizing the knowledge in LMs. Besides, we propose the Orion (\underline{o}pen \underline{r}ule \underline{i}nducti\underline{on}) system to automatically mine open rules from LMs without supervision of annotated rules. We conducted extensive experiments to verify the quality and quantity of the inducted open rules. Surprisingly, when applying the open rules in downstream tasks (i.e. relation extraction), these automatically inducted rules even outperformed the manually annotated rules.

paragraphs: Rules offer an understandable way to express knowledge, derive further conclusions, and communicate with other reasoning systems. The paper argues that existing rule induction is constrained in two ways: knowledge-base methods stay within a fixed knowledge base, while supervised language-model methods inherit patterns from their annotated training rules.

The authors formulate open rule induction as extracting open rules from knowledge contained in language models. Their Orion system mines such rules automatically without supervision from annotated rules. The intended change is to exploit the expressive capacity of language models without requiring the discovered rules to follow the templates supplied by a rule-annotation dataset.

Experiments assess both the quality and quantity of the induced rules. When used for downstream relation extraction, the automatically obtained rules outperform manually annotated rules in the reported evaluation. This provides evidence that the mined rules can be useful beyond the induction process itself. The result supports language models as a source for discovering usable rules, rather than only generating variations of supervised examples.
summary.tldr: Orion mines open rules from language models without annotated-rule supervision and demonstrates their usefulness for relation extraction.

title: Open Rule Induction

abstract: We study privacy in a distributed learning framework, where clients collaboratively build a learning model iteratively throughinteractions with a server from whom we need privacy. Motivated by stochastic optimization and the federated learning (FL) paradigm, we focus on the case where a small fraction of data samples are randomly sub-sampled in each round to participate in the learning process, which also enables privacy amplification. To obtain even stronger local privacy guarantees, we study this in the shuffle privacy model, where each client randomizes its response using a local differentially private (LDP) mechanism and the server only receives a random permutation (shuffle) of the clients' responses without theirassociation to each client. The principal result of this paper is a privacy-optimization performance trade-off for discrete randomization mechanisms in this sub-sampled shuffle privacy model. This is enabledthrough a new theoretical technique to analyze the Renyi Differential Privacy (RDP) of the sub-sampled shuffle model. We numerically demonstrate that, for important regimes, with composition our boundyields significant improvement in privacy guarantee over the state-of-the-art approximate Differential Privacy (DP) guarantee (with strong composition) for sub-sampled shuffled models. We also demonstrate numerically significant improvement in privacy-learning performance operating point using real data sets. Despite these advances, an open question is to bridge the gap between lower and upper privacy bounds in our RDP analysis.

paragraphs: The paper examines distributed learning in which clients collaborate through a server while needing privacy from that server. Each round randomly selects a small fraction of data samples. Clients randomize their responses using local differential privacy, and the server receives a shuffled collection of responses without the association between each response and its client.

The authors develop a new analysis of Rényi differential privacy for this combination of subsampling and shuffling. Their principal result describes a tradeoff between privacy and optimization performance for discrete randomization mechanisms. The analysis also supports accounting for privacy across repeated rounds, which is central to iterative learning.

Numerical results show that, in important regimes, the composed bounds improve substantially over previous approximate differential privacy guarantees using strong composition. Experiments with real datasets also show better privacy-learning performance tradeoffs. The paper explicitly leaves a gap between its lower and upper privacy bounds unresolved, so the improved accounting does not settle the exact privacy limits of the analyzed setting.
summary.tldr: A new Rényi privacy analysis improves guarantees and privacy-learning tradeoffs for distributed learning that combines subsampling, local randomization, and shuffling.

title: Renyi Differential Privacy of The Subsampled Shuffle Model In Distributed Learning

abstract: Training models that perform well under distribution shifts is a central challenge in machine learning. In this paper, we introduce a modeling framework where, in addition to training data, we have partial structural knowledge of the shifted test distribution. We employ the principle of minimum discriminating information to embed the available prior knowledge, and use distributionally robust optimization to account for uncertainty due to the limited samples. By leveraging large deviation results, we obtain explicit generalization bounds with respect to the unknown shifted distribution. Lastly, we demonstrate the versatility of our framework by demonstrating it on two rather distinct applications: (1) training classifiers on systematically biased data and (2) off-policy evaluation in Markov Decision Processes.

paragraphs: A model trained on one distribution may be evaluated on another, making ordinary training-data evidence insufficient for assessing its performance. This paper studies a setting where the learner also possesses partial structural knowledge about the shifted test distribution. That extra knowledge is an explicit ingredient of the framework, even though the full test distribution remains unknown.

The method uses the principle of minimum discriminating information to incorporate this prior knowledge. It then applies distributionally robust optimization to account for uncertainty caused by having only a limited sample. These components address different sources of information: structural knowledge constrains how the test distribution is understood, while robust optimization handles remaining sampling uncertainty.

Using large-deviation results, the authors derive explicit generalization bounds relative to the unknown shifted distribution. They demonstrate the framework in two distinct applications: classification from systematically biased data and off-policy evaluation in Markov decision processes. The contribution is a way to connect partial knowledge of distribution shift to formal performance bounds, with applications spanning prediction and policy evaluation.
summary.tldr: The framework combines partial knowledge of a shifted test distribution with robust optimization to derive explicit generalization bounds.

title: Robust Generalization despite Distribution Shift via Minimum Discriminating Information

abstract: A large amount of recent research has the far-reaching goal of finding training methods for deep neural networks that can serve as alternatives to backpropagation~(BP). A prominent example is predictive coding (PC), which is a neuroscience-inspired method that performs inference on hierarchical Gaussian generative models. These methods, however, fail to keep up with modern neural networks, as they are unable to replicate the dynamics of complex layers and activation functions. In this work, we solve this problem by generalizing PC to arbitrary probability distributions, enabling the training of architectures, such as transformers, that are hard to approximate with only Gaussian assumptions. We perform three experimental analyses. First, we study the gap between our method and the standard formulation of PC on multiple toy examples. Second, we test the reconstruction quality on variational autoencoders, where our method reaches the same reconstruction quality as BP. Third, we show that our method allows us to train transformer networks and achieve performance comparable with BP on conditional language models. More broadly, this method allows neuroscience-inspired learning to be applied to multiple domains, since the internal distributions can be flexibly adapted to the data, tasks, and architectures used.

paragraphs: Predictive coding is a neuroscience-inspired approach to neural-network training that traditionally performs inference in hierarchical Gaussian generative models. Those distributional assumptions make it difficult to reproduce the behavior of complex layers and activation functions. This paper broadens predictive coding to accommodate arbitrary probability distributions.

That generalization allows internal distributions to fit the architecture and task more flexibly. In particular, it enables training Transformer architectures that are difficult to approximate using only Gaussian assumptions. The authors first investigate differences between the generalized method and standard predictive coding on several toy examples, then evaluate it on larger model families.

For variational autoencoders, the method reaches the same reconstruction quality as backpropagation in the reported experiments. For conditional language modeling, it trains Transformers to performance comparable with backpropagation. These findings support a wider practical scope for predictive coding: loosening its distributional assumptions makes the approach compatible with architectures and tasks beyond those readily captured by its conventional Gaussian formulation.
summary.tldr: Generalizing predictive coding beyond Gaussian distributions enables Transformer training and matches or approaches backpropagation performance in the reported tasks.

title: Predictive Coding beyond Gaussian Distributions

abstract: Biases in existing datasets used to train algorithmic decision rules can raise ethical and economic concerns due to the resulting disparate treatment of different groups. We propose an algorithm for sequentially debiasing such datasets through adaptive and bounded exploration in a classification problem with costly and censored feedback. Exploration in this context means that at times, and to a judiciously-chosen extent, the decision maker deviates from its (current) loss-minimizing rule, and instead accepts some individuals that would otherwise be rejected, so as to reduce statistical data biases. Our proposed algorithm includes parameters that can be used to balance between the ultimate goal of removing data biases -- which will in turn lead to more accurate and fair decisions, and the exploration risks incurred to achieve this goal. We analytically show that such exploration can help debias data in certain distributions. We further investigate how fairness criteria can work in conjunction with our data debiasing algorithm. We illustrate the performance of our algorithm using experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets.

We propose an algorithm for sequentially debiasing such datasets through adaptive and bounded exploration in a classification problem with costly and censored feedback. Exploration in this context means that at times, and to a judiciously-chosen extent, the decision maker deviates from its (current) loss-minimizing rule, and instead accepts some individuals that would otherwise be rejected, so as to reduce statistical data biases. Our proposed algorithm includes parameters that can be used to balance between the ultimate goal of removing data biases -- which will in turn lead to more accurate and fair decisions, and the exploration risks incurred to achieve this goal. We analytically show that such exploration can help debias data in certain distributions. We further investigate how fairness criteria can work in conjunction with our data debiasing algorithm. We illustrate the performance of our algorithm using experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: A decision system can inherit biased data while also influencing which new outcomes become observable. This paper studies classification with costly, censored feedback: the learner cannot freely obtain all the information it would like. Its goal is to improve the dataset over time through deliberately chosen exploration.

Exploration means occasionally accepting people whom the current rule would reject. These departures from the rule are adaptive and bounded, so the decision maker controls how much exploration occurs. The algorithm includes parameters for balancing the aim of reducing statistical bias against the risks incurred while gathering additional feedback. This makes data collection itself part of the learning problem.

The authors analytically establish that this strategy can debias data for certain distributions, rather than claiming that exploration always removes bias. They also examine how fairness criteria can operate alongside the algorithm and illustrate its behavior on synthetic and real-world datasets. The contribution connects fairer decision making to the process that creates the available evidence, with an explicit tradeoff between learning opportunities and exploration risk.
summary.tldr: Bounded, adaptive departures from a classification rule can reduce dataset bias under certain distributions while controlling exploration risk.

title: Adaptive Data Debiasing through Bounded Exploration

abstract: We consider the fixed-budget best arm identification problem where the goal is to find the arm of the largest mean with a fixed number of samples. It is known that the probability of misidentifying the best arm is exponentially small to the number of rounds. However, limited characterizations have been discussed on the rate (exponent) of this value. In this paper, we characterize the minimax optimal rate as a result of an optimization over all possible parameters. We introduce two rates, $R^{\mathrm{go}}$ and $R^{\mathrm{go}}_{\infty}$, corresponding to lower bounds on the probability of misidentification, each of which is associated with a proposed algorithm. The rate $R^{\mathrm{go}}$ is associated with $R^{\mathrm{go}}$-tracking, which can be efficiently implemented by a neural network and is shown to outperform existing algorithms. However, this rate requires a nontrivial condition to be achievable. To address this issue, we introduce the second rate $R^{\mathrm{go}}_\infty$. We show that this rate is indeed achievable by introducing a conceptual algorithm called delayed optimal tracking (DOT).

Both contribute to understanding the fundamental difficulty of allocating a fixed sampling budget.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes minimax error rates for fixed-budget best-arm identification and develops tracking algorithms associated with two such rates.

title: Minimax Optimal Algorithms for Fixed-Budget Best Arm Identification

abstract: Augmented Reality or AR filters on selfies have become very popular on social media platforms for a variety of applications, including marketing, entertainment and aesthetics. Given the wide adoption of AR face filters and the importance of faces in our social structures and relations, there is increased interest by the scientific community to analyze the impact of such filters from a psychological, artistic and sociological perspective. However, there are few quantitative analyses in this area mainly due to a lack of publicly available datasets of facial images with applied AR filters. The proprietary, close nature of most social media platforms does not allow users, scientists and practitioners to access the code and the details of the available AR face filters. Scraping faces from these platforms to collect data is ethically unacceptable and should, therefore, be avoided in research. In this paper, we present OpenFilter, a flexible framework to apply AR filters available in social media platforms on existing large collections of human faces. Moreover, we share FairBeauty and B-LFW, two beautified versions of the publicly available FairFace and LFW datasets and we outline insights derived from the analysis of these beautified datasets.

The paper identifies proprietary platforms and limited access to filter implementations as obstacles. It also rejects scraping faces from those platforms as an ethically acceptable way to assemble research data.

OpenFilter provides a framework for applying filters available on social-media platforms to existing large collections of face images. This gives researchers a way to create filtered datasets from existing image resources. The approach directly addresses the shortage of research material that has constrained psychological, artistic, and sociological analysis of these widely used visual transformations.

The authors also release FairBeauty and B-LFW, beautified versions of the public FairFace and LFW datasets, and outline insights from analyzing them. These resources make the framework's contribution concrete: researchers gain both a method for applying filters and datasets containing the resulting transformations. The stated contribution supports quantitative study of filter effects without establishing any particular psychological or social outcome in the abstract.
summary.tldr: OpenFilter applies social-media face filters to existing image collections and releases two beautified datasets to support research.

title: OpenFilter: A Framework to Democratize Research Access to Social Media AR Filters

abstract: Black-box attacks can generate adversarial examples without accessing the parameters of target model, largely exacerbating the threats of deployed deep neural networks (DNNs). However, previous works state that black-box attacks fail to mislead target models when their training data and outputs are inaccessible. In this work, we argue that black-box attacks can pose practical attacks in this extremely restrictive scenario where only several test samples are available. Specifically, we find that attacking the shallow layers of DNNs trained on a few test samples can generate powerful adversarial examples. As only a few samples are required, we refer to these attacks as lightweight black-box attacks. The main challenge to promoting lightweight attacks is to mitigate the adverse impact caused by the approximation error of shallow layers. As it is hard to mitigate the approximation error with few available samples, we propose Error TransFormer (ETF) for lightweight attacks. Namely, ETF transforms the approximation error in the parameter space into a perturbation in the feature space and alleviates the error by disturbing features. In experiments, lightweight black-box attacks with the proposed ETF achieve surprising results. For example, even if only 1 sample per category available, the attack success rate in lightweight black-box attacks is only about 3% lower than that of the black-box attacks with complete training data.

paragraphs: This paper studies adversarial attacks under a restrictive access setting: the attacker cannot inspect the target model’s parameters, training data, or outputs and has only a few test samples. The authors find that attacking shallow layers of networks trained on those limited samples can nevertheless produce effective adversarial examples.

They call this setting lightweight black-box attack. A central obstacle is approximation error in the shallow layers, which is difficult to reduce with so little data. The result challenges the view that withholding training data and model outputs necessarily prevents effective black-box attacks when a few test samples remain available.
summary.tldr: ETF enables effective black-box attacks from very few test samples by addressing shallow-layer approximation error through feature perturbations.

title: Towards Lightweight Black-Box Attack Against Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Widely observed neural scaling laws, in which error falls off as a power of the training set size, model size, or both, have driven substantial performance improvements in deep learning. However, these improvements through scaling alone require considerable costs in compute and energy. Here we focus on the scaling of error with dataset size and show how in theory we can break beyond power law scaling and potentially even reduce it to exponential scaling instead if we have access to a high-quality data pruning metric that ranks the order in which training examples should be discarded to achieve any pruned dataset size. We then test this improved scaling prediction with pruned dataset size empirically, and indeed observe better than power law scaling in practice on ResNets trained on CIFAR-10, SVHN, and ImageNet. Next, given the importance of finding high-quality pruning metrics, we perform the first large-scale benchmarking study of ten different data pruning metrics on ImageNet. We find most existing high performing metrics scale poorly to ImageNet, while the best are computationally intensive and require labels for every image. We therefore developed a new simple, cheap and scalable self-supervised pruning metric that demonstrates comparable performance to the best supervised metrics. Overall, our work suggests that the discovery of good data-pruning metrics may provide a viable path forward to substantially improved neural scaling laws, thereby reducing the resource costs of modern deep learning.
