paragraphs: DP-LLM addresses how an on-device language model should adapt when queries come with different latency and accuracy requirements. Multi-scale quantization makes runtime adaptation possible by overlaying model variants that use different numerical bitwidths. The remaining challenge is choosing a configuration that provides a useful balance between model performance and the time needed to generate an answer.

The paper's key observation is that a layer's sensitivity to numerical precision changes across decoding steps. A precision allocation that suits one stage of generation may therefore be less suitable at another. DP-LLM uses input values to assign precision dynamically to individual layers, extending the idea of mixed precision into a decision that changes during generation.

Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks report a better performance-latency trade-off than prior approaches. The finding supports using the current computation to guide precision allocation rather than treating layer sensitivity as fixed throughout decoding. Its practical significance is more adaptable use of the available precision choices when serving language models under runtime constraints.
summary.tldr: DP-LLM dynamically adjusts each layer's numerical precision during decoding to improve the performance-latency trade-off.

title: DP-LLM: Runtime Model Adaptation with Dynamic Layer-wise Precision Assignment

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel optimizer state compression algorithm, namely \textbf{$\pi$-Quant}, which leverages the properties of irrational numbers (\eg $\pi$) for memory-efficient training. The core idea is based on our mathematical findings, which show that a pair of parameters can be represented by a single rotation angle using the complex rotation scheme. Building on this insight, we map the parameters into a complex space and perform quantization using the corresponding rotation angles. To efficiently integrate it into optimization process, we develop an efficient system of geometric equations that computes the precise rotation angles with linear complexity. We evaluate $\pi$-Quant on a wide range of tasks. Our experiments show that it can reduce the bit-width of parameters to 3.32-bit, achieving a 41.8\% decrease in GPU memory usage, all while maintaining full accuracy. \textcolor{blue}{We have submitted the code in supplementary materials}.

paragraphs: This paper introduces π-Quant, an optimizer-state compression algorithm intended to reduce the memory needed for training. Its starting point is a mathematical representation result: using a complex rotation scheme with properties of irrational numbers, a pair of parameters can be represented through a single rotation angle.

The algorithm maps parameters into complex space and quantizes their associated rotation angles. This changes the representation on which compression operates, making the geometry of paired values central to the method. To integrate the scheme efficiently into optimization, the authors develop geometric equations that calculate the required angles precisely with linear complexity.

Across a wide range of evaluated tasks, the authors report reducing parameter bit width to 3.32 bits and lowering GPU memory usage by 41.8% while maintaining full accuracy. These are empirical results for the evaluated settings. The contribution joins a mathematical encoding idea with an efficient angle-computation procedure, showing how a compact representation can translate into substantial training-memory savings without an observed accuracy reduction in those experiments.
summary.tldr: π-Quant compresses optimizer states through complex rotation angles, reporting 41.8% lower GPU memory usage while preserving accuracy in its experiments.

title: Irrational Complex Rotations Empower Low-bit Optimizers

abstract: Covariate shift is a unconventional learning scenario in which training and testing data have different distributions. A general principle to solve the problem is to make the training data distribution similar to the test one, such that classifiers computed on the former generalizes well to the latter. Current approaches typically target on the sample distribution in the input space, however, for kernel-based learning methods, the algorithm performance depends directly on the geometry of the kernel-induced feature space. Motivated by this, we propose to match data distributions in the Hilbert space, which, given a pre-defined empirical kernel map, can be formulated as aligning kernel matrices across domains. In particular, to evaluate similarity of kernel matrices defined on arbitrarily different samples, the novel concept of surrogate kernel is introduced based on the Mercer's theorem. Our approach caters the model adaptation specifically to kernel-based learning mechanism, and demonstrates promising results on several real-world applications.

paragraphs: When training and testing data follow different distributions, a classifier may struggle to transfer what it has learned. A common response is to make the training distribution resemble the test distribution. This paper argues that, for kernel methods, the relevant comparison should account for the feature space created by the kernel, because its geometry directly affects learning.

The authors propose matching distributions in that Hilbert space. Given a predefined empirical kernel map, the task becomes one of aligning kernel matrices across domains. These matrices describe relationships among samples, but comparing them is challenging when they are defined over different sample collections. The paper introduces surrogate kernels, based on Mercer’s theorem, to evaluate their similarity.

This approach connects adaptation to the representation actually used by the kernel learner. Its significance is the choice of where distribution matching occurs and how otherwise differently indexed kernel matrices can be compared. The abstract reports promising results on several real-world applications, supporting the usefulness of adapting to kernel-space geometry in the settings examined.
summary.tldr: Surrogate kernels enable distribution matching in the feature space used by kernel learners under covariate shift.

title: Covariate Shift in Hilbert Space: A Solution via Sorrogate Kernels

abstract: We characterize a family of regularized loss minimization problems that satisfy three properties: scaled uniform convergence, super-norm regularization, and norm-loss monotonicity. We show several theoretical guarantees within this framework, including loss consistency, norm consistency, sparsistency (i.e. support recovery) as well as sign consistency. A number of regularization problems can be shown to fall within our framework and we provide several examples. Our results can be seen as a concise summary of existing guarantees but we also extend them to new settings. Our formulation enables us to assume very little about the hypothesis class, data distribution, the loss, or the regularization. In particular, many of our results do not require a bounded hypothesis class, or identically distributed samples. Similarly, we do not assume boundedness, convexity or smoothness of the loss nor the regularizer. We only assume approximate optimality of the empirical minimizer. In terms of recovery, in contrast to existing results, our sparsistency and sign consistency results do not require knowledge of the sub-differential of the objective function.

paragraphs: Regularized learning combines a measure of prediction error with a penalty on the chosen model. This paper asks when solutions to such problems reliably approach the desired population solution as more data become available. It organizes the analysis around three properties: scaled uniform convergence, super-norm regularization, and norm-loss monotonicity. Together, these define the family of problems covered by the framework.

The guarantees address several distinct kinds of success. Loss consistency concerns predictive performance, while norm consistency concerns convergence measured through a norm. Sparsistency means recovering which components belong in the model, and sign consistency concerns recovering their signs. The framework gathers existing guarantees into one formulation and extends them to additional settings.

Its breadth comes from avoiding several assumptions often used in separate analyses. Many results allow unbounded hypothesis classes or samples that are not identically distributed. The loss and regularizer need not be bounded, convex, or smooth, and empirical optimization may be approximate. These conclusions remain conditional on the framework’s defining properties; the paper does not claim consistency for arbitrary regularized learning problems.
summary.tldr: A common framework establishes several forms of consistency for regularized learning under broad, explicitly defined conditions.

title: A Unified Framework for Consistency of Regularized Loss Minimizers

abstract: Unknown constraints arise in many types of expensive black-box optimization problems. Several methods have been proposed recently for performing Bayesian optimization with constraints, based on the expected improvement (EI) heuristic. However, EI can lead to pathologies when used with constraints. For example, in the case of decoupled constraints—i.e., when one can independently evaluate the objective or the constraints—EI can encounter a pathology that prevents exploration. Additionally, computing EI requires a current best solution, which may not exist if none of the data collected so far satisfy the constraints. By contrast, information-based approaches do not suffer from these failure modes. In this paper, we present a new information-based method called Predictive Entropy Search with Constraints (PESC). We analyze the performance of PESC and show that it compares favorably to EI-based approaches on synthetic and benchmark problems, as well as several real-world examples. We demonstrate that PESC is an effective algorithm that provides a promising direction towards a unified solution for constrained Bayesian optimization.

Additionally, computing EI requires a current best solution, which may not exist if none of the data collected so far satisfy the constraints. By contrast, information-based approaches do not suffer from these failure modes. In this paper, we present a new information-based method called Predictive Entropy Search with Constraints (PESC). paragraphs: Expensive black-box optimization becomes harder when the conditions defining an acceptable solution are also unknown. This paper examines problems with using expected improvement to choose evaluations in that setting. In particular, objective and constraint evaluations may be available independently, creating a need to decide which kind of information to acquire.

The authors describe two failure modes. With independently evaluated constraints, expected improvement can encounter a pathology that prevents exploration. It also requires a current best solution, which may be unavailable when no observed point satisfies the constraints. Information-based approaches avoid these particular difficulties because their evaluation criterion does not rely on the same improvement calculation.

The proposed method, Predictive Entropy Search with Constraints, applies this information-based perspective to constrained Bayesian optimization. Evaluations on synthetic problems, benchmarks, and real-world examples compare favorably with expected-improvement methods. The findings support PESC as an effective approach and a promising step toward a unified treatment of constrained optimization, rather than establishing a complete universal solution.
summary.tldr: PESC uses information-based evaluation to handle unknown constraints and avoid specific exploration failures of expected improvement.

title: Predictive Entropy Search for Bayesian Optimization with Unknown Constraints

abstract: In this paper, we attack the anomaly detection problem by directly modeling the data distribution with deep architectures. We hence propose deep structured energy based models (DSEBMs), where the energy function is the output of a deterministic deep neural network with structure. We develop novel model architectures to integrate EBMs with different types of data such as static data, sequential data, and spatial data, and apply appropriate model architectures to adapt to the data structure. Our training algorithm is built upon the recent development of score matching (Hyvarinen, 2005), which connects an EBM with a regularized autoencoder, eliminating the need for complicated sampling method. Statistically sound decision criterion can be derived for anomaly detection purpose from the perspective of the energy landscape of the data distribution. We investigate two decision criteria for performing anomaly detection: the energy score and the reconstruction error. Extensive empirical studies on benchmark anomaly detection tasks demonstrate that our proposed model consistently matches or outperforms all the competing methods.

paragraphs: This paper approaches anomaly detection by learning the distribution of the data with a deep energy-based model. A structured, deterministic neural network produces the energy function. The authors develop architectures for static, sequential, and spatial data, so the model can reflect the organization of the observations it receives.

Training uses score matching and its connection between energy-based models and regularized autoencoders. This connection removes the need for complicated sampling procedures in the proposed training method. It also brings together two perspectives on unusual observations: their position in the learned energy landscape and the error incurred when reconstructing them.

The authors investigate both energy scores and reconstruction errors as criteria for deciding whether an observation is anomalous. They describe a statistically grounded criterion derived from the energy landscape and evaluate the models on benchmark anomaly-detection tasks. Across those empirical studies, their method consistently matches or exceeds the competing approaches. The results support the proposed combination of structure-aware architectures, score-matching training, and anomaly decisions based on the learned distribution.
summary.tldr: Structured deep energy models detect anomalies using energy or reconstruction scores and perform strongly on the evaluated benchmarks.

title: Deep Structured Energy Based Models for Anomaly Detection

abstract: We develop the method of stochastic modified equations (SME), in which stochastic gradient algorithms are approximated in the weak sense by continuous-time stochastic differential equations. We exploit the continuous formulation together with optimal control theory to derive novel adaptive hyper-parameter adjustment policies. Our algorithms have competitive performance with the added benefit of being robust to varying models and datasets. This provides a general methodology for the analysis and design of stochastic gradient algorithms.
originalAbstract: We develop the method of stochastic modified equations (SME), in which stochastic gradient algorithms are approximated in the weak sense by continuous-time stochastic differential equations. We exploit the continuous formulation together with optimal control theory to derive novel adaptive hyper-parameter adjustment policies. Our algorithms have competitive performance with the added benefit of being robust to varying models and datasets. This provides a general methodology for the analysis and design of stochastic gradient algorithms.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient algorithms evolve through discrete, random updates. This paper develops stochastic modified equations as a way to study those updates using continuous-time stochastic differential equations. The approximation is in the weak sense, so the continuous formulation serves as a probabilistic description of the algorithm rather than an assertion that individual trajectories coincide.

The authors use this formulation together with optimal control theory to derive adaptive policies for adjusting hyperparameters. This connects analysis and algorithm design: the continuous description provides a setting in which adjustment rules can be derived, and those rules become part of the stochastic gradient procedure.

The resulting algorithms achieve competitive performance and are reported to remain robust across varying models and datasets. The contribution is therefore both a collection of adaptive methods and a general methodology for understanding and designing stochastic gradient algorithms. Its significance lies in turning a mathematical approximation into actionable training policies, with empirical results supporting the usefulness of that connection.
summary.tldr: Continuous stochastic approximations and optimal control yield adaptive gradient algorithms with competitive performance across varied models and datasets.

title: Stochastic Modified Equations and Adaptive Stochastic Gradient Algorithms

abstract: Many applications require forecasts for a hierarchy comprising a set of time series along with aggregates of subsets of these series. Hierarchical forecasting require not only good prediction accuracy at each level of the hierarchy, but also the coherency between different levels — the property that forecasts add up appropriately across the hierarchy. A fundamental limitation of prior research is the focus on forecasting the mean of each time series. We consider the situation where probabilistic forecasts are needed for each series in the hierarchy, and propose an algorithm to compute predictive distributions rather than mean forecasts only. Our algorithm has the advantage of synthesizing information from different levels in the hierarchy through a sparse forecast combination and a probabilistic hierarchical aggregation. We evaluate the accuracy of our forecasting algorithm on both simulated data and large-scale electricity smart meter data. The results show consistent performance gains compared to state-of-the art methods.

paragraphs: Hierarchical forecasting involves related time series and aggregates formed from subsets of those series. A useful forecast must be accurate at each level while also respecting the relationships between levels. This consistency requirement, called coherence, means that forecasts must add up appropriately throughout the hierarchy.

The paper extends the focus from predicting means to producing predictive distributions. A distribution expresses uncertainty about future outcomes, so the task requires more than making individual point predictions consistent. The proposed algorithm combines information from different hierarchy levels through sparse forecast combination and probabilistic hierarchical aggregation. These components allow forecasts at multiple levels to contribute to the resulting distributions.

The authors evaluate the algorithm on simulated data and large-scale electricity smart meter data. They report consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art methods in those evaluations. The contribution matters where users need both uncertainty estimates and compatible forecasts across aggregation levels: it treats these as connected requirements and uses information distributed across the hierarchy to improve the forecasting process.
summary.tldr: The paper produces coherent predictive distributions for hierarchical time series by combining information across aggregation levels.

title: Coherent Probabilistic Forecasts for Hierarchical Time Series

abstract: Inspired by many applications of bipartite matching in online advertising and machine learning, we study a simple and natural iterative proportional allocation algorithm: Maintain a priority score $\priority_a$ for each node $a\in \mathds{A}$ on one side of the bipartition, initialized as $\priority_a=1$. Iteratively allocate the nodes $i\in \impressions$ on the other side to eligible nodes in $\mathds{A}$ in proportion of their priority scores. After each round, for each node $a\in \mathds{A}$, decrease or increase the score $\priority_a$ based on whether it is over- or under- allocated. Our first result is that this simple, distributed algorithm converges to a $(1-\epsilon)$-approximate fractional $b$-matching solution in $O({\log n\over \epsilon^2} )$ rounds. We also extend the proportional allocation algorithm and convergence results to the maximum weighted matching problem, and show that the algorithm can be naturally tuned to produce maximum matching with high entropy . High entropy, in turn, implies additional desirable properties of this matching, e.g., it satisfies certain diversity and fairness (aka anonymity) properties that are desirable in a variety of applications in online advertising and machine learning.

Iteratively allocate the nodes $i\in \impressions$ on the other side to eligible nodes in $\mathds{A}$ in proportion of their priority scores. paragraphs: Bipartite matching allocates items on one side of a graph to eligible recipients on the other. The paper studies a simple distributed procedure that assigns each recipient a priority score, initially equal for everyone. Items are allocated in proportion to those scores, providing a direct rule for sharing available opportunities.

After each round, scores decrease for recipients receiving too much allocation and increase for those receiving too little. The authors prove that this process reaches a fractional b-matching within a factor of 1 minus epsilon of optimal in O(log(n)/epsilon²) rounds. They also extend the proportional allocation approach and its convergence results to maximum weighted matching.

The algorithm can additionally be tuned to produce maximum matchings with high entropy. In this setting, high entropy implies certain diversity and fairness properties, including anonymity, that are useful in advertising and machine learning applications. The contribution combines a lightweight allocation mechanism with approximation guarantees and a way to favor a more diverse distribution of assignments.
summary.tldr: Iterative proportional allocation efficiently approximates fractional matching and can produce high-entropy matchings with specified diversity and fairness properties.

title: Proportional Allocation: Simple, Distributed, and Diverse Matching with High Entropy

abstract: We introduce a framework based on bilevel programming that unifies gradient-based hyperparameter optimization and meta-learning. We show that an approximate version of the bilevel problem can be solved by taking into explicit account the optimization dynamics for the inner objective. Depending on the specific setting, the outer variables take either the meaning of hyperparameters in a supervised learning problem or parameters of a meta-learner. We provide sufficient conditions under which solutions of the approximate problem converge to those of the exact problem. We instantiate our approach for meta-learning in the case of deep learning where representation layers are treated as hyperparameters shared across a set of training episodes. In experiments, we confirm our theoretical findings, present encouraging results for few-shot learning and contrast the bilevel approach against classical approaches for learning-to-learn.

Depending on the specific setting, the outer variables take either the meaning of hyperparameters in a supervised learning problem or parameters of a meta-learner. paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization and meta-learning both involve choices that influence another learning process. This paper places them in a common bilevel framework: an inner objective describes one optimization problem, while outer variables govern choices around it. Depending on the application, those outer variables represent supervised-learning hyperparameters or parameters of a meta-learner.

The approach solves an approximate bilevel problem by explicitly accounting for the optimization dynamics of the inner objective. The authors provide sufficient conditions under which solutions of this approximation converge to solutions of the exact problem. This gives a conditional theoretical justification for using the approximation, rather than asserting that every approximate formulation will recover an exact solution.

For deep meta-learning, the paper treats representation layers as hyperparameters shared across training episodes. Experiments support the theoretical findings, report encouraging few-shot learning results, and compare the approach with classical learning-to-learn methods. Together, these contributions connect a general optimization formulation with a concrete way to learn representations shared across episodes.
summary.tldr: A bilevel optimization framework unifies hyperparameter optimization and meta-learning, with sufficient conditions for convergence of approximate solutions.

title: Bilevel Programming for Hyperparameter Optimization and Meta-Learning

abstract: We study generalization properties of distributed algorithms in the setting of nonparametric regression over a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). We investigate distributed stochastic gradient methods (SGM), with mini-batches and multi-passes over the data. We show that optimal generalization error bounds can be retained for distributed SGM provided that the partition level is not too large. Our results are superior to the state-of-the-art theory, covering the cases that the regression function may not be in the hypothesis spaces. Particularly, our results show that distributed SGM has a smaller theoretical computational complexity, compared with distributed kernel ridge regression (KRR) and classic SGM.

The theory also covers cases where the true regression function does not belong to the chosen hypothesis space.

The significance is a joint statistical and computational result. Within the analyzed conditions, distributed training can reduce the theoretical work required while retaining an optimal bound on generalization error.
summary.tldr: Distributed multi-pass stochastic gradient methods retain optimal regression guarantees when data partitioning is sufficiently limited.

title: Optimal Distributed Learning with Multi-pass Stochastic Gradient Methods

abstract: Many interesting applications of reinforcement learning (RL) involve MDPs that include numerous “dead-end" states. Upon reaching a dead-end state, the agent continues to interact with the environment in a dead-end trajectory before reaching an undesired terminal state, regardless of whatever actions are chosen. The situation is even worse when existence of many dead-end states is coupled with distant positive rewards from any initial state (we term this as Bridge Effect). Hence, conventional exploration techniques often incur prohibitively many training steps before convergence. To deal with the bridge effect, we propose a condition for exploration, called security. We next establish formal results that translate the security condition into the learning problem of an auxiliary value function. This new value function is used to cap “any" given exploration policy and is guaranteed to make it secure. As a special case, we use this theory and introduce secure random-walk. We next extend our results to the deep RL settings by identifying and addressing two main challenges that arise. Finally, we empirically compare secure random-walk with standard benchmarks in two sets of experiments including the Atari game of Montezuma’s Revenge.

The central contribution is the connection between an exploration requirement and a learnable value function that can regulate exploration.
summary.tldr: An auxiliary value function can constrain exploration to satisfy a formal security condition in environments with dead ends and distant rewards.

title: Dead-ends and Secure Exploration in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study the problem of knowledge graph (KG) embedding. A widely-established assumption to this problem is that similar entities are likely to have similar relational roles. However, existing related methods derive KG embeddings mainly based on triple-level learning, which lack the capability of capturing long-term relational dependencies of entities. Moreover, triple-level learning is insufficient for the propagation of semantic information among entities, especially for the case of cross-KG embedding. In this paper, we propose recurrent skipping networks (RSNs), which employ a skipping mechanism to bridge the gaps between entities. RSNs integrate recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with residual learning to efficiently capture the long-term relational dependencies within and between KGs. We design an end-to-end framework to support RSNs on different tasks. Our experimental results showed that RSNs outperformed state-of-the-art embedding-based methods for entity alignment and achieved competitive performance for KG completion.

This paper highlights a weakness of learning mainly from individual triples: it does not adequately capture longer relational dependencies or propagate semantic information among entities. The authors identify this as especially relevant when representations must connect information across different knowledge graphs.

Their recurrent skipping networks combine recurrent neural networks with residual learning. A skipping mechanism bridges gaps between entities, helping the model capture relational dependencies over longer spans both within and between graphs. The approach builds on the established assumption that similar entities are likely to occupy similar relational roles.

The authors package the networks in an end-to-end framework supporting different tasks. Experiments show better entity-alignment performance than state-of-the-art embedding-based methods and competitive performance on knowledge-graph completion. These outcomes distinguish the strongest reported gain from the broader applicability claim: the method leads the compared alignment approaches, while completion results show that the same framework remains competitive on another graph task.
summary.tldr: Recurrent skipping networks capture longer relational dependencies, improving entity alignment while remaining competitive on knowledge-graph completion.

title: Learning to Exploit Long-term Relational Dependencies in Knowledge Graphs

abstract: In the age of Internet of Things (IoT), embedded devices ranging from ARM Cortex M0s with hundreds of KB of RAM to Arduinos with 2KB RAM are expected to perform increasingly sophisticated classification tasks, such as voice and gesture recognition, activity tracking, and biometric security. While convolutional neural networks (CNNs), together with spectrogram preprocessing, are a natural solution to many of these classification tasks, storage of the network’s activations often exceeds the hard memory constraints of embedded platforms. This paper presents memory-optimal direct convolutions as a way to push classification accuracy as high as possible given strict hardware memory constraints at the expense of extra compute. We therefore explore the opposite end of the compute-memory trade-off curve from standard approaches that minimize latency. We validate the memory-optimal CNN technique with an Arduino implementation of the 10-class MNIST classification task, fitting the network specification, weights, and activations entirely within 2KB SRAM and achieving a state-of-the-art classification accuracy for small-scale embedded systems of 99.15%.

paragraphs: Small embedded devices increasingly need to run classification systems, but their memory may be too limited to hold a convolutional network's intermediate activations. This paper treats that storage constraint as the central design problem. The goal is to achieve as much classification accuracy as possible within a strict memory budget.

The proposed memory-optimal direct convolutions trade additional computation for reduced memory requirements. This deliberately explores a different operating point from approaches designed primarily to minimize latency. The motivation is practical: for a device with a hard memory ceiling, an approach that uses more computation can make a useful network fit at all.

The authors validate the technique with an Arduino implementation of ten-class MNIST classification. The network specification, weights, and activations all fit within 2KB of SRAM, while classification accuracy reaches 99.15%. They report this as state-of-the-art accuracy for small-scale embedded systems. The demonstration links the compute-memory trade-off to an actual implementation, with the extra computation remaining an explicit cost of the approach.
summary.tldr: Memory-optimal convolutions trade extra computation for storage savings, enabling 99.15% MNIST accuracy with the full network contained in 2KB SRAM.

title: Memory-Optimal Direct Convolutions for Maximizing Classification Accuracy in Embedded Applications

abstract: To be effective in sequential data processing, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are required to keep track of past events by creating memories. While the relation between memories and the network’s hidden state dynamics was established over the last decade, previous works in this direction were of a predominantly descriptive nature focusing mainly on locating the dynamical objects of interest. In particular, it remained unclear how dynamical observables affect the performance, how they form and whether they can be manipulated. Here, we utilize different training protocols, datasets and architectures to obtain a range of networks solving a delayed classification task with similar performance, alongside substantial differences in their ability to extrapolate for longer delays. We analyze the dynamics of the network’s hidden state, and uncover the reasons for this difference. Each memory is found to be associated with a nearly steady state of the dynamics which we refer to as a ’slow point’. Slow point speeds predict extrapolation performance across all datasets, protocols and architectures tested. Furthermore, by tracking the formation of the slow points we are able to understand the origin of differences between training protocols. Finally, we propose a novel regularization technique that is based on the relation between hidden state speeds and memory longevity. Our technique manipulates these speeds, thereby leading to a dramatic improvement in memory robustness over time, and could pave the way for a new class of regularization methods.

The predictive evidence is established across the settings tested in the paper.
summary.tldr: Hidden-state slow-point speeds predict memory longevity in the tested recurrent networks and motivate regularization that substantially improves memory robustness.

title: Understanding and Controlling Memory in Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: We consider classification in the presence of class-dependent asymmetric label noise with unknown noise probabilities. In this setting, identifiability conditions are known, but additional assumptions were shown to be required for finite sample rates, and so far only the parametric rate has been obtained. Assuming these identifiability conditions, together with a measure-smoothness condition on the regression function and Tsybakov’s margin condition, we show that the Robust kNN classifier of Gao et al. attains, the mini-max optimal rates of the noise-free setting, up to a log factor, even when trained on data with unknown asymmetric label noise. Hence, our results provide a solid theoretical backing for this empirically successful algorithm. By contrast the standard kNN is not even consistent in the setting of asymmetric label noise. A key idea in our analysis is a simple kNN based method for estimating the maximum of a function that requires far less assumptions than existing mode estimators do, and which may be of independent interest for noise proportion estimation and randomised optimisation problems.

paragraphs: Label errors need not occur equally often across classes. This paper studies classification when labels are corrupted at unknown, class-dependent rates. That asymmetry matters: the abstract states that ordinary k-nearest-neighbor classification is not even consistent in this setting, so additional data alone does not ensure recovery of the desired classifier.

The authors analyze the existing Robust kNN classifier under identifiability assumptions, a measure-smoothness condition on the regression function, and Tsybakov's margin condition. Under these assumptions, its rates match the minimax-optimal rates of the noise-free problem up to a logarithmic factor. Thus, the stated noise model need not worsen the fundamental rate beyond that factor when these conditions hold.

It requires substantially fewer assumptions than existing mode estimators and may also help with noise-proportion estimation or randomized optimization. The main result supplies theoretical support for an empirically successful classifier, while the auxiliary estimation method offers a potentially useful contribution beyond classification.
summary.tldr: Under identifiability, smoothness, and margin assumptions, Robust kNN nearly matches optimal noise-free rates despite unknown asymmetric label corruption.

title: Fast Rates for a kNN Classifier Robust to Unknown Asymmetric Label Noise

abstract: Labeling training data is a key bottleneck in the modern machine learning pipeline. Recent weak supervision approaches combine labels from multiple noisy sources by estimating their accuracies without access to ground truth labels; however, estimating the dependencies among these sources is a critical challenge. We focus on a robust PCA-based algorithm for learning these dependency structures, establish improved theoretical recovery rates, and outperform existing methods on various real-world tasks. Under certain conditions, we show that the amount of unlabeled data needed can scale sublinearly or even logarithmically with the number of sources m, improving over previous efforts that ignore the sparsity pattern in the dependency structure and scale linearly in m. We provide an information-theoretic lower bound on the minimum sample complexity of the weak supervision setting. Our method outperforms weak supervision approaches that assume conditionally-independent sources by up to 4.64 F1 points and previous structure learning approaches by up to 4.41 F1 points on real-world relation extraction and image classification tasks.

paragraphs: Weak supervision combines labels from multiple noisy sources without requiring ground-truth labels to estimate their accuracies. A major challenge is that those sources may depend on one another. This paper studies how to learn that dependency structure, so the combined model can account for relationships among its sources.

The authors analyze an algorithm based on robust principal component analysis and establish improved recovery rates. Under certain conditions, the required amount of unlabeled data grows sublinearly, or even logarithmically, with the number of sources. These results exploit the sparsity pattern of dependencies, improving on earlier analyses with linear scaling. An information-theoretic lower bound also characterizes the minimum sample requirements of the weak-supervision setting.

On real-world relation extraction and image classification tasks, the method improves over approaches assuming conditionally independent sources by up to 4.64 F1 points. It improves over previous structure-learning approaches by up to 4.41 points. Together, the theoretical and empirical results show why modeling source dependencies can improve both data requirements and predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Learning sparse dependencies among noisy labeling sources can reduce unlabeled-data requirements under stated conditions and improve weak-supervision accuracy.

title: Learning Dependency Structures for Weak Supervision Models

abstract: We study regularization in the context of small sample-size learning with over-parametrized neural networks. Specifically, we shift focus from architectural properties, such as norms on the network weights, to properties of the internal representations before a linear classifier. Specifically, we impose a topological constraint on samples drawn from the probability measure induced in that space. This provably leads to mass concentration effects around the representations of training instances, i.e., a property beneficial for generalization. By leveraging previous work to impose topological constrains in a neural network setting, we provide empirical evidence (across various vision benchmarks) to support our claim for better generalization.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to regularize overparameterized neural networks when only a small training sample is available. It focuses on the internal representations immediately before a linear classifier. The proposed approach controls properties of the distribution in that representation space, shifting attention toward the geometry of learned features.

The authors impose a topological constraint on samples drawn from the probability measure induced in this space. They prove that the constraint produces concentration of probability mass around the representations of training examples. This supplies a mathematical link between the imposed structural condition and how the learned representation distribution is organized.

The paper identifies this concentration as beneficial for generalization and uses previous work to implement topological constraints in neural networks. Experiments across several vision benchmarks provide evidence for improved generalization. The contribution joins a theoretical concentration result with an empirical learning argument: shaping the representation distribution can be a useful form of regularization for networks trained with limited data.
summary.tldr: Topological constraints on internal representations provably concentrate probability mass near training representations and empirically improve generalization in small-sample vision learning.

title: Topologically Densified Distributions

abstract: The point estimates of ReLU classification networks—arguably the most widely used neural network architecture—have been shown to yield arbitrarily high confidence far away from the training data. This architecture, in conjunction with a maximum a posteriori estimation scheme, is thus not calibrated nor robust. Approximate Bayesian inference has been empirically demonstrated to improve predictive uncertainty in neural networks, although the theoretical analysis of such Bayesian approximations is limited. We theoretically analyze approximate Gaussian distributions on the weights of ReLU networks and show that they fix the overconfidence problem. Furthermore, we show that even a simplistic, thus cheap, Bayesian approximation, also fixes these issues. This indicates that a sufficient condition for a calibrated uncertainty on a ReLU network is “to be a bit Bayesian”. These theoretical results validate the usage of last-layer Bayesian approximation and motivate a range of a fidelity-cost trade-off. We further validate these findings empirically via various standard experiments using common deep ReLU networks and Laplace approximations.

paragraphs: ReLU classifiers represented by a single set of fitted weights can become arbitrarily confident far from their training data. Such confidence is problematic because the prediction may concern inputs unlike those used to learn the model. This paper examines whether approximate Bayesian treatment of the weights can resolve that overconfidence.

The authors theoretically analyze Gaussian approximations to distributions over network weights. They show that these approximations fix the studied overconfidence problem, and that even a simple, inexpensive Bayesian approximation can suffice. The result gives theoretical support to treating only the last layer in a Bayesian way, creating room to balance approximation fidelity against computational cost.

Experiments with common deep ReLU networks and Laplace approximations further support the theoretical findings. The central message is that resolving this problem need not require an elaborate Bayesian treatment of every network component. The stated condition is sufficient: the work supports particular approximate Bayesian approaches without establishing that they are the only possible route to calibrated uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Gaussian Bayesian weight approximations, including inexpensive last-layer approaches, can fix the studied overconfidence problem in ReLU classifiers.

title: Being Bayesian, Even Just a Bit, Fixes Overconfidence in ReLU Networks

abstract: We study the problem of Robust Outlier Arm Identification (ROAI), where the goal is to identify arms whose expected rewards deviate substantially from the majority, by adaptively sampling from their reward distributions. We compute the outlier threshold using the median and median absolute deviation of the expected rewards. This is a robust choice for the threshold compared to using the mean and standard deviation, since it can identify outlier arms even in the presence of extreme outlier values. Our setting is different from existing pure exploration problems where the threshold is pre-specified as a given value or rank. This is useful in applications where the goal is to identify the set of promising items but the cardinality of this set is unknown, such as finding promising drugs for a new disease or identifying items favored by a population. We propose two $\delta$-PAC algorithms for ROAI, which includes the first UCB-style algorithm for outlier detection, and derive upper bounds on their sample complexity. We also prove a matching, up to logarithmic factors, worst case lower bound for the problem, indicating that our upper bounds are generally unimprovable. Experimental results show that our algorithms are both robust and about $5$x sample efficient compared to state-of-the-art.

The learner adaptively samples their reward distributions to identify them. Unlike problems with a supplied numerical threshold or target rank, this setting derives its threshold from the collection of expected rewards, allowing the number of identified items to be unknown in advance.

The formulation is intended for applications such as identifying promising drugs or population-favored items, where the goal is to discover a set rather than choose a predetermined number.

Experiments report robustness and roughly fivefold better sample efficiency than state-of-the-art methods in the evaluated comparisons.
summary.tldr: Robust, data-dependent thresholds enable adaptive outlier identification with near-matching sample-complexity bounds.

title: Robust Outlier Arm Identification

abstract: The activations of language transformers like GPT-2 have been shown to linearly map onto brain activity during speech comprehension. However, the nature of these activations remains largely unknown and presumably conflate distinct linguistic classes. Here, we propose a taxonomy to factorize the high-dimensional activations of language models into four combinatorial classes: lexical, compositional, syntactic, and semantic representations. We then introduce a statistical method to decompose, through the lens of GPT-2’s activations, the brain activity of 345 subjects recorded with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) during the listening of 4.6 hours of narrated text. The results highlight two findings. First, compositional representations recruit a more widespread cortical network than lexical ones, and encompass the bilateral temporal, parietal and prefrontal cortices. Second, contrary to previous claims, syntax and semantics are not associated with separated modules, but, instead, appear to share a common and distributed neural substrate. Overall, this study introduces a versatile framework to isolate, in the brain activity, the distributed representations of linguistic constructs.

paragraphs: Language-transformer activations can be linearly mapped to brain activity during speech comprehension, but those activations combine multiple kinds of linguistic information. This paper develops a way to separate that information so researchers can investigate which aspects of language correspond to different patterns of brain activity.

The authors organize representations along lexical, compositional, syntactic, and semantic categories. They introduce a statistical method that uses GPT-2 activations to decompose fMRI activity from 345 people listening to 4.6 hours of narrated text. The language model serves as a lens for distinguishing linguistic constructs within the recorded activity.

summary.tldr: A GPT-2-based analysis of brain activity suggests that syntax and semantics share distributed neural representations.

title: Disentangling syntax and semantics in the brain with deep networks

abstract: In this paper, we devise a distributional framework on actor-critic as a solution to distributional instability, action type restriction, and conflation between samples and statistics. We propose a new method that minimizes the Cram{é}r distance with the multi-step Bellman target distribution generated from a novel Sample-Replacement algorithm denoted SR(\lambda), which learns the correct value distribution under multiple Bellman operations. Parameterizing a value distribution with Gaussian Mixture Model further improves the efficiency and the performance of the method, which we name GMAC. We empirically show that GMAC captures the correct representation of value distributions and improves the performance of a conventional actor-critic method with low computational cost, in both discrete and continuous action spaces using Arcade Learning Environment (ALE) and PyBullet environment.

paragraphs: This paper develops an actor-critic framework that represents a distribution of values rather than only a value statistic. It targets instability in distributional learning, restrictions on supported action types, and confusion between samples and statistics. The goal is to make distributional information useful within actor-critic learning while addressing these obstacles in one framework.

The method minimizes the Cramér distance to a target distribution constructed using multiple Bellman steps. A new Sample-Replacement procedure, SR(λ), generates that target and learns the correct value distribution under multiple Bellman operations. The authors then represent the value distribution with a Gaussian mixture model, obtaining the method they call GMAC and improving its efficiency and performance.

Experiments in the Arcade Learning Environment and PyBullet show that GMAC captures the correct representation of value distributions and improves a conventional actor-critic method at low computational cost. The evaluations include discrete and continuous actions. These findings support using the proposed distributional target and representation across both action settings examined by the authors.
summary.tldr: GMAC combines sample-replacement targets and Gaussian mixture value distributions to improve actor-critic learning in tested discrete and continuous environments.

title: GMAC: A Distributional Perspective on Actor-Critic Framework

abstract: A key problem in computational biology is discovering the gene expression changes that regulate cell fate transitions, in which one cell type turns into another. However, each individual cell cannot be tracked longitudinally, and cells at the same point in real time may be at different stages of the transition process. This can be viewed as a problem of learning the behavior of a dynamical system from observations whose times are unknown. Additionally, a single progenitor cell type often bifurcates into multiple child cell types, further complicating the problem of modeling the dynamics. To address this problem, we developed an approach called variational mixtures of ordinary differential equations. By using a simple family of ODEs informed by the biochemistry of gene expression to constrain the likelihood of a deep generative model, we can simultaneously infer the latent time and latent state of each cell and predict its future gene expression state. The model can be interpreted as a mixture of ODEs whose parameters vary continuously across a latent space of cell states. Our approach dramatically improves data fit, latent time inference, and future cell state estimation of single-cell gene expression data compared to previous approaches.

title: Variational Mixtures of ODEs for Inferring Cellular Gene Expression Dynamics

abstract: Learning-augmented algorithms—in which, traditional algorithms are augmented with machine-learned predictions—have emerged as a framework to go beyond worst-case analysis. The overarching goal is to design algorithms that perform near-optimally when the predictions are accurate yet retain certain worst-case guarantees irrespective of the accuracy of the predictions. This framework has been successfully applied to online problems such as caching where the predictions can be used to alleviate uncertainties. In this paper we introduce and study the setting in which the learning-augmented algorithm can utilize the predictions parsimoniously. We consider the caching problem—which has been extensively studied in the learning-augmented setting—and show that one can achieve quantitatively similar results but only using a sublinear number of predictions.

paragraphs: Learning-augmented algorithms use machine-learned predictions to improve traditional decision procedures. The goal is to benefit when predictions are accurate while retaining worst-case guarantees when they are unreliable. Caching is a natural setting for this idea because decisions must be made despite uncertainty about future requests.

This paper adds a resource question: how often does the algorithm actually need to use predictions? It introduces a setting in which prediction use is deliberately limited and studies that setting for caching. The focus is therefore on obtaining the value of predictive information while reducing the amount of such information consumed.

The authors show that quantitatively similar results are possible with only a sublinear number of predictions. Sublinear use means the prediction count grows more slowly than the scale of the request sequence. The result establishes that prediction access need not grow proportionally to every caching decision to retain comparable learning-augmented guarantees. It makes prediction usage itself part of the algorithm-design problem, alongside performance when predictions are accurate or inaccurate.
summary.tldr: Learning-augmented caching can retain quantitatively similar guarantees while using only a sublinear number of predictions.

title: Parsimonious Learning-Augmented Caching

abstract: We pursue tractable Bayesian analysis of generalized linear models (GLMs) for categorical data. GLMs have been difficult to scale to more than a few dozen categories due to non-conjugacy or strong posterior dependencies when using conjugate auxiliary variable methods. We define a new class of GLMs for categorical data called categorical-from-binary (CB) models. Each CB model has a likelihood that is bounded by the product of binary likelihoods, suggesting a natural posterior approximation. This approximation makes inference straightforward and fast; using well-known auxiliary variables for probit or logistic regression, the product of binary models admits conjugate closed-form variational inference that is embarrassingly parallel across categories and invariant to category ordering. Moreover, an independent binary model simultaneously approximates multiple CB models. Bayesian model averaging over these can improve the quality of the approximation for any given dataset. We show that our approach scales to thousands of categories, outperforming posterior estimation competitors like Automatic Differentiation Variational Inference (ADVI) and No U-Turn Sampling (NUTS) in the time required to achieve fixed prediction quality.

paragraphs: Bayesian generalized linear models for categorical outcomes can become difficult to scale when there are many categories. The paper identifies two obstacles: likelihoods that resist convenient Bayesian updates and strong posterior dependencies in auxiliary-variable approaches. It introduces categorical-from-binary models to make approximate inference more tractable while retaining a categorical prediction problem.

Each model has a likelihood bounded by a product of binary likelihoods, motivating an independent binary approximation to the posterior. With established auxiliary variables for probit or logistic regression, this construction permits closed-form variational updates. Computation can proceed independently across categories, and the result does not depend on how the categories are ordered.

The authors demonstrate scaling to thousands of categories and faster attainment of a fixed prediction quality than ADVI and NUTS. The reported advantage is thus computational efficiency at comparable predictive quality, rather than a claim of exact posterior recovery.
summary.tldr: Categorical-from-binary models enable fast, parallel Bayesian approximation across thousands of categories through independent binary inference.

title: Easy Variational Inference for Categorical Models via an Independent Binary Approximation

abstract: Transformers have shown remarkable progress on computer vision tasks in the past year. Compared to their CNN counterparts, transformers usually need the help of distillation to achieve comparable results on middle or small sized datasets. Meanwhile, recent researches discover that when transformers are trained with supervised and self-supervised manner respectively, the captured patterns are quite different both qualitatively and quantitatively. These findings motivate us to introduce an self-supervised teaching assistant (SSTA) besides the commonly used supervised teacher to improve the performance of transformers. Specifically, we propose a head-level knowledge distillation method that selects the most important head of the supervised teacher and self-supervised teaching assistant, and let the student mimic the attention distribution of these two heads, so as to make the student focus on the relationship between tokens deemed by the teacher and the teacher assistant. Extensive experiments verify the effectiveness of SSTA and demonstrate that the proposed SSTA is a good compensation to the supervised teacher. Meanwhile, some analytical experiments towards multiple perspectives (e.g. prediction, shape bias, robustness, and transferability to downstream tasks) with supervised teachers, self-supervised teaching assistants and students are inductive and may inspire future researches.

paragraphs: Vision transformers often rely on distillation to perform comparably to convolutional networks on small or medium-sized datasets. The paper builds on observations that supervised and self-supervised transformers capture different patterns. It asks whether a self-supervised model can provide complementary guidance alongside the supervised teacher commonly used during student training.

The proposed self-supervised teaching assistant supplies that second source of guidance through head-level knowledge distillation. The method selects the most important attention head from each of the supervised teacher and self-supervised assistant. The student learns to match both attention distributions, directing it toward relationships between input tokens emphasized by the two sources.

Extensive experiments support the assistant’s effectiveness as a complement to the supervised teacher. Additional analyses examine predictions, shape bias, robustness, and transfer to downstream tasks across teachers, assistants, and students. These analyses provide further perspectives on the learned models, while the main empirical finding is that combining the two forms of teaching improves transformer performance.
summary.tldr: A self-supervised teaching assistant complements a supervised teacher by guiding a vision transformer student to match selected attention heads from both.

title: Self-supervised Models are Good Teaching Assistants for Vision Transformers

abstract: Tandem mass spectrometry is the only high-throughput method for analyzing the protein content of complex biological samples and is thus the primary technology driving the growth of the field of proteomics. A key outstanding challenge in this field involves identifying the sequence of amino acids -the peptide- responsible for generating each observed spectrum, without making use of prior knowledge in the form of a peptide sequence database. Although various machine learning methods have been developed to address this de novo sequencing problem, challenges that arise when modeling tandem mass spectra have led to complex models that combine multiple neural networks and post-processing steps. We propose a simple yet powerful method for de novo peptide sequencing, Casanovo, that uses a transformer framework to map directly from a sequence of observed peaks (a mass spectrum) to a sequence of amino acids (a peptide). Our experiments show that Casanovo achieves state-of-the-art performance on a benchmark dataset using a standard cross-species evaluation framework which involves testing with spectra with never-before-seen peptide labels. Casanovo not only achieves superior performance but does so at a fraction of the model complexity and inference time required by other methods.

paragraphs: Tandem mass spectrometry produces spectra that researchers use to study the protein content of biological samples. A central challenge is identifying the amino acid sequence responsible for each spectrum. De novo sequencing tackles this without consulting a peptide sequence database, making the task one of inferring a sequence directly from the observed measurements.

The paper introduces Casanovo, which uses a transformer to map a sequence of spectral peaks directly to a sequence of amino acids. This provides a simpler modeling approach to a problem for which previous machine learning systems have combined multiple neural networks and post-processing stages. The transformation from measured peaks to peptide sequence is the core prediction task.

On a benchmark dataset, Casanovo achieves state-of-the-art performance under a standard cross-species evaluation that includes peptide labels never seen during training. It also requires only a fraction of the model complexity and inference time of other methods. These findings support the direct transformer formulation as both accurate and efficient in the evaluated setting, including the challenge of predicting previously unseen peptide sequences.
summary.tldr: Casanovo directly translates mass spectra into peptide sequences with a transformer, achieving strong benchmark accuracy with lower complexity and inference time.

title: De novo mass spectrometry peptide sequencing with a transformer model

abstract: In this work we propose a HyperTransformer, a Transformer-based model for supervised and semi-supervised few-shot learning that generates weights of a convolutional neural network (CNN) directly from support samples. Since the dependence of a small generated CNN model on a specific task is encoded by a high-capacity Transformer model, we effectively decouple the complexity of the large task space from the complexity of individual tasks. Our method is particularly effective for small target CNN architectures where learning a fixed universal task-independent embedding is not optimal and better performance is attained when the information about the task can modulate all model parameters. For larger models we discover that generating the last layer alone allows us to produce competitive or better results than those obtained with state-of-the-art methods while being end-to-end differentiable.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning requires adapting to a task from a small collection of support examples. HyperTransformer tackles this by using a Transformer to generate the weights of a convolutional neural network directly from those examples. The method covers both supervised and semi-supervised versions of the problem, making model generation the means of task adaptation.

The design separates the capacity needed to understand many possible tasks from the capacity needed to solve any one task. A large Transformer represents the relationship between support examples and model parameters, while the generated CNN can remain small. The paper finds this particularly effective for small CNNs, where letting task information influence all parameters performs better than relying on a fixed, task-independent embedding.

For larger target networks, the authors find that generating only the final layer can already match or improve on state-of-the-art results. This variant also remains differentiable from end to end. Together, the findings show that task-conditioned weight generation can be useful at different model sizes, with the appropriate extent of parameter generation changing between the small and larger architectures studied.
summary.tldr: HyperTransformer generates task-specific CNN weights from a few support examples, allowing compact models to adapt throughout their parameters.

title: HyperTransformer: Model Generation for Supervised and Semi-Supervised Few-Shot Learning

abstract: Large-scale multimodal generative modeling has created milestones in text-to-image and text-to-video generation. Its application to audio still lags behind for two main reasons: the lack of large-scale datasets with high-quality text-audio pairs, and the complexity of modeling long continuous audio data. In this work, we propose Make-An-Audio with a prompt-enhanced diffusion model that addresses these gaps by 1) introducing pseudo prompt enhancement with a distill-then-reprogram approach, it alleviates data scarcity with orders of magnitude concept compositions by using language-free audios; 2) leveraging spectrogram autoencoder to predict the self-supervised audio representation instead of waveforms. Together with robust contrastive language-audio pretraining (CLAP) representations, Make-An-Audio achieves state-of-the-art results in both objective and subjective benchmark evaluation. Moreover, we present its controllability and generalization for X-to-Audio with "No Modality Left Behind", for the first time unlocking the ability to generate high-definition, high-fidelity audios given a user-defined modality input. Audio samples are available at https://Make-An-Audio.github.io

paragraphs: Generating audio from text faces two obstacles highlighted by this paper: limited high-quality paired text and audio, and the difficulty of modeling long continuous sound signals. Make-An-Audio addresses both within a diffusion-based generation system. Its design combines a strategy for expanding useful prompt information with a more manageable representation of audio.

The first component creates enhanced pseudo prompts through a distill-then-reprogram procedure, making use of audio without accompanying language. This alleviates paired-data scarcity by enabling many concept compositions. The second uses a spectrogram autoencoder so that generation predicts a learned audio representation instead of directly predicting waveforms. Contrastive language-audio pretraining supplies representations connecting language and sound.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on both objective and subjective benchmark evaluations. They also demonstrate controllability and generalization beyond text-conditioned generation through an X-to-Audio capability described as accepting user-defined input modalities. Together, the findings support combining prompt enhancement and representation-based generation to improve audio synthesis, while the reported broader-input demonstrations extend the system’s stated scope beyond text prompts.
summary.tldr: Make-An-Audio combines pseudo-prompt enhancement and learned audio representations to improve diffusion-based audio generation.

title: Make-An-Audio: Text-To-Audio Generation with Prompt-Enhanced Diffusion Models

abstract: Modern deep learning models with great expressive power can be trained to overfit the training data but still generalize well. This phenomenon is referred to as benign overfitting. Recently, a few studies have attempted to theoretically understand benign overfitting in neural networks. However, these works are either limited to neural networks with smooth activation functions or to the neural tangent kernel regime. How and when benign overfitting can occur in ReLU neural networks remains an open problem. In this work, we seek to answer this question by establishing algorithm-dependent risk bounds for learning two-layer ReLU convolutional neural networks with label-flipping noise. We show that, under mild conditions, the neural network trained by gradient descent can achieve near-zero training loss and Bayes optimal test risk. Our result also reveals a sharp transition between benign and harmful overfitting under different conditions on data distribution in terms of test risk. Experiments on synthetic data back up our theory.

paragraphs: Benign overfitting occurs when a model fits its training data extremely closely yet still predicts well on new data. This paper asks when that behavior is possible for networks using ReLU activations. Earlier theoretical treatments had focused on smooth activations or the neural tangent kernel regime, leaving an important gap for ReLU networks.

The authors analyze two-layer convolutional networks trained by gradient descent when some training labels have been flipped. They derive risk bounds that depend on the learning algorithm. Under conditions described as mild, the trained network can achieve almost zero training loss while attaining Bayes-optimal test risk: the best prediction risk available for the underlying data distribution.

The analysis also identifies a sharp change between benign and harmful overfitting as conditions on the data distribution vary. Fitting noisy training labels therefore need not have the same effect in every setting. Synthetic-data experiments support the theoretical results. The contribution is a conditional explanation of successful overfitting in this specific ReLU architecture, including when its test performance can deteriorate.
summary.tldr: For two-layer ReLU convolutional networks with label noise, the paper establishes conditions separating benign from harmful overfitting.

title: Benign Overfitting in Two-layer ReLU Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: The ability to accurately recognize, localize and separate sound sources is fundamental to any audio-visual perception task. Historically, these abilities were tackled separately, with several methods developed independently for each task. However, given the interconnected nature of source localization, separation, and recognition, independent models are likely to yield suboptimal performance as they fail to capture the interdependence between these tasks. To address this problem, we propose a unified audio-visual learning framework (dubbed OneAVM) that integrates audio and visual cues for joint localization, separation, and recognition. OneAVM comprises a shared audio-visual encoder and task-specific decoders trained with three objectives. The first objective aligns audio and visual representations through a localized audio-visual correspondence loss. The second tackles visual source separation using a traditional mix-and-separate framework. Finally, the third objective reinforces visual feature separation and localization by mixing images in pixel space and aligning their representations with those of all corresponding sound sources. Extensive experiments on MUSIC, VGG-Instruments, VGG-Music, and VGGSound datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of OneAVM for all three tasks, audio-visual source localization, separation, and nearest neighbor recognition, and empirically demonstrate a strong positive transfer between them.

paragraphs: Finding where a sound comes from, separating it from other sounds, and recognizing its source are closely connected tasks. OneAVM trains them together using audio and images. A shared encoder builds representations used by separate task-specific decoders, allowing the learning objectives to influence the same underlying features.

The framework combines three objectives. One aligns sounds with their corresponding image regions. Another uses a mix-and-separate procedure to learn source separation with visual information. The third mixes images directly in pixel space and aligns the resulting representations with all corresponding sound sources. This last objective is designed to strengthen both visual feature separation and localization.

Experiments on MUSIC, VGG-Instruments, VGG-Music, and VGGSound support the framework’s effectiveness for localization, separation, and nearest-neighbor recognition. The authors also observe strong positive transfer between these tasks: training them together helps their performance in the evaluated settings. The central finding is that their shared structure can be useful training information, rather than something each independently trained model must rediscover.
summary.tldr: OneAVM jointly learns sound localization, separation, and recognition, with experiments showing that the tasks benefit one another.

title: A Unified Audio-Visual Learning Framework for Localization, Separation, and Recognition

abstract: Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) are discriminative models that directly model the class posterior $p(y|\mathbf{x})$ for semi-supervised classification of graph data. While being effective, as a representation learning approach, the node representations extracted from a GCN often miss useful information for effective clustering, because the objectives are different. In this work, we design normalizing flows that replace GCN layers, leading to a generative model that models both the class conditional likelihood $p(\mathbf{x}|y)$ and the class prior $p(y)$. The resulting neural network, GC-Flow, retains the graph convolution operations while being equipped with a Gaussian mixture representation space. It enjoys two benefits: it not only maintains the predictive power of GCN, but also produces well-separated clusters, due to the structuring of the representation space. We demonstrate these benefits on a variety of benchmark data sets. Moreover, we show that additional parameterization, such as that on the adjacency matrix used for graph convolutions, yields additional improvement in clustering.

paragraphs: A graph network trained to predict node classes does not necessarily produce representations that work well for clustering. Classification and clustering reward different properties, so useful grouping information can be absent from features learned for label prediction. GC-Flow addresses this mismatch by changing the probabilistic model behind graph representation learning.

The method replaces graph convolutional network layers with normalizing flows while retaining graph convolution operations. Instead of directly modeling class probabilities given node features, it models feature likelihoods conditioned on classes together with class probabilities. Its representation space follows a Gaussian mixture structure, giving the learned features an explicit organization that supports separated groups.

Benchmark experiments demonstrate that GC-Flow retains classification predictive power while producing well-separated clusters. The authors also find further clustering gains from additional parameterization, including parameterizing the adjacency matrix used in graph convolutions. The contribution shows how a generative objective and structured representation space can align graph learning more closely with clustering while preserving useful prediction capabilities.
summary.tldr: GC-Flow combines graph convolutions with normalizing flows and a Gaussian mixture representation to improve clustering while preserving predictive power.

title: GC-Flow: A Graph-Based Flow Network for Effective Clustering

abstract: This paper considers the problem of learning single ReLU neuron with squared loss (a.k.a., ReLU regression) in the overparameterized regime, where the input dimension can exceed the number of samples. We analyze a Perceptron-type algorithm called GLM-tron [Kakade et al. 2011], and provide its dimension-free risk upper bounds for high-dimensional ReLU regression in both well-specified and misspecified settings. Our risk bounds recover several existing results as special cases. Moreover, in the well-specified setting, we also provide an instance-wise matching risk lower bound for GLM-tron. Our upper and lower risk bounds provide a sharp characterization of the high-dimensional ReLU regression problems that can be learned via GLM-tron. On the other hand, we provide some negative results for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for ReLU regression with symmetric Bernoulli data: if the model is well-specified, the excess risk of SGD is provably no better than that of GLM-tron ignoring constant factors, for each problem instance; and in the noiseless case, GLM-tron can achieve a small risk while SGD unavoidably suffers from a constant risk in expectation. These results together suggest that GLM-tron might be more preferable than SGD for high-dimensional ReLU regression.
