These results together suggest that GLM-tron might be more preferable than SGD for high-dimensional ReLU regression.

paragraphs: Learning even a single ReLU neuron raises meaningful questions when input dimension exceeds the number of examples. This paper studies that setting under squared loss, analyzing the Perceptron-type algorithm GLM-tron. The goal is to characterize prediction risk with a finite amount of data rather than relying only on eventual convergence.

The authors establish dimension-free risk upper bounds in both well-specified and misspecified settings. When the model is well-specified, they also give a matching lower bound for each problem instance. Together, these results sharply describe which high-dimensional ReLU regression problems GLM-tron can learn, while recovering several earlier results as special cases.

The comparison with stochastic gradient descent is made for symmetric Bernoulli data. In the well-specified setting, SGD’s excess risk is no better than GLM-tron’s up to constant factors on each instance. In the noiseless case, GLM-tron can obtain small risk while SGD retains constant expected risk. These findings support GLM-tron as a potentially preferable choice for this problem class; the stated data and model conditions are essential to interpreting the comparison.
summary.tldr: Sharp risk bounds for GLM-tron and conditional negative results for SGD favor GLM-tron in the studied high-dimensional ReLU regression settings.

title: Finite-Sample Analysis of Learning High-Dimensional Single ReLU Neuron

abstract: LLMs have been found to memorize training textual sequences and regurgitate verbatim said sequences during text generation time. This fact is known to be the cause of privacy and related (e.g., copyright) problems. Unlearning in LLMs then takes the form of devising new algorithms that will properly deal with these side-effects of memorized data, while not hurting the model’s utility. We offer a fresh perspective towards this goal, namely, that each textual sequence to be forgotten should be treated differently when being unlearned based on its degree of memorization within the LLM. We contribute a new metric for measuring unlearning quality, an adversarial attack showing that SOTA algorithms lacking this perspective fail for privacy, and two new unlearning methods based on Gradient Ascent and Task Arithmetic, respectively. A comprehensive performance evaluation across an extensive suite of NLP tasks then mapped the solution space, identifying the best solutions under different scales in model capacities and forget set sizes and quantified the gains of the new approaches.

paragraphs: Language models can reproduce memorized training passages, creating privacy and related copyright concerns. Unlearning seeks to remove such memorized material while preserving useful model capabilities. This paper argues that the removal process should account for how strongly each individual sequence is memorized, rather than applying the same treatment across the entire set to be forgotten.

The authors contribute a measure of unlearning quality and an adversarial attack showing privacy failures in state-of-the-art algorithms that lack this sequence-specific perspective. They also introduce two unlearning methods, one based on gradient ascent and the other on task arithmetic. Both incorporate the central idea that different sequences warrant different unlearning treatment.

An extensive evaluation across natural-language tasks examines the resulting balance between forgetting and utility. It compares solutions at different model capacities and forget-set sizes, identifies the best options within those settings, and quantifies gains from the proposed approaches. The findings make the choice of unlearning method sensitive to both the model and the material being removed, while the attack provides a direct test of whether apparent forgetting withstands adversarial probing.
summary.tldr: Sequence-specific unlearning accounts for memorization strength and improves the evaluated tradeoffs between forgetting, privacy, and model utility.

title: To Each (Textual Sequence) Its Own: Improving Memorized-Data Unlearning in Large Language Models

abstract: Visual reprogramming (VR) is a prompting technique that aims to re-purpose a pre-trained model (e.g., a classifier on ImageNet) to target tasks (e.g., medical data prediction) by learning a small-scale pattern added into input images instead of tuning considerable parameters within the model. The location of the pattern within input samples is usually determined by a pre-defined mask shared across all samples. In this paper, we show that the shared mask potentially limits VR’s generalization and increases its approximation error due to the lack of sample-level adaptation. Motivated by this finding, we design a new framework for VR called sample-specific multi-channel masks (SMM). Specifically, SMM employs a lightweight ConvNet and patch-wise interpolation to generate sample-specific three-channel masks instead of a shared and pre-defined mask. Since we generate different masks for individual samples, SMM is theoretically shown to reduce approximation error for the target tasks compared with existing state-of-the-art VR methods. We also empirically demonstrate its performance gain on both ResNet and ViT. The success of SMM further highlights the broader applicability of VR in leveraging the latent knowledge of pre-trained models for various target tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/tmlr-group/SMM.

paragraphs: Visual reprogramming adapts a pretrained model by adding a learned pattern to input images, avoiding the need to tune many internal model parameters. A mask usually specifies where that pattern appears, and existing approaches often share the same predefined mask across images. This paper shows that such sharing can limit generalization and increase approximation error.

The proposed sample-specific multi-channel mask framework, SMM, makes the mask depend on the individual image. A lightweight convolutional network and patch-wise interpolation generate a separate three-channel mask for each sample. The key change is therefore in how the prompt is placed across the input, adding adaptation at the sample level.

The authors theoretically show reduced target-task approximation error compared with existing state-of-the-art visual reprogramming methods. They also demonstrate empirical performance gains with both ResNet and Vision Transformer backbones. These findings support input-dependent masks as a way to improve the use of pretrained knowledge through visual prompting, while keeping the adaptation focused on the input pattern and its placement.
summary.tldr: SMM improves visual reprogramming by generating a separate three-channel prompt mask for each input image.

title: Sample-specific Masks for Visual Reprogramming-based Prompting

abstract: Multi-task reinforcement learning (RL) faces the significant challenge of varying task difficulties, often leading to negative transfer when simpler tasks overshadow the learning of more complex ones. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel algorithm, Scheduled Multi-Task Training (SMT), that strategically prioritizes more challenging tasks, thereby enhancing overall learning efficiency. SMT introduces a dynamic task prioritization strategy, underpinned by an effective metric for assessing task difficulty. This metric ensures an efficient and targeted allocation of training resources, significantly improving learning outcomes. Additionally, SMT incorporates a reset mechanism that periodically reinitializes key network parameters to mitigate the simplicity bias, further enhancing the adaptability and robustness of the learning process across diverse tasks. The efficacy of SMT’s scheduling method is validated by significantly improving performance on challenging Meta-World benchmarks.

paragraphs: Learning several reinforcement-learning tasks together creates a resource-allocation problem when those tasks differ in difficulty. Easier tasks can dominate training and interfere with learning harder ones, producing negative transfer. Scheduled Multi-Task Training, or SMT, addresses this imbalance by giving challenging tasks greater priority during learning.

SMT uses a task-difficulty metric to update its priorities dynamically. That connects the allocation of training resources to how demanding the tasks are, instead of allowing simpler tasks to overshadow them. The algorithm also periodically reinitializes key network parameters. This reset mechanism is intended to reduce the tendency to favor simple tasks and improve adaptability across the task collection.

The paper reports significant performance improvements on challenging Meta-World benchmarks, validating the scheduling approach in those evaluations. The findings support treating the order and emphasis of training as part of the learning algorithm itself. SMT combines dynamic prioritization with parameter resets to address both resource imbalance and the simplicity bias that can develop during shared training.
summary.tldr: SMT improves multi-task reinforcement learning by dynamically prioritizing difficult tasks and periodically resetting key network parameters.

title: Hard Tasks First: Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning Through Task Scheduling

abstract: Bayesian reinforcement learning (RL) offers a principled and elegant approach for sequential decision making under uncertainty. Most notably, Bayesian agents do not face an exploration/exploitation dilemma, a major pathology of frequentist methods. However theoretical understanding of model-free approaches is lacking. In this paper, we introduce a novel Bayesian model-free formulation and the first analysis showing that model-free approaches can yield Bayes-optimal policies. We show all existing model-free approaches make approximations that yield policies that can be arbitrarily Bayes-suboptimal. As a first step towards model-free Bayes optimality, we introduce the Bayesian exploration network (BEN) which uses normalising flows to model both the aleatoric uncertainty (via density estimation) and epistemic uncertainty (via variational inference) in the Bellman operator. In the limit of complete optimisation, BEN learns true Bayes-optimal policies, but like in variational expectation-maximisation, partial optimisation renders our approach tractable. Empirical results demonstrate that BEN can learn true Bayes-optimal policies in tasks where existing model-free approaches fail.

paragraphs: Bayesian reinforcement learning treats uncertainty as part of sequential decision-making. This paper asks whether model-free methods can achieve Bayes-optimal policies, addressing a gap in their theoretical understanding. The authors introduce a Bayesian model-free formulation and show that such optimality is possible, while existing model-free approximations can produce arbitrarily Bayes-suboptimal policies.

Their proposed Bayesian exploration network, BEN, models two kinds of uncertainty in the Bellman operator. Aleatoric uncertainty concerns randomness represented through density estimation; epistemic uncertainty concerns uncertainty in knowledge, represented through variational inference. BEN uses normalizing flows for both, making uncertainty modeling central to how it learns decisions.

The optimality statement has an important condition: BEN learns genuinely Bayes-optimal policies in the limit of complete optimization. Partial optimization makes the method tractable but does not carry that same unconditional conclusion. Empirically, the authors show that BEN can learn Bayes-optimal policies on tasks where existing model-free approaches fail. The contribution combines a theoretical route to optimality with a practical approximation strategy.
summary.tldr: BEN models two forms of uncertainty to pursue model-free Bayesian reinforcement learning, with Bayes-optimality guaranteed in the limit of complete optimization.

title: Bayesian Exploration Networks

abstract: Can we model Non-Euclidean graphs as pure language or even Euclidean vectors while retaining their inherent information? The Non-Euclidean property have posed a long term challenge in graph modeling. Despite recent graph neural networks and graph transformers efforts encoding graphs as Euclidean vectors, recovering the original graph from vectors remains a challenge. In this paper, we introduce GraphsGPT, featuring an Graph2Seq encoder that transforms Non-Euclidean graphs into learnable Graph Words in the Euclidean space, along with a GraphGPT decoder that reconstructs the original graph from Graph Words to ensure information equivalence. We pretrain GraphsGPT on $100$M molecules and yield some interesting findings: (1) The pretrained Graph2Seq excels in graph representation learning, achieving state-of-the-art results on $8/9$ graph classification and regression tasks. (2) The pretrained GraphGPT serves as a strong graph generator, demonstrated by its strong ability to perform both few-shot and conditional graph generation. (3) Graph2Seq+GraphGPT enables effective graph mixup in the Euclidean space, overcoming previously known Non-Euclidean challenges. (4) The edge-centric pretraining framework GraphsGPT demonstrates its efficacy in graph domain tasks, excelling in both representation and generation. Code is available at https://github.com/A4Bio/GraphsGPT.

paragraphs: Graphs describe relationships that do not naturally form an ordinary sequence or vector. Converting them into vectors can make them easier to process, but recovering the original graph remains difficult. GraphsGPT addresses this problem with a paired encoder and decoder, making reconstruction central to the representation rather than treating vector production as the endpoint.

The Graph2Seq encoder translates a graph into learned vector representations called Graph Words. The GraphGPT decoder reconstructs the graph from those representations, supporting the paper’s goal of preserving its information. The combined system also enables graph mixup in vector space: graph representations can be combined in a space where ordinary vector operations are available.

After pretraining on 100 million molecules, the encoder achieves state-of-the-art results on eight of nine classification and regression tasks. The decoder also demonstrates strong few-shot and conditional generation. Together, these findings support the usefulness of the edge-focused pretraining framework for both understanding graphs and producing them, with reconstruction connecting the two capabilities.
summary.tldr: GraphsGPT converts graphs into learned vector tokens and reconstructs them, supporting strong graph prediction, generation, and mixup.

title: A Graph is Worth $K$ Words: Euclideanizing Graph using Pure Transformer

abstract: Large Language Models’ success in text generation has also made them better at code generation and coding tasks. While a lot of work has demonstrated their remarkable performance on tasks such as code completion and editing, it is still unclear as to why. We help bridge this gap by exploring to what degree auto-regressive models understand the logical constructs of the underlying programs. We propose Counterfactual Analysis for Programming Concept Predicates (CACP) as a counterfactual testing framework to evaluate whether Large Code Models understand programming concepts. With only black-box access to the model, we use CACP to evaluate ten popular Large Code Models for four different programming concepts. Our findings suggest that current models lack understanding of concepts such as data flow and control flow.

paragraphs: Strong code completion and editing performance leaves an underlying question unanswered: how well do code models understand the logical constructs in the programs they process? This paper investigates that question directly. Its focus is the degree of programming concept understanding exhibited by autoregressive models, rather than their success at producing code alone.

The authors introduce Counterfactual Analysis for Programming Concept Predicates, abbreviated CACP. It is a testing framework that uses counterfactual analysis to evaluate programming concepts. The method needs only black-box access to a model, so the evaluation does not depend on inspecting its internal representations or parameters. This makes the proposed test applicable through the model’s observable behavior.

Using CACP, the authors evaluate ten popular large code models on four programming concepts. Their findings suggest that current models lack understanding of concepts including data flow and control flow. The result is evidence about conceptual understanding under this evaluation, and it explains why impressive coding task performance alone does not settle the question of whether a model grasps program logic.
summary.tldr: Black-box counterfactual tests of ten code models suggest gaps in understanding programming concepts such as data flow and control flow.

title: Do Large Code Models Understand Programming Concepts? Counterfactual Analysis for Code Predicates

abstract: Model inversion, which aims to reconstruct the original training data from pre-trained discriminative models, is especially useful when the original training data is unavailable due to privacy, usage rights, or size constraints. However, existing dense inversion methods attempt to reconstruct the entire image area, making them extremely inefficient when inverting high-resolution images from large-scale Vision Transformers (ViTs). We further identify two underlying causes of this inefficiency: the redundant inversion of noisy backgrounds and the unintended inversion of spurious correlations—a phenomenon we term “hallucination” in model inversion. To address these limitations, we propose a novel sparse model inversion strategy, as a plug-and-play extension to speed up existing dense inversion methods with no need for modifying their original loss functions. Specifically, we selectively invert semantic foregrounds while stopping the inversion of noisy backgrounds and potential spurious correlations. Through both theoretical and empirical studies, we validate the efficacy of our approach in achieving significant inversion acceleration (up to $\times$3.79) while maintaining comparable or even enhanced downstream performance in data-free model quantization and data-free knowledge transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/Egg-Hu/SMI.

paragraphs: Model inversion seeks to reconstruct training data from a pretrained discriminative model when the original data is unavailable. For large vision transformers and high-resolution images, reconstructing every image region can be costly. This paper identifies wasted effort in noisy backgrounds and in spurious correlations that it calls inversion hallucinations.

Sparse Model Inversion focuses reconstruction on semantic foregrounds while stopping work on noisy backgrounds and potential spurious correlations. It is designed as an extension to existing dense inversion procedures and does not require changes to their original loss functions. The approach changes which parts of the image receive inversion effort.

Theoretical and empirical studies support the method, with reported acceleration reaching 3.79 times. Downstream results in data-free model quantization and knowledge transfer remain comparable or improve. This matters because faster reconstruction is useful only if the generated data still serves its intended purpose. The stated results suggest that selectively reconstructing meaningful foreground content can save substantial computation while preserving the usefulness of inverted data for those applications.
summary.tldr: Sparse Model Inversion accelerates image reconstruction by focusing on semantic foregrounds while preserving or improving performance in tested data-free applications.

title: Sparse Model Inversion: Efficient Inversion of Vision Transformers for Data-Free Applications

abstract: Despite the impressive capabilities of large language models (LLMs) across diverse applications, they still suffer from trustworthiness issues, such as hallucinations and misalignments. Retrieval-augmented language models (RAG) have been proposed to enhance the credibility of generations by grounding external knowledge, but the theoretical understandings of their generation risks remains unexplored. In this paper, we answer: 1) whether RAG can indeed lead to low generation risks, 2) how to provide provable guarantees on the generation risks of RAG and vanilla LLMs, and 3) what sufficient conditions enable RAG models to reduce generation risks. We propose C-RAG, the first framework to certify generation risks for RAG models. Specifically, we provide conformal risk analysis for RAG models and certify an upper confidence bound of generation risks, which we refer to as conformal generation risk. We also provide theoretical guarantees on conformal generation risks for general bounded risk functions under test distribution shifts. We prove that RAG achieves a lower conformal generation risk than that of a single LLM when the quality of the retrieval model and transformer is non-trivial. Our intensive empirical results demonstrate the soundness and tightness of our conformal generation risk guarantees across four widely-used NLP datasets on four state-of-the-art retrieval models.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented language models use external information to support their answers, but grounding an answer does not by itself quantify its risk. This paper develops C-RAG to provide a statistical certificate for generation risk. It asks both how to bound that risk and when retrieval can provably improve the bound relative to a language model operating alone.

C-RAG uses conformal risk analysis to establish an upper confidence bound, called conformal generation risk. The framework accommodates general bounded risk functions and includes theoretical guarantees under shifts in the test distribution. This makes the contribution broader than a guarantee tied to one particular way of measuring problematic generations.

The authors prove a lower conformal generation risk for retrieval augmentation when the retrieval model and transformer satisfy a non-trivial quality condition. That condition is central: the result establishes sufficient circumstances for improvement. Experiments across four NLP datasets and four retrieval models support the soundness and tightness of the reported bounds, suggesting that the certificates can be informative as well as theoretically justified.
summary.tldr: C-RAG certifies upper bounds on generation risk and identifies sufficient quality conditions under which retrieval augmentation improves those bounds.

title: C-RAG: Certified Generation Risks for Retrieval-Augmented Language Models

abstract: This paper studies clustering algorithms for dynamically evolving graphs $\{G_t\}$, in which new edges (and potential new vertices) are added into a graph, and the underlying cluster structure of the graph can gradually change. The paper proves that, under some mild condition on the cluster-structure, the clusters of the final graph $G_T$ of $n_T$ vertices at time $T$ can be well approximated by a dynamic variant of the spectral clustering algorithm. The algorithm runs in amortised update time $O(1)$ and query time $o(n_T)$. Experimental studies on both synthetic and real-world datasets further confirm the practicality of our designed algorithm.

The paper proves that, under some mild condition on the cluster-structure, the clusters of the final graph $G_T$ of $n_T$ vertices at time $T$ can be well approximated by a dynamic variant of the spectral clustering algorithm. paragraphs: The paper studies clustering when a graph grows over time. New edges arrive, new vertices may appear, and the communities underlying the graph can gradually change. The goal is to keep track of that evolving cluster structure efficiently while retaining a mathematical guarantee about the quality of the resulting approximation.

The proposed method is a dynamic version of spectral clustering. Under a condition on the graph's cluster structure, described by the authors as mild, they prove that it can closely approximate the clusters of the final graph. The guarantee therefore accommodates gradual structural change, while depending on the stated cluster-structure condition.

The algorithm has constant amortized update time, meaning its update cost averages to a constant across a sequence of changes. Its query time grows sublinearly with the number of vertices in the final graph. These are distinct guarantees for maintaining information and answering queries. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets further support the method's practicality, connecting its theoretical efficiency to tested uses on evolving graphs.
summary.tldr: A dynamic spectral clustering method provides conditional approximation guarantees with constant amortized updates and sublinear query time.

title: Dynamic Spectral Clustering with Provable Approximation Guarantee

abstract: Dataset distillation aims to synthesize a small number of images per class (IPC) from a large dataset to approximate full dataset training with minimal performance loss. While effective in very small IPC ranges, many distillation methods become less effective, even underperforming random sample selection, as IPC increases. Our examination of state-of-the-art trajectory-matching based distillation methods across various IPC scales reveals that these methods struggle to incorporate the complex, rare features of harder samples into the synthetic dataset even with the increased IPC, resulting in a persistent coverage gap between easy and hard test samples. Motivated by such observations, we introduce SelMatch, a novel distillation method that effectively scales with IPC. SelMatch uses selection-based initialization and partial updates through trajectory matching to manage the synthetic dataset’s desired difficulty level tailored to IPC scales. When tested on CIFAR-10/100 and TinyImageNet, SelMatch consistently outperforms leading selection-only and distillation-only methods across subset ratios from 5% to 30%.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation creates a small image collection intended to approximate training on a much larger dataset. Yet increasing the number of images per class does not always improve existing methods effectively; some can fall below random sample selection. This paper investigates why trajectory-matching distillation struggles as the available distilled dataset grows.

The authors find that these methods have difficulty incorporating the complex, uncommon features found in harder examples. As a result, a coverage gap between easy and hard test samples persists even with more images. SelMatch addresses this through selection-based initialization and partial updates using trajectory matching, adjusting the desired difficulty of the synthetic dataset to its size.

Evaluations on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet show consistent gains over leading selection-only and distillation-only approaches for subset sizes from five to thirty percent. The results suggest that allocating more examples is useful when the method also preserves and incorporates challenging information. SelMatch's contribution is to combine sample selection with controlled distillation updates to improve scaling across those dataset sizes.
summary.tldr: SelMatch combines selected initialization with partial distillation updates to better capture difficult examples as distilled datasets grow.

title: SelMatch: Effectively Scaling Up Dataset Distillation via Selection-Based Initialization and Partial Updates by Trajectory Matching

abstract: Recommender system aims to recommend items or information that may interest users based on their behaviors and preferences. However, there may be sampling selection bias in the data collection process, i.e., the collected data is not a representative of the target population. Many debiasing methods are developed based on pseudo-labelings. Nevertheless, the validity of these methods relies heavily on accurate pseudo-labelings (i.e., the imputed labels), which is difficult to satisfy in practice. In this paper, we theoretically propose several novel doubly robust estimators that are unbiased when either (a) the pseudo-labelings deviate from the true labels with an arbitrary user-specific inductive bias, item-specific inductive bias, or a combination of both, or (b) the learned propensities are accurate. We further propose a propensity reconstruction learning approach that adaptively updates the constraint weights using an attention mechanism and effectively controls the variance. Extensive experiments show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art on one semi-synthetic and three real-world datasets.

Many debiasing methods are developed based on pseudo-labelings. Nevertheless, the validity of these methods relies heavily on accurate pseudo-labelings (i.e., the imputed labels), which is difficult to satisfy in practice. In this paper, we theoretically propose several novel doubly robust estimators that are unbiased when either (a) the pseudo-labelings deviate from the true labels with an arbitrary user-specific inductive bias, item-specific inductive bias, or a combination of both, or (b) the learned propensities are accurate. We further propose a propensity reconstruction learning approach that adaptively updates the constraint weights using an attention mechanism and effectively controls the variance. Extensive experiments show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art on one semi-synthetic and three real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Recommendation data can be biased because observed user behavior does not represent the target population. Some correction methods fill in missing labels, but their validity depends heavily on those imputed labels being accurate. This paper develops estimators that tolerate particular forms of systematic imputation error while preserving an unbiasedness guarantee.

The proposed doubly robust estimators are unbiased under either of two conditions. One permits arbitrary user-specific bias, item-specific bias, or a combination of both in the imputed labels. The other requires accurate learned propensities. The relaxation concerns these specified forms of bias; it does not make unrestricted imputation errors harmless.

The authors also introduce propensity reconstruction learning, using attention to adaptively update constraint weights and control variance. Experiments on one semi-synthetic dataset and three real-world datasets show improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines a weaker imputation requirement with a practical training approach, addressing both the validity of bias correction and the variability that can complicate its use in collaborative filtering.
summary.tldr: New doubly robust estimators tolerate specified user- and item-dependent imputation biases or remain unbiased when learned propensities are accurate.

title: Relaxing the Accurate Imputation Assumption in Doubly Robust Learning for Debiased Collaborative Filtering

abstract: Mastering multiple tasks through exploration and learning in an environment poses a significant challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Unsupervised RL has been introduced to address this challenge by training policies with intrinsic rewards rather than extrinsic rewards. However, current intrinsic reward designs and unsupervised RL algorithms often overlook the heterogeneous nature of collected samples, thereby diminishing their sample efficiency. To overcome this limitation, in this paper, we proposed a reward-free RL algorithm called GFA-RFE. The key idea behind our algorithm is an uncertainty-aware intrinsic reward for exploring the environment and an uncertainty-weighted learning process to handle heterogeneous uncertainty in different samples. Theoretically, we show that in order to find an $\epsilon$-optimal policy, GFA-RFE needs to collect $\tilde{O} (H^2 \log N_{\mathcal{F}} (\epsilon) \text{dim} (\mathcal{F}) / \epsilon^2 )$ number of episodes, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the value function class with covering number $N_{\mathcal{F}} (\epsilon)$ and generalized eluder dimension $\text{dim} (\mathcal{F})$. Such a result outperforms all existing reward-free RL algorithms. We further implement and evaluate GFA-RFE across various domains and tasks in the DeepMind Control Suite. Experiment results show that GFA-RFE outperforms or is comparable to the performance of state-of-the-art unsupervised RL algorithms.

paragraphs: Reward-free reinforcement learning explores an environment without relying on task-specific external rewards during exploration. The resulting experience can support learning for multiple tasks. This paper argues that existing approaches often overlook differences in uncertainty among collected samples, reducing how efficiently they use experience.

An uncertainty-aware intrinsic reward guides exploration, while an uncertainty-weighted learning process handles samples with different uncertainty levels. This connects the choice of what experience to collect with the treatment of that experience during learning. The approach uses a general value-function class, allowing the theoretical analysis to express complexity through properties of that class.

The stated episode bound scales with the square of the horizon, the logarithm of the function class’s covering number, and its generalized eluder dimension, divided by the square of the target error, up to suppressed logarithmic factors. The authors report an improvement over existing reward-free bounds. Across DeepMind Control Suite domains and tasks, GFA-RFE outperforms or matches state-of-the-art unsupervised reinforcement-learning methods, supporting the practical value of accounting for heterogeneous uncertainty.
summary.tldr: GFA-RFE uses uncertainty to guide exploration and weight learning, improving the stated sample-complexity bound and achieving competitive empirical performance.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Reward-Free Exploration with General Function Approximation

abstract: A current limitation of video generative video models is that they generate plausible looking frames, but poor motion — an issue that is not well captured by FVD and other popular methods for evaluating generated videos. Here we go beyond FVD by developing a metric which better measures plausible object interactions and motion. Our novel approach is based on auto-encoding point tracks and yields motion features that can be used to not only compare distributions of videos (as few as one generated and one ground truth, or as many as two datasets), but also for evaluating motion of single videos. We show that using point tracks instead of pixel reconstruction or action recognition features results in a metric which is markedly more sensitive to temporal distortions in synthetic data, and can predict human evaluations of temporal consistency and realism in generated videos obtained from open-source models better than a wide range of alternatives. We also show that by using a point track representation, we can spatiotemporally localize generative video inconsistencies, providing extra interpretability of generated video errors relative to prior work. An overview of the results and link to the code can be found on the project page: trajan-paper.github.io.

Its central choice is to represent motion through point tracks, following positions through a video.

The method learns motion features by auto-encoding those tracks. These features support comparisons ranging from one generated video against one ground-truth video to comparisons between entire datasets. They can also assess the motion of a single video. This gives the representation uses beyond a single aggregate score comparing two collections of clips.

They also better predict human judgments of temporal consistency and realism for videos from open-source generators than a wide range of alternatives. Because the representation retains where and when motion occurs, it can localize inconsistencies in space and time, helping explain the errors behind an assessment.
summary.tldr: A point-track-based video metric better captures motion errors and human judgments while locating inconsistencies in space and time.

title: Direct Motion Models for Assessing Generated Videos

abstract: We present an approach to model-based RL that achieves a new state of the art performance on the challenging Craftax-classic benchmark, an open-world 2D survival game that requires agents to exhibit a wide range of general abilities—such as strong generalization, deep exploration, and long-term reasoning. With a series of careful design choices aimed at improving sample efficiency, our MBRL algorithm achieves a reward of 69.66% after only 1M environment steps, significantly outperforming DreamerV3, which achieves $53.2%$, and, for the first time, exceeds human performance of 65.0%. Our method starts by constructing a SOTA model-free baseline, using a novel policy architecture that combines CNNs and RNNs. We then add three improvements to the standard MBRL setup: (a) "Dyna with warmup", which trains the policy on real and imaginary data, (b) "nearest neighbor tokenizer" on image patches, which improves the scheme to create the transformer world model (TWM) inputs, and (c) "block teacher forcing", which allows the TWM to reason jointly about the future tokens of the next timestep.

paragraphs: This paper improves model-based reinforcement learning for Craftax-classic, an open-world survival game requiring exploration, generalization, and long-term reasoning. The approach targets sample efficiency: learning strong behavior from a limited number of interactions with the environment. It begins with a strong model-free policy architecture that combines convolutional and recurrent neural networks.

The authors then introduce three changes to the model-based setup. Dyna with warmup trains the policy using both real experience and imagined data. A nearest-neighbor tokenizer changes how image patches become inputs to the transformer world model. Block teacher forcing allows that world model to reason jointly about the future tokens belonging to the next timestep.

After one million environment steps, the method reaches a reported reward of 69.66%, compared with 53.2% for DreamerV3 and 65.0% for human performance. The authors describe this as a new state of the art and the first result above human performance on the benchmark. The findings connect improvements in policy design, imagined training, and world-model representation to more efficient learning in this setting.
summary.tldr: Policy and transformer world-model improvements achieve 69.66% reward on Craftax-classic after one million environment steps, exceeding the reported human benchmark.

title: Improving Transformer World Models for Data-Efficient RL

abstract: A fundamental challenge in formal theorem proving by LLMs is the lack of high-quality training data. Although reinforcement learning or expert iteration partially mitigates this issue by alternating between LLM generating proofs and finetuning them on correctly generated ones, performance quickly plateaus due to the scarcity of correct proofs (sparse rewards). To keep improving the models with limited data, we draw inspiration from mathematicians, who continuously develop new results, partly by proposing novel conjectures or exercises (which are often variants of known results) and attempting to solve them. We design the Self-play Theorem Prover (STP) that simultaneously takes on two roles, conjecturer and prover, each providing training signals to the other. The conjecturer is trained iteratively on previously generated conjectures that are barely provable by the current prover, which incentivizes it to generate increasingly challenging conjectures over time. The prover attempts to prove the conjectures with standard expert iteration. We evaluate STP with both Lean and Isabelle formal versifiers. With 51.3 billion tokens generated during the training in Lean, STP proves 28.5% of the statements in the LeanWorkbook dataset, doubling the previous best result of 13.1% achieved through expert iteration. The final model achieves state-of-the-art performance among whole-proof generation methods on miniF2F-test (65.0%), ProofNet-test (23.9%) and PutnamBench (8/644) with pass@3200.

summary.tldr: STP improves formal theorem proving through self-play between a conjecturer that proposes challenging statements and a prover that learns to solve them.

title: STP: Self-play LLM Theorem Provers with Iterative Conjecturing and Proving

abstract: Motivated by applications in online bidding and sleeping bandits, we examine the problem of contextual bandits with cross learning, where the learner observes the loss associated with the action across all possible contexts, not just the current round’s context. Our focus is on a setting where losses are chosen adversarially, and contexts are sampled i.i.d. from a specific distribution. This problem was first studied by Balseiro et al. (2019), who proposed an algorithm that achieves near-optimal regret under the assumption that the context distribution is known in advance. However, this assumption is often unrealistic. To address this issue, Schneider & Zimmert (2023) recently proposed a new algorithm that achieves nearly optimal expected regret. It is well-known that expected regret can be significantly weaker than high-probability bounds. In this paper, we present a novel, in-depth analysis of their algorithm and demonstrate that it actually achieves near-optimal regret with high probability. There are steps in the original analysis by Schneider & Zimmert (2023) that lead only to an expected bound by nature. In our analysis, we introduce several new insights. Specifically, we make extensive use of the weak dependency structure between different epochs, which was overlooked in previous analyses. Additionally, standard martingale inequalities are not directly applicable, so we refine martingale inequalities to complete our analysis.

paragraphs: In contextual bandits with cross learning, choosing an action reveals its loss across every possible context, not just the context currently encountered. The paper studies adversarially chosen losses with contexts sampled independently from a fixed distribution. That distribution is unknown to the learner, removing an assumption used in earlier near-optimal results.

An existing algorithm already achieves nearly optimal expected regret in this setting. This paper strengthens the understanding of that same algorithm by showing near-optimal regret with high probability. The distinction matters because an average guarantee can coexist with substantially worse outcomes on some runs, whereas a high-probability result controls how often poor outcomes occur.

The new analysis uses weak dependencies between different epochs that earlier arguments did not exploit. It also refines martingale inequalities because standard versions cannot be applied directly. The contribution is therefore a stronger reliability guarantee supported by new proof techniques, rather than a replacement learning algorithm. The result remains tied to the stated assumptions about adversarial losses and independently sampled contexts.
summary.tldr: A new analysis upgrades an existing cross-learning bandit algorithm from near-optimal expected regret to a near-optimal high-probability guarantee.

title: High Probability Bound for Cross-Learning Contextual Bandits with Unknown Context Distributions

abstract: In two-sided platforms (e.g., video streaming or e-commerce), viewers and providers engage in interactive dynamics: viewers benefit from increases in provider populations, while providers benefit from increases in viewer population. Despite the importance of such “population effects” on long-term platform health, recommendation policies do not generally take the participation dynamics into account. This paper thus studies the dynamics and recommender policy design on two-sided platforms under the population effects for the first time. Our control- and game-theoretic findings warn against the use of the standard “myopic-greedy” policy and shed light on the importance of provider-side considerations (i.e., effectively distributing exposure among provider groups) to improve social welfare via population growth. We also present a simple algorithm to optimize long-term social welfare by taking the population effects into account, and demonstrate its effectiveness in synthetic and real-data experiments. Our experiment code is available at https://github.com/sdean-group/dynamics-two-sided-market.

paragraphs: On a two-sided platform, viewers and providers influence each other’s reasons to participate. More providers can benefit viewers, while more viewers can benefit providers. This paper studies how recommendation policies should account for those population effects when the objective is the platform’s long-term social welfare.

The analysis uses control and game theory to examine participation dynamics. Its findings warn against a myopic-greedy policy that prioritizes immediate gains. They also emphasize how exposure is distributed among provider groups: recommendation choices affect the provider side, which can influence population growth and, through that growth, the welfare of both sides.

The authors introduce a simple algorithm that incorporates population effects when optimizing long-term social welfare. Synthetic experiments and experiments using real data demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution broadens the recommendation objective to include how current decisions shape future participation. In this view, allocating exposure is part of managing an evolving interaction between the two populations, with consequences that extend beyond the immediate benefit of an individual recommendation.
summary.tldr: Accounting for how recommendations influence viewer and provider participation can improve long-term platform welfare, with provider exposure playing a central role.

title: Policy Design for Two-sided Platforms with Participation Dynamics

abstract: As Diffusion Models (DM) generate increasingly realistic images, related issues such as copyright and misuse have become a growing concern. Watermarking is one of the promising solutions. Existing methods inject the watermark into the single-domain of initial Gaussian noise for generation, which suffers from unsatisfactory robustness. This paper presents the first dual-domain DM watermarking approach using a pipelined injector to consistently embed watermarks in both the spatial and frequency domains. To further boost robustness against certain image manipulations and advanced attacks, we introduce a model-independent learnable Gaussian Noise Restorer (GNR) to refine Gaussian noise extracted from manipulated images and enhance detection robustness by integrating the detection scores of both watermarks. GaussMarker efficiently achieves state-of-the-art performance under eight image distortions and four advanced attacks across three versions of Stable Diffusion with better recall and lower false positive rates, as preferred in real applications.

paragraphs: Watermarks can help identify images produced by diffusion models, but image modifications can make those marks difficult to detect. Existing approaches embed a watermark in one domain of the initial Gaussian noise used for generation. GaussMarker instead embeds watermarks in both spatial and frequency domains through a coordinated injection pipeline.

The detection process also includes a learned Gaussian Noise Restorer. It refines noise recovered from manipulated images, aiming to recover a more useful detection signal. This component is model-independent, and the method combines detection scores from both watermarks to strengthen robustness against certain modifications and advanced attacks.

The authors evaluate GaussMarker across three versions of Stable Diffusion, eight image distortions, and four advanced attacks. They report efficient state-of-the-art performance with better recall and lower false positive rates. Those two outcomes matter together: more watermarked images are detected while fewer unwatermarked images are incorrectly flagged. The results support combining complementary watermark domains with noise restoration for the tested detection conditions.
summary.tldr: GaussMarker combines spatial and frequency watermarks with learned noise restoration to improve detection after image distortions and attacks.

title: GaussMarker: Robust Dual-Domain Watermark for Diffusion Models

abstract: This paper proposes Constrained Exploitability Descent (CED), a model-free offline reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm for solving adversarial Markov games (MGs). CED combines the game-theoretical approach of Exploitability Descent (ED) with policy constraint methods from offline RL. While policy constraints can perturb the optimal pure-strategy solutions in single-agent scenarios, we find the side effect less detrimental in adversarial games, where the optimal policy can be a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium. We theoretically prove that, under the uniform coverage assumption on the dataset, CED converges to a stationary point in deterministic two-player zero-sum Markov games. We further prove that the min-player policy at the stationary point follows the property of mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium in MGs. Compared to the model-based ED method that optimizes the max-player policy, our CED method no longer relies on a generalized gradient. Experiments in matrix games, a tree-form game, and an infinite-horizon soccer game verify that CED can find an equilibrium policy for the min-player as long as the offline dataset guarantees uniform coverage. Besides, CED achieves a significantly lower NashConv compared to an existing pessimism-based method and can gradually improve the behavior policy even under non-uniform data coverages. When combined with neural networks, CED also outperforms behavior cloning and offline self-play in a large-scale two-team robotic combat game.

paragraphs: Constrained Exploitability Descent, or CED, learns strategies for adversarial Markov games from an existing dataset without building an environment model. It combines exploitability descent with policy constraints from offline reinforcement learning. The authors argue that these constraints can be less harmful in adversarial games, where an optimal solution may randomize among actions, than in single-agent problems with optimal pure strategies.

The theoretical guarantees depend on uniform dataset coverage and deterministic, two-player, zero-sum Markov games. Under those conditions, CED converges to a stationary point, and the minimizing player's policy there has the stated mixed-strategy Nash-equilibrium property. Under non-uniform coverage, CED can still progressively improve the behavior policy. With neural networks, it also outperforms behavior cloning and offline self-play in a large two-team robotic combat game.
summary.tldr: CED combines offline policy constraints with exploitability descent, with equilibrium-related guarantees under uniform coverage in deterministic two-player zero-sum games.

title: Constrained Exploitability Descent: An Offline Reinforcement Learning Method for Finding Mixed-Strategy Nash Equilibrium

abstract: Standard multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithms are vulnerable to sim-to-real gaps. To address this, distributionally robust Markov games (RMGs) have been proposed to enhance robustness in MARL by optimizing the worst-case performance when game dynamics shift within a prescribed uncertainty set. RMGs remains under-explored, from reasonable problem formulation to the development of sample-efficient algorithms. Two notorious and open challenges are the formulation of the uncertainty set and whether the corresponding RMGs can overcome the curse of multiagency, where the sample complexity scales exponentially with the number of agents. In this work, we propose a natural class of RMGs inspired by behavioral economics, where each agent’s uncertainty set is shaped by both the environment and the integrated behavior of other agents. We first establish the well-posedness of this class of RMGs by proving the existence of game-theoretic solutions such as robust Nash equilibria and coarse correlated equilibria (CCE). Assuming access to a generative model, we then introduce a sample-efficient algorithm for learning the CCE whose sample complexity scales polynomially with all relevant parameters. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm to break the curse of multiagency for RMGs, regardless of the uncertainty set formulation.

paragraphs: Multi-agent reinforcement learning can fail when the environment differs from the one used for training. Robust Markov games address this by optimizing performance under the worst dynamics allowed by a specified uncertainty set. A central difficulty is choosing that set while avoiding sample requirements that grow exponentially with the number of agents.

The paper proposes a class of games in which each agent's uncertainty reflects both the environment and the combined behavior of other agents. The formulation draws inspiration from behavioral economics. The authors prove that robust Nash equilibria and coarse correlated equilibria exist, establishing that the proposed games have meaningful game-theoretic solutions.

Assuming access to a generative model, the authors then provide an algorithm for learning a coarse correlated equilibrium with sample complexity polynomial in all relevant parameters. For this formulation and access assumption, the result avoids exponential scaling with agent count. The authors describe it as the first such result for robust Markov games, to their knowledge; the algorithmic guarantee concerns coarse correlated equilibria specifically.
summary.tldr: A new robust Markov-game formulation admits equilibrium learning with polynomial sample complexity, assuming access to a generative model.

title: Breaking the Curse of Multiagency in Robust Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) plays a crucial role in domains such as knowledge-based visual question answering (KB-VQA), where models should effectively integrate additional knowledge to generate a response. However, existing vision and language models (VLMs) are not inherently designed for context-augmented generation, limiting their effectiveness in such tasks. While synthetic data generation has recently gained attention for training large VLMs, its application for context-augmented generation remains underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce SKVQA, a large-scale synthetic multimodal dataset containing over 2 million visual question-answer pairs, each associated with external knowledge sources to determine the final answer. Compared to previous datasets, SKVQA exhibits 11$\times$ more unique questions, greater domain diversity, and a broader spectrum of image sources. Through human evaluations, we confirm the high quality of the generated question-answer pairs and their contextual relevance. Extensive experiments show that SKVQA serves both as a challenging benchmark for knowledge-based VQA and as an effective training resource for adapting generative multimodal models to context-augmented generation. Our results further indicate that models trained on SKVQA demonstrate enhanced generalization in both context-aware VQA and multimodal RAG settings.

paragraphs: Some visual questions require both an image and outside knowledge. Models must learn to integrate that added context, yet vision-language models are not inherently designed for this form of generation. summary.tldr: SKVQA supplies over two million synthetic visual question-answer pairs with external knowledge to train and evaluate context-aware multimodal models.

title: SK-VQA: Synthetic Knowledge Generation at Scale for Training Context-Augmented Multimodal LLMs

abstract: Learning-to-optimize leverages machine learning to accelerate optimization algorithms. While empirical results show tremendous improvements compared to classical optimization algorithms, theoretical guarantees are mostly lacking, such that the outcome cannot be reliably assured. Especially, convergence is hardly studied in learning-to-optimize, because conventional convergence guarantees in optimization are based on geometric arguments, which cannot be applied easily to learned algorithms. Thus, we develop a probabilistic framework that resembles classical optimization and allows for transferring geometric arguments into learning-to-optimize. Based on our new proof-strategy, our main theorem is a generalization result for parametric classes of potentially non-smooth, non-convex loss functions and establishes the convergence of learned optimization algorithms to critical points with high probability. This effectively generalizes the results of a worst-case analysis into a probabilistic framework, and frees the design of the learned algorithm from using safeguards.

paragraphs: Learning-to-optimize trains algorithms to carry out optimization more effectively. Although these learned algorithms can deliver substantial empirical improvements, their convergence is harder to justify theoretically. Classical convergence proofs often depend on geometric properties of the optimization process, and those arguments do not transfer easily to algorithms whose behavior is learned.

The paper develops a probabilistic framework that retains enough of the structure of classical optimization to reuse geometric reasoning. Its new proof strategy supports a generalization theorem for parameterized families of loss functions, including losses that may be non-smooth or non-convex. The theorem establishes convergence of learned optimization algorithms to critical points with high probability.

This provides a way to connect learned optimization behavior with mathematical convergence guarantees beyond the cases directly analyzed during design. The result concerns critical points rather than a claim of finding globally optimal solutions. By recasting worst-case reasoning probabilistically, the framework also allows learned algorithms to be designed without the safeguards that would otherwise constrain their construction.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic framework establishes high-probability convergence to critical points for learned optimizers across parameterized loss families.

title: A Generalization Result for Convergence in Learning-to-Optimize

abstract: Modern policy gradient algorithms, such as TRPO and PPO, outperform vanilla policy gradient in many RL tasks. Questioning the common belief that enforcing approximate trust regions leads to steady policy improvement in practice, we show that the more critical factor is the enhanced value estimation accuracy from more value update steps in each iteration. To demonstrate, we show that by simply increasing the number of value update steps per iteration, vanilla policy gradient itself can achieve performance comparable to or better than PPO in all the standard continuous control benchmark environments. Importantly, this simple change to vanilla policy gradient is significantly more robust to hyperparameter choices, opening up the possibility that RL algorithms may still become more effective and easier to use.

paragraphs: This paper revisits why modern policy gradient methods often outperform vanilla policy gradient. A common explanation emphasizes approximately restricting how much the policy changes at each update. The authors question that account and investigate another difference: how much effort each iteration spends improving estimates of the value of states or behavior.

Their intervention is straightforward: increase the number of value estimation updates per iteration while using vanilla policy gradient. The study identifies the resulting improvement in value accuracy as a more critical factor in practical performance than the approximate trust-region explanation it examines. This focuses attention on the quality of the estimates supporting policy learning, rather than only the rule used to change the policy.

Across the standard continuous-control benchmark environments evaluated, the modified vanilla method matches or exceeds PPO. The authors also report substantially greater robustness to hyperparameter choices. These findings suggest that a simple allocation of more updates to value estimation can materially improve a basic algorithm, opening a possible route toward reinforcement learning methods that are both effective and easier to tune.
summary.tldr: More value estimation updates let vanilla policy gradient match or outperform PPO on the evaluated continuous-control benchmarks with greater tuning robustness.

title: Improving Value Estimation Critically Enhances Vanilla Policy Gradient

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are considered promising energy-efficient models due to their dynamic capability to process spatial-temporal spike information. Existing work has demonstrated that SNNs exhibit temporal heterogeneity, which leads to diverse outputs of SNNs at different time steps and has the potential to enhance their performance. Although SNNs obtained by direct training methods achieve state-of-the-art performance, current methods introduce limited temporal heterogeneity through the dynamics of spiking neurons or network structures. They lack the improvement of temporal heterogeneity through the lens of the gradient. In this paper, we first conclude that the diversity of the temporal logit gradients in current methods is limited. This leads to insufficient temporal heterogeneity and results in temporally miscalibrated SNNs with degraded performance. Based on the above analysis, we propose a Temporal Model Calibration (TMC) method, which can be seen as a logit gradient rescaling mechanism across time steps. Experimental results show that our method can improve the temporal logit gradient diversity and generate temporally calibrated SNNs with enhanced performance. In particular, our method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on ImageNet, DVSCIFAR10, and N-Caltech101. Codes are available at https://github.com/zju-bmi-lab/TMC.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks produce outputs across multiple time steps, and variation between those outputs can support better performance. Existing training methods create some temporal diversity through neuron dynamics and architecture. This paper argues that limited diversity in the gradients of temporal logits leaves another source of useful variation underused.

Temporal Model Calibration rescales logit gradients across time steps. The authors connect insufficient gradient diversity to temporal miscalibration, then design the rescaling mechanism to improve both. This targets the training signal directly rather than relying only on a different spiking-neuron model or network structure.

Experiments show greater temporal gradient diversity and better-performing, temporally calibrated networks. The method reaches state-of-the-art accuracy on ImageNet, DVSCIFAR10, and N-Caltech101 in the reported comparisons. The contribution concerns training quality and accuracy; although spiking networks are motivated partly by energy efficiency, the abstract does not report a measured energy reduction from this calibration procedure.
summary.tldr: Temporal Model Calibration rescales gradients across time to improve spiking-network diversity, calibration, and benchmark accuracy.

title: Training High Performance Spiking Neural Network by Temporal Model Calibration

abstract: As scaling large language models faces prohibitive costs, multi-agent systems emerge as a promising alternative, though challenged by static knowledge assumptions and coordination inefficiencies. We introduce Knowledge-Aware Bayesian Bandits (KABB), a novel framework that enhances multi-agent system coordination through semantic understanding and dynamic adaptation. The framework features three key innovations: a customized knowledge distance model for deep semantic understanding, a dual-adaptation mechanism for continuous expert optimization, and a knowledge-aware Thompson Sampling strategy for efficient expert selection. Extensive evaluation demonstrates KABB achieves an optimal cost-performance balance, maintaining high performance while keeping computational demands relatively low in multi-agent coordination.

The framework features three key innovations: a customized knowledge distance model for deep semantic understanding, a dual-adaptation mechanism for continuous expert optimization, and a knowledge-aware Thompson Sampling strategy for efficient expert selection. Extensive evaluation demonstrates KABB achieves an optimal cost-performance balance, maintaining high performance while keeping computational demands relatively low in multi-agent coordination.

paragraphs: Using multiple expert agents is a promising alternative to continually scaling a single large language model, but coordination can become a source of inefficiency. A coordinating system must decide which experts to involve while accounting for what they know. This paper addresses weaknesses in coordination approaches that assume knowledge is static or do not adapt expert selection effectively.

Knowledge-Aware Bayesian Bandits, or KABB, combines three components. A customized knowledge-distance model supplies semantic information for coordination. A dual-adaptation mechanism supports continuous expert optimization. A knowledge-aware Thompson Sampling strategy handles expert selection. Together, these components connect the representation of expert knowledge with an adaptive process for deciding which experts to use.

The reported evaluation finds an optimal cost-performance balance, maintaining high performance with relatively low computational demands in multi-agent coordination. The significance is the connection between semantic understanding and ongoing adaptation: the framework uses knowledge information within the selection process itself. Its stated findings support this combination as a way to coordinate experts efficiently in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: KABB combines semantic knowledge modeling, expert adaptation, and Bayesian selection to improve the cost-performance balance of multi-agent coordination.

title: KABB: Knowledge-Aware Bayesian Bandits for Dynamic Expert Coordination in Multi-Agent Systems

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) recently showed strong capacity in integrating data among multiple modalities, empowered by generalizable attention architecture. Advanced methods predominantly focus on language-centric tuning while less exploring multimodal tokens mixed through attention, posing challenges in high-level tasks that require fine-grained cognition and emotion understanding. In this work, we identify the attention deficit disorder problem in multimodal learning, caused by inconsistent cross-modal attention and layer-by-layer decayed attention activation. To address this, we propose a novel attention mechanism, termed MOdular Duplex Attention (MODA), simultaneously conducting the inner-modal refinement and inter-modal interaction. MODA employs a correct-after-align strategy to effectively decouple modality alignment from cross-layer token mixing. In the alignment phase, tokens are mapped to duplex modality spaces based on the basis vectors, enabling the interaction between visual and language modality. Further, the correctness of attention scores is ensured through adaptive masked attention, which enhances the model’s flexibility by allowing customizable masking patterns for different modalities. Extensive experiments on 21 benchmark datasets verify the effectiveness of MODA in perception, cognition, and emotion tasks.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models must combine visual and language information through attention. This paper identifies two problems in that process: inconsistent attention across modalities and attention activation that weakens across layers. The authors argue that these problems hinder tasks involving detailed cognition and emotion understanding, areas that language-centered tuning has explored less directly.

MODA addresses both refinement within a modality and interaction between modalities. Its correct-after-align strategy separates modality alignment from token mixing across layers. During alignment, basis vectors map tokens into duplex modality spaces so that visual and language information can interact. Adaptive masked attention then corrects attention scores using masking patterns that can be customized for different modalities.

The authors evaluate MODA on twenty-one benchmark datasets spanning perception, cognition, and emotion tasks, reporting evidence of its effectiveness. The approach makes the handling of multimodal tokens an explicit architectural concern. Its significance is that alignment and subsequent attention correction are coordinated while remaining distinct parts of how the model combines information.
summary.tldr: MODA coordinates modality alignment and adaptive attention correction to improve multimodal perception, cognition, and emotion understanding.

title: MODA: MOdular Duplex Attention for Multimodal Perception, Cognition, and Emotion Understanding

abstract: Self-improving agents aim to continuously acquire new capabilities with minimal supervision. However, current approaches face two key limitations: their self-improvement processes are often rigid, fail to generalize across tasks domains, and struggle to scale with increasing agent capabilities. We argue that effective self-improvement requires intrinsic metacognitive learning, defined as an agent’s $\textit{intrinsic}$ ability to actively evaluate, reflect on, and adapt its own learning processes. Drawing inspiration from human metacognition, we introduce a formal framework comprising three components: $\textit{metacognitive knowledge}$ (self-assessment of capabilities, tasks, and learning strategies), $\textit{metacognitive planning}$ (deciding what and how to learn), and $\textit{metacognitive evaluation}$ (reflecting on learning experiences to improve future learning). Analyzing existing self-improving agents, we find they rely predominantly on $\textit{extrinsic}$ metacognitive mechanisms, which are fixed, human-designed loops that limit scalability and adaptability. Examining each component, we contend that many ingredients for intrinsic metacognition are already present. Finally, we explore how to optimally distribute metacognitive responsibilities between humans and agents, and robustly evaluate and improve intrinsic metacognitive learning, key challenges that must be addressed to enable truly sustained, generalized, and aligned self-improvement.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that sustained self-improvement requires agents to evaluate and adapt their own learning processes. Current approaches often use rigid improvement procedures that transfer poorly between task domains and struggle as capabilities grow. The authors call the proposed internal capacity intrinsic metacognitive learning, drawing inspiration from how humans reflect on their own learning.

Their framework contains three components. Metacognitive knowledge covers an agent’s assessment of its capabilities, tasks, and learning strategies. Metacognitive planning determines what to learn and how to approach it. Metacognitive evaluation reflects on learning experiences so that future learning can improve. Together, these components describe control over the learning process itself.

Analyzing existing agents, the authors find that metacognitive control is mostly supplied through fixed, human-designed loops. They argue that many ingredients for more intrinsic control are already available, while identifying important remaining questions. These include distributing responsibilities between people and agents and evaluating the resulting learning reliably. The framework is intended to guide progress toward sustained, generalizable, aligned improvement rather than establish that such improvement has already been achieved.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that self-improving agents need internal capacities to assess, plan, and revise how they learn.

title: Position: Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning

abstract: We study a stylized social learning dynamics where self-interested agents collectively follow a simple multi-armed bandit protocol. Each agent controls an "episode": a short sequence of consecutive decisions. Motivating applications include users repeatedly interacting with an AI, or repeatedly shopping at a marketplace. While agents are incentivized to explore within their respective episodes, we show that the aggregate exploration fails: e.g., its Bayesian regret grows linearly over time. In fact, such failure is a (very) typical case, not just a worst-case scenario. This conclusion persists even if an agent’s per-episode utility is some fixed function of the per-round outcomes: e.g., $\min$ or $\max$, not just the sum. Thus, externally driven exploration is needed even when some amount of exploration happens organically.

paragraphs: When people repeatedly use an AI system or shop in a marketplace, trying unfamiliar options can benefit their later decisions. This paper models that situation as a shared multi-armed bandit process in which each self-interested agent controls a short episode of consecutive choices. Because an agent makes several decisions, it can have a personal incentive to explore during its episode.

The central result is that this individual incentive does not ensure effective exploration for the population over time. Under the studied dynamics, aggregate learning can fail, with Bayesian regret growing linearly. That means the cumulative cost of imperfect decisions keeps growing at a constant-order rate. The authors establish that this failure is typical in their setting, rather than confined to a specially constructed worst case.

The conclusion also persists when episode utility is a fixed function such as the minimum or maximum round outcome, rather than a sum. Within this model, organic exploration therefore does not remove the need for externally driven exploration.
summary.tldr: In the studied social-learning model, personally useful exploration within short episodes still fails to produce effective collective learning.

title: Bandit Social Learning with Exploration Episodes

abstract: Mixture of Experts (MoE) has emerged as a mainstream architecture for Large Language Models (LLMs), balancing computational efficiency with model scalability. While prior work has explored increasing tensor-level sparsity via finer-grained expert configurations during pre-training, we identify significant unexploited sparsity at both the tensor and neuron levels during post-training and inference. To leverage this, we propose complete expert partition for post-training and threshold-based token-expert dropping for inference. These techniques improve the Mixtral-8$\times$7B model’s average accuracy by 1% across nine downstream benchmarks (notably 4% on GSM8K). To further optimize the accuracy-efficiency trade-off for inference, we introduce dual-threshold token-expert dropping with partial expert partition and reconstruction. Our approach yields a 1.19$\times$ MoE speedup and a 0.5% accuracy gain on Mixtral-8$\times$7B when combining post-training and inference optimizations. For inference-only optimization on OLMoE-Instruct and DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat, we achieve up to 1.41$\times$ MoE speedup with a negligible accuracy loss ($<$0.5%).

title: Mining Tensor/Neuron-Level Sparsity to Maximize Mixture-of-Experts Potential in Post-Training and Inference

abstract: We investigate the capabilities and scalability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in optimization modeling, a domain requiring structured reasoning and precise formulation. To this end, we introduce OPT-ENGINE, an extensible benchmark framework with quantifiable and controllable complexity. OPT-ENGINE spans ten canonical Operations Research problems, systematically scaling from Linear Programming to Mixed-Integer Programming, providing a structured environment to probe the limits of automated problem formulation and solving. Utilizing OPT-Engine, we address three pivotal research questions. First, we examine whether Pure-Text Reasoning (PTR) via classical Chain-of-Thought can efficiently tackle optimization tasks, finding that PTR suffers from a critical robustness gap as task complexity increases. Second, we examine whether integrating external computational tools can mitigate PTR’s arithmetic weaknesses and improve performance. Our results show that while such tools aid local calculations, they still fail to adhere to global optimization constraints. Finally, we pinpoint that for the current SOTA paradigm, Solver-integrated Reasoning (SIR), the automated formulation of constraints represents the primary bottleneck. These findings clarify current paradigms’ limitations and provide a structured roadmap for developing next-generation LLMs for optimization modeling. We release our code and data to facilitate future research (https://github.com/Cardinal-Operations/OPTEngine).
