paragraphs: OPT-Engine evaluates how well language models formulate and solve optimization problems as complexity increases. Its benchmark spans ten canonical operations-research problems, with controlled progression from linear programming to mixed-integer programming. This structure allows the authors to examine where different reasoning approaches begin to break down.

The study first tests pure text reasoning through chain-of-thought and finds a substantial robustness gap at higher complexity. Adding computational tools helps with local arithmetic, but the evaluated systems still fail to respect global optimization constraints. Correctly calculating an individual quantity therefore does not establish that a complete proposed solution satisfies the problem.

For solver-integrated reasoning, the authors identify automated constraint formulation as the main bottleneck. A solver depends on the mathematical problem it receives, so this finding places emphasis on translating task requirements into accurate constraints. Together, the results distinguish weaknesses in calculation from weaknesses in formulation and provide a controlled framework for evaluating future progress on both.
summary.tldr: OPT-Engine scales optimization-task complexity and identifies constraint formulation as the key bottleneck for solver-integrated language-model reasoning.

title: OPT-Engine: Benchmarking the Limits of LLMs in Optimization Modeling via Complexity Scaling

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) frequently produce hallucinations (i.e., assertions that contradict the image or facts), undermining reliability in high-risk applications. Existing detection approaches typically feed images and texts jointly and estimate hallucination scores by measuring the consistency of model outputs. However, because the visual module often lags behind the language module in understanding and reasoning, MLLMs can repeatedly produce similar yet incorrect answers, yielding overestimated trustworthiness and missed detections. To address this, we propose a simple yet effective model-agnostic method, dubbed Decoupled Object-level Understanding and Bridging via vMF-based Trustworthiness (DOUBT). DOUBT first employs Object-level Understanding and Bridging (OUB), a two-step prompting scheme that decouples object recognition from relational reasoning by prompting the model to identify objects and then reason based on them. It further introduces a von Mises-Fisher (vMF)-based trustworthiness metric, which is more stable than semantic entropy metrics in small-sample settings. Extensive experiments and ablation studies on multiple benchmarks show that DOUBT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating its robustness and generalizability for hallucination detection in MLLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/XLearning-SCU/2026-ICML-DOUBT.

paragraphs: DOUBT targets a weakness in detecting hallucinations from multimodal language models: repeated answers can agree with one another while still being wrong. The authors attribute this partly to a mismatch between visual and language capabilities. When visual understanding is weaker, consistency across generated answers can exaggerate trustworthiness and cause detectors to miss errors.

A von Mises–Fisher-based metric then assesses trustworthiness, with greater reported stability than semantic-entropy metrics when only a small number of samples are available.

The approach is model-agnostic, and the authors evaluate it through multiple benchmarks and ablation studies. They report consistent improvements over leading detection baselines. The findings support separating stages of visual reasoning and improving small-sample trust estimation as complementary ways to detect hallucinations more reliably.
summary.tldr: DOUBT separates object recognition from relational reasoning and uses a more stable trust metric to detect multimodal hallucinations.

title: DOUBT: Decoupled Object-level Understanding and Bridging via vMF-based Trustworthiness for Hallucination Detection in MLLMs

abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models remain computationally intensive: generating a single image typically requires dozens of passes through large transformer backbones (e.g., SDXL uses 50 evaluations of a 2.6B-parameter model). Few-step variants reduce the step count to 2–8 but still rely on large, full-precision backbones, making inference impractical on resource-constrained platforms. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods are further hampered by their dependence on full-precision calibration. We introduce Q-Sched, a scheduler-level PTQ approach that adapts the diffusion sampler while keeping the quantized weights fixed. By adjusting the few-step sampling trajectory with quantization-aware preconditioning coefficients, Q-Sched matches or surpasses full-precision quality while delivering a 4$\times$ reduction in model size and preserving a single reusable checkpoint across bit-widths. To learn these coefficients, we propose a reference-free Joint Alignment–Quality (JAQ) loss, which combines text–image compatibility with an image-quality objective for fine-grained control. JAQ requires only a handful of calibration prompts and avoids any full-precision inference during calibration. Empirically, Q-Sched yields substantial gains: a 15.5% FID improvement over the FP16 4-step Latent Consistency Model and a 16.6% improvement over the FP16 8-step Phased Consistency Model, demonstrating that quantization and few-step distillation are complementary for high-fidelity generation. A large-scale user study with 80,000+ annotations further validates these results on both FLUX.1[schnell] and SDXL-Turbo. Code: https://github.com/enyac-group/q-sched

title: Q-Sched: Pushing the Boundaries of Few-Step Diffusion Models with Quantization-Aware Scheduling

abstract: In safety-critical domains where online data collection is infeasible, offline reinforcement learning (RL) is attractive only if policies achieve high returns without catastrophic lower-tail risk. Prior work on risk-averse offline RL achieves safety at the cost of value- or model-based pessimism, and restricted policy classes that limit policy expressiveness, whereas diffusion/flow-based expressive generative policies have largely been used in risk-neutral settings. We introduce Risk-Aware Multimodal Actor-Critic (RAMAC), a simple, modular, model-free framework that couples an expressive generative actor (e.g., diffusion/flow) with a distributional critic and optimizes a composite objective that combines Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) with behavioral cloning (BC), enabling risk-sensitive learning in complex multimodal scenarios. Since out-of-distribution (OOD) actions are a major driver of catastrophic failures in offline RL, we further provide an objective-level analysis showing that controlling behavior divergence via BC suppresses OOD actions and stabilizes CVaR. Instantiating RAMAC with a diffusion actor, we illustrate these insights on a 2-D risky bandit and evaluate on Stochastic-D4RL, observing consistent gains in CVaR$_{0.1}$ while maintaining strong returns.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from existing data without gathering new experience. In safety-critical settings, a high average return is insufficient if a policy also produces disastrous outcomes. RAMAC targets this lower-tail risk while retaining an expressive policy capable of representing multiple distinct action patterns.

The framework combines a generative actor, such as a diffusion or flow model, with a distributional critic. Its objective joins Conditional Value-at-Risk, which emphasizes poor outcomes, with behavioral cloning. The latter keeps the learned behavior closer to the recorded data. An objective-level analysis shows that controlling this divergence suppresses out-of-distribution actions and stabilizes the risk objective.

The authors instantiate RAMAC with a diffusion actor, illustrate the mechanism on a two-dimensional risky bandit, and evaluate it on Stochastic-D4RL. They observe consistent gains in CVaR at the 0.1 level while maintaining strong returns. These results support combining expressive policies with behavior regularization to improve lower-tail outcomes without abandoning the objective of achieving useful overall performance.
summary.tldr: RAMAC combines expressive generative policies, lower-tail risk optimization, and behavioral cloning to improve risk-sensitive offline reinforcement learning.

title: RAMAC: Multimodal Risk-Aware Offline Reinforcement Learning and the Role of Behavior Regularization

abstract: Achieving a provable exponential quantum speedup for an important machine learning task has been a central research goal since the seminal HHL quantum algorithm for solving linear systems and the subsequent quantum recommender systems algorithm by Kerenidis and Prakash. These algorithms were initially believed to be strong candidates for exponential speedups, but a lower bound ruling out similar classical improvements remained absent. In breakthrough work by Tang, it was demonstrated that this lack of progress in classical lower bounds was for good reasons. Concretely, she gave a classical counterpart of the quantum recommender systems algorithm, reducing the quantum advantage to a mere polynomial. Her approach is quite general and was named quantum-inspired classical algorithms. Since then, almost all the initially exponential quantum machine learning speedups have been reduced to polynomial via new quantum-inspired classical algorithms. From the current state-of-affairs, it is unclear whether we can hope for exponential quantum speedups for any natural machine learning task. In this work, we present the first such provable exponential separation between quantum and quantum-inspired classical algorithms for the basic problem of solving a linear system when the input matrix is well-conditioned and has sparse rows and columns.

paragraphs: The paper addresses whether quantum computing can offer a provable exponential advantage for solving linear systems, a basic computational problem relevant to machine learning. Earlier quantum algorithms appeared to offer such advantages, but establishing a separation also required showing that comparable classical methods could not achieve similar improvements. Without that lower-bound evidence, the size of the advantage remained uncertain.

Quantum-inspired classical algorithms made this issue concrete. These methods reproduced important benefits of earlier quantum algorithms using classical computation, reducing many proposed exponential advantages to polynomial ones. The paper therefore focuses on distinguishing quantum algorithms from this particularly relevant class of classical competitors, rather than merely comparing against an older classical implementation.

The stated result is an exponential separation for linear systems whose input matrices are well-conditioned and have sparse rows and columns. Those matrix conditions define the setting of the claim. The contribution is a proof that an exponential gap survives quantum-inspired classical approaches in this setting, providing a positive answer for a natural computational task after many earlier candidate advantages had narrowed.
summary.tldr: The paper proves an exponential quantum advantage over quantum-inspired classical algorithms for linear systems with well-conditioned matrices and sparse rows and columns.

title: An Exponential Separation Between Quantum and Quantum-Inspired Classical Algorithms for Linear Systems

abstract: Large vision–language models (LVLMs) perform well on multimodal tasks, but their ability to reason and precisely align visual and textual information still has room for improvement. In this study, we show that external visual cues, such as symbols or grid lines, help LVLMs form more accurate connections between visual components, such as objects, and their corresponding textual descriptions, improving their grounding and reasoning abilities. We introduce the concept of Grounding IDs, which are latent identifiers that arise within the model as a result of external cues structuring both visual and textual modalities. Our analysis reveals that partition-inducing external cues lead to Grounding IDs that make better alignment between corresponding visual and text representations, helping the model focus on relevant information. We find that Grounding IDs enhance attention between related components, improving cross-modal grounding and reducing hallucinations. Overall, our results show that Grounding IDs are a key mechanism that enables external cues to improve cross-modal alignment, reduce errors, and enhance the overall performance of LVLMs across a range of multimodal tasks.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can struggle to connect a particular visual object with the right textual description. This paper investigates why external visual cues, such as symbols and grid lines, improve those connections. The authors find that cues which divide or structure the input help models align visual components with corresponding language.

They describe the resulting internal mechanism as Grounding IDs: latent identifiers that emerge when external cues structure both modalities. These identifiers improve alignment between matching visual and textual representations and help direct attention toward relevant information. The proposed explanation links an observable input change to a change in how the model internally binds related components.

The analysis finds stronger attention between related components, improved cross-modal grounding, and fewer hallucinations. Across a range of multimodal tasks, these effects accompany better reasoning and overall performance. The contribution is therefore more than demonstrating that visual annotations help: it identifies Grounding IDs as a key mechanism through which partition-inducing cues organize representations and reduce errors.
summary.tldr: External visual cues induce latent Grounding IDs that improve image-text alignment, focus attention, and reduce hallucinations.

title: Uncovering Grounding IDs: How External Cues Shape Multi-Modal Binding

abstract: We present HOI-PAGE, a new approach that prioritizes part-level affordance reasoning to generate high-fidelity 4D human-object interactions (HOIs) from text prompts in a zero-shot fashion. In contrast to prior works that focus on global, whole body-object motion synthesis, our approach explicitly reasons about the underlying part-level mechanics of interactions using large language models (LLMs). We capture this reasoning in a structured part affordance graph (PAG) representation, serving as a high-level interaction scaffolding to guide a three-stage synthesis: first, decomposing input 3D objects into semantic parts; then, generating reference HOI videos from text prompts to extract part-based motion constraints; and finally, optimizing for 4D HOI motion sequences that mimic the reference dynamics while satisfying part-level contact constraints. Extensive experiments show that our approach is flexible and capable of generating complex multi-object or multi-person interaction sequences, with significantly improved realism and text alignment for zero-shot 4D HOI generation.

paragraphs: Generating a believable human–object interaction requires more than arranging whole bodies and objects along plausible paths. The interacting parts must make suitable contact and move consistently with the intended action. HOI-PAGE makes these part-level relationships central to generating time-varying 3D interactions from text in a zero-shot setting.

The method uses a language model to reason about part affordances: how particular parts can participate in an interaction. It records this reasoning in a structured part affordance graph. That graph guides three stages: dividing input 3D objects into meaningful parts, generating reference interaction videos and extracting part-based motion constraints, and optimizing the final motion sequences.

The final optimization aims to follow the reference dynamics while satisfying contact constraints between relevant parts. Experiments show that the approach can generate complex sequences involving multiple objects or multiple people, with significantly improved realism and alignment with the text. The results support structured part-level reasoning as useful guidance for coordinating detailed contact with the overall motion requested by a prompt.
summary.tldr: HOI-PAGE uses structured reasoning about interacting body and object parts to improve zero-shot generation of realistic 4D interactions.

title: HOI-PAGE: Zero-Shot Human-Object Interaction Generation with Part Affordance Guidance

abstract: While large vision-language models (LVLMs) have shown remarkable adaptability to downstream applications, their fine-tuning process remains susceptible to bias under long-tailed data. Compared to zero-shot scenarios, fine-tuning LVLMs on imbalanced datasets often yields limited performance improvements on tail data. This is because LVLMs tend to rapidly overfit the head data at an early fine-tuning stage, thereby impairing the learning of the tail data while simultaneously failing to exploit their quantitative advantage. Furthermore, in many downstream LVLM scenarios, quantified long-tailed prior knowledge of data distribution is often unavailable, significantly limiting the applicability of traditional long-tailed techniques that rely heavily on such information. To address these issues, we propose the Adaptive Token Refinement (ATR), a novel framework that adaptively refines the learning process of LVLMs under long-tailed data. Specifically, ATR consists of two token-level operations applied to output and input tokens, respectively: 1) a bounded adaptive loss that dynamically filters and reweights output tokens to mitigate overfitting on head data, and 2) a visual token mask strategy that augments the probability paths of input tokens to enhance long-tailed performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ATR consistently enhance both performance and generalization for long-tailed LVLMs fine-tuning.

paragraphs: When training data contains many common examples and relatively few rare ones, fine-tuning a large vision-language model can reinforce the imbalance. The paper identifies early overfitting to frequent data as a problem: it interferes with learning rare cases while also failing to make full use of the abundant examples.

Adaptive Token Refinement addresses this through two operations at the token level. On the output side, a bounded adaptive loss dynamically filters and reweights tokens to reduce overfitting to frequent data. On the input side, a visual token masking strategy augments the probability paths available during learning. Together, these operations adjust both the supervision the model receives and the visual input it learns from.

The motivation also reflects a practical constraint: downstream datasets often lack quantified information about their imbalance, limiting methods that depend on such prior knowledge. Experiments report consistent improvements in performance and generalization for long-tailed fine-tuning. The contribution is an adaptive training framework aimed at improving learning across the imbalance, including the poorly served rare examples.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Token Refinement adjusts output-token learning and visual inputs to improve vision-language fine-tuning on imbalanced data.

title: Adaptive Token Refinement in Long-Tailed Large Vision-Language Models Fine-Tuning

abstract: We study online configuration selection with admission control problem, which arises in LLM serving, GPU scheduling, and revenue management. In a planning horizon with $T$ periods, we consider a two-layer framework for the decisions made within each time period. In the first layer, the decision maker selects one of the $K$ configurations (ex. quantization, parallelism, fare class) which induces distribution over the reward-resource pair of the incoming request. In the second layer, the decision maker observes the request and then decides whether to accept it or not. Benchmarking this framework requires care. We introduce a switching-aware fluid oracle that accounts for the value of mixing configurations over time, provably upper-bounding any online policy. We derive a max-min formulation for evaluating the benchmark, and we characterize saddle points of the max-min problem via primal-dual optimality conditions linking equilibrium, feasibility, and complementarity. This guides the design of SP-UCB–OLP algorithm, which solves an optimistic saddle point problem and achieves $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$ regret.

Examples include choosing an LLM serving configuration or a fare class. The first decision changes the distribution of possible rewards and resource demands; the second uses the observed request to decide whether accepting it is worthwhile.

The authors show why evaluating this joint problem requires a benchmark that accounts for changing configurations over time. Their switching-aware fluid oracle includes the value of mixing configurations and provably upper-bounds what any online policy can achieve. They formulate its evaluation as a max-min problem and characterize its saddle points through conditions connecting feasibility, equilibrium, and complementary resource constraints.

These mathematical conditions guide SP-UCB–OLP, which selects decisions by solving an optimistic saddle-point problem. Its regret guarantee scales as roughly the square root of K times T, up to logarithmic factors, where K counts configurations and T counts periods. The result gives a theoretical performance guarantee for coordinating configuration choice with admission decisions.
summary.tldr: A two-stage online algorithm coordinates configuration choices and request acceptance with a regret guarantee against a switching-aware benchmark.

title: A Two-Layer Framework for Joint Online Configuration Selection and Admission Control

abstract: Text-guided stylized image generation has yielded promising advances by leveraging the powerful capabilities of text-to-image diffusion models. However, the inherent coupling of style and content information within the reference image presents a significant challenge. To address this, we propose StyleDistillation, a novel approach grounded in two key observations about the CLIP embedding space from a style perspective. By leveraging a lightweight StyleDistiller module, combined with carefully designed optimization objectives based on geometric and semantic priors, we can extract fine-grained style representation from the reference image. Additionally, we introduce a Prompt Alignment Enhancement mechanism during inference, which significantly improves the control that text prompts exert over the generated images. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves outstanding performance in both style reproduction and prompt alignment. Furthermore, StyleDistillation supports various personalized operations, including style editing and style fusion, highlighting its substantial potential for diverse applications.

paragraphs: A reference image provides both an aesthetic style and particular visual content. For text-guided stylization, those two sources of information can become entangled, making it difficult to reproduce the desired style while following a new prompt. StyleDistillation addresses this by extracting a more focused representation of style from the reference.

The method builds on two observations about style in CLIP’s embedding space. A lightweight StyleDistiller module uses optimization objectives informed by geometric and semantic priors to extract fine-grained style information. During inference, a separate Prompt Alignment Enhancement mechanism strengthens the influence of the text prompt on the generated image, complementing the representation learned from the reference.

Experiments report strong performance in both style reproduction and prompt alignment. The framework also supports personalized operations such as editing a style and combining styles. These outcomes matter together because successful stylization requires control over appearance and over what the image depicts. The paper’s contribution is a coordinated approach to those requirements, pairing style extraction with an explicit mechanism for maintaining textual control during generation.
summary.tldr: StyleDistillation extracts fine-grained reference-image style and strengthens prompt alignment to support controlled stylization, style editing, and style fusion.

title: StyleDistillation: A New Insight of Image Style Enables Personalized Aesthetic Manipulation

abstract: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) person search aims to transfer a model trained on a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain without using target annotations. However, existing UDA methods frequently neglect the issue of scale inconsistency between the source and target domains. This inconsistency arises from variations in camera height, tilt angle, focal length, and scene layout. To address this challenge, we propose a Scale-Aware Consistent Alignment Learning (SCALE) framework. Specifically, we propose a Scale-aware Domain Harmonization (SDH) module, which adaptively harmonizes semantic and structural scales through cross-path interaction and consistency refinement to alleviate cross-domain scale inconsistency. To further reduce pseudo-label noise, we introduce a Bidirectional Cluster Regularization (BCR) strategy, which improves pseudo-label reliability by refining the clustering results through a second regularized clustering step. By collaboratively alleviating the impact of scale misalignment and enhancing pseudo-label reliability, our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on two benchmark person search datasets, with 82.3% mAP and 84.0% top-1 on the CUHK-SYSU dataset, 41.7% mAP and 82.4% top-1 on the PRW dataset. Our source code is available at https://github.com/whhbdmu/SCALE.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation for person search transfers a model from labeled source images to a target domain without target annotations. Camera height, tilt, focal length, and scene layout can change the scales at which people and their features appear. The paper argues that existing methods often overlook this mismatch, leaving an important source of transfer difficulty unresolved.

SCALE introduces a scale-aware harmonization module that aligns semantic and structural scales through interaction across processing paths and consistency refinement. It also addresses noisy pseudo-labels, the automatically inferred labels used when target annotations are unavailable. A bidirectional cluster regularization strategy performs a second, regularized clustering step to improve the reliability of those labels.

Its contribution is the coordinated treatment of scale mismatch and pseudo-label quality. The reported results indicate that improving both representation alignment and target supervision can strengthen transfer in this setting.
summary.tldr: SCALE improves person-search domain adaptation by aligning image scales and refining the pseudo-labels used for unlabeled target data.

title: Scale-Aware Domain Harmonization for Domain Adaptation Person Search

abstract: Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) is a widely used paradigm for accelerating inference in few-step video diffusion models. However, DMD-style training faces a structural bottleneck: the student-side auxiliary score network (the fake score) must closely track a continuously evolving generator. Updating the fake score too frequently increases training cost and can over-emphasize inner-loop tracking, while infrequent updates lead to tracking lag that destabilizes training and degrades generation consistency. To address this issue, we propose Score Gradient Matching Distillation (SGMD). SGMD adopts a fake-score perspective by directly optimizing the fake score toward the teacher, while using teacher stop-gradient Fisher as a stable distribution-matching objective. We provide a gradient analysis that motivates this objective choice under ideal tracking. Building on this, SGMD introduces a pair of dual potentials: negative-residual (NR) for outer-loop correction and residual-contraction (RC) for inner-loop tracking. Empirically, compared to DMD, SGMD achieves an approximately $\sim 3\times$ training speedup and substantially improves motion dynamics for 4-step distilled models while preserving temporal consistency.

Frequent updates are costly, while infrequent updates create tracking lag that can destabilize learning and reduce consistency.

Score Gradient Matching Distillation changes how this auxiliary network and the generator are optimized. It directly trains the fake score toward the teacher and uses a teacher stop-gradient Fisher objective for distribution matching. A gradient analysis motivates that objective under ideal tracking. The method then introduces two complementary potentials: negative-residual correction for the outer loop and residual-contraction tracking for the inner loop.

This design targets the interaction between updating the generator and keeping its auxiliary score estimate current. Compared with DMD, experiments report approximately threefold faster training and substantially improved motion dynamics for four-step distilled video models, while preserving temporal consistency. The speed claim concerns distillation training, and the theoretical motivation explicitly relies on ideal tracking; the practical results show benefits in the evaluated training setting.
summary.tldr: SGMD improves auxiliary score tracking during video distillation, reporting roughly threefold faster training and better four-step motion dynamics.

title: SGMD: Score Gradient Matching Distillation for Few-Step Video Diffusion Distillation

abstract: Semi-supervised graph anomaly detection (GAD), which assumes a subset of labeled normal nodes for training, is widely studied. However, existing methods learn normality only from these labeled nodes, often overfitting their patterns and causing high detection errors, such as many false positives. To overcome this limitation, we propose $GraphNC$, a graph normality calibration framework that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to calibrate the normality from a teacher (a pre-trained semi-supervised GAD model) jointly in anomaly score and representation spaces. GraphNC includes two main components, anomaly score distribution alignment ($ScoreDA$) and perturbation-based normality regularization ($NormReg$). ScoreDA optimizes our model’s anomaly scores by aligning them with the teacher’s score distribution. Because the teacher provides accurate scores for most normal nodes and some anomalies, this alignment pulls the scores of the two classes toward opposite ends, making them more separable. To reduce the impact of inaccurate teacher scores, NormReg regularizes normality in the representation space, making normal node representations more compact via a perturbation-guided consistency loss applied only to the labeled nodes. Comprehensive experiments on six benchmarks demonstrate that GraphNC (1) consistently and substantially enhances the performance of teacher models from different GAD methods (2) achieves new state-of-the-art performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/mala-lab/GraphNC.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised graph anomaly detection learns from a subset of nodes labeled normal. Learning normality only from that subset can overfit its patterns, causing other normal nodes to be flagged incorrectly. GraphNC calibrates an existing detector using both labeled and unlabeled data, working on anomaly scores and internal representations together.

Its score-distribution alignment component uses a pretrained detector as a teacher. The method relies on that teacher providing accurate scores for most normal nodes and some anomalies; aligning with its score distribution helps separate the classes. A second component addresses inaccurate teacher scores by regularizing representations through perturbation-guided consistency on labeled nodes only, making normal representations more compact.

These two components provide complementary guidance: the teacher contributes information across the data, while known normal nodes anchor representation regularization. Experiments on six benchmarks show consistent, substantial improvements to teachers drawn from different anomaly-detection methods and report new state-of-the-art performance. The findings support normality calibration as a way to improve existing detectors beyond the patterns present in their labeled training subset.
summary.tldr: GraphNC improves graph anomaly detectors by calibrating teacher scores with unlabeled data and stabilizing representations of labeled normal nodes.

title: Normality Calibration in Semi-supervised Graph Anomaly Detection

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) have shown strong potential in scaling language models efficiently by activating only a small subset of experts per input. However, their deployment remains limited due to the high memory overhead associated with storing all expert parameters, particularly as the number of experts increases. To address this challenge, prior works have explored expert dropping and merging strategies; however, they often suffer from notable performance drop especially at high compression ratios due to their reliance on coarse-grained tensor- or expert-level operations. In this paper, we introduce PuzzleMoE, the first MoE merging method to enable fine-grained element-wise merging while achieving both high accuracy and inference speed, via two key innovations: First, PuzzleMoE performs sparse expert merging by identifying element-wise weight redundancy and specialization. It introduces a dual-mask approach to capture both shared and expert-specific salient parameters. Second, to avoid the overhead of storing masks and signs, we introduce a bit-packed encoding scheme that reuses underutilized exponent bits, enabling efficient MoE inference on GPUs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PuzzleMoE outperforms prior MoE compression methods by up to 16.7% on MMLU at 50% compression ratio, and achieves up to 1.80$\times$ end-to-end inference throughput gain.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models activate only a small fraction of their experts for an input, but deployment still requires storing all expert parameters. Removing or merging whole experts can reduce memory needs while damaging performance, particularly under heavy compression. PuzzleMoE targets redundancy at the finer level of individual weight elements.

Its sparse merging procedure uses two masks to capture both parameters that can be shared and salient parameters specific to individual experts. This allows compression to reflect differences within experts instead of treating each expert or tensor as one indivisible unit. Preserving expert-specific elements is part of the method's approach to maintaining accuracy.

Fine-grained merging also creates storage and execution overhead from masks and signs. PuzzleMoE addresses this with a bit-packed encoding that reuses underutilized exponent bits for efficient GPU inference. Experiments report improvements over prior compression methods of up to 16.7% on MMLU at a 50% compression ratio, along with up to 1.80-fold end-to-end throughput gains. The contribution combines a finer compression decision with an encoding designed to make that decision computationally useful.
summary.tldr: PuzzleMoE combines element-wise expert merging with bit-packed storage to improve compressed MoE accuracy and inference throughput.

title: PuzzleMoE: Efficient Compression of Large Mixture-of-Experts Models via Fine-Grained Expert Merging and Bit-packed Inference

abstract: Time series is a pervasive data type across various application domains, rendering the reasonable solving of diverse time series tasks a long-standing goal. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs), especially their reasoning abilities unlocked through reinforcement learning (RL), have opened new opportunities for tackling tasks with long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. However, leveraging LLM reasoning for time series remains infancy, hindered by the absence of carefully curated time series CoT data for training, limited data efficiency caused by underexplored data scheduling, and the lack of RL algorithms tailored for exploiting such time series CoT data. In this paper, we introduce VeriTime, a framework that tailors LLMs for time series reasoning through data synthesis, data scheduling, and RL training. First, we propose a data synthesis pipeline that constructs a time series–text multimodal dataset with process-verifiable annotations. Second, we design a data scheduling mechanism that arranges training samples according to a principled hierarchy of difficulty and task taxonomy. Third, we develop a two-stage reinforcement finetuning featuring fine-grained, multi-objective rewards that leverages verifiable process-level CoT data. Extensive experiments show that VeriTime substantially boosts LLM performance across diverse time series reasoning tasks. Notably, it enables compact 3B–4B models to achieve reasoning capabilities on par with or exceeding those of larger proprietary LLMs.

paragraphs: Language models offer new possibilities for reasoning about time series, but training them requires suitable examples and rewards. VeriTime addresses three connected needs: reasoning data whose intermediate process can be checked, an effective order for presenting that data, and reinforcement learning that makes use of process-level supervision.

The framework first synthesizes a multimodal dataset pairing time series with text and process-verifiable annotations. It then schedules examples using a hierarchy of difficulty and a taxonomy of tasks. Finally, two-stage reinforcement fine-tuning applies detailed, multi-objective rewards to the verifiable reasoning data, connecting the structure of the training examples with the feedback used to learn from them.

Experiments report substantial improvements across diverse time-series reasoning tasks. In the evaluated setting, compact models with 3B–4B parameters match or exceed the reasoning capabilities of larger proprietary models. The findings support the combined value of data synthesis, scheduling, and tailored reinforcement learning: the framework improves how reasoning examples are created, when they are encountered, and how their intermediate steps contribute to training.
summary.tldr: VeriTime combines verifiable time-series reasoning data, structured scheduling, and tailored reinforcement learning to strengthen compact language models.

title: Time Series Reasoning via Process-Verifiable Thinking Data Synthesis and Scheduling for Tailored LLM Reasoning

abstract: Collaborative and content-based filtering are two paradigms that have beenapplied in the context of recommender systems and user preference prediction.This paper proposes a novel, unified approach that systematically integratesall available training information such as past user-item ratings as well asattributes of items or users to learn a prediction function. The keyingredient of our method is the design of a suitable kernel or similarityfunction between user-item pairs that allows simultaneous generalizationacross the user and item dimensions. We propose an on-line algorithm (JRank)that generalizes perceptron learning. Experimental results on the EachMoviedata set show significant improvements over standard approaches.

The keyingredient of our method is the design of a suitable kernel or similarityfunction between user-item pairs that allows simultaneous generalizationacross the user and item dimensions. We propose an on-line algorithm (JRank)that generalizes perceptron learning. Experimental results on the EachMoviedata set show significant improvements over standard approaches.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems can learn from past user ratings and from descriptive attributes of users or items. This paper proposes a unified method that systematically incorporates these forms of training information into one prediction function. Its aim is to bring collaborative and content-based filtering into a common learning approach.

The key design choice is a kernel, or similarity function, between user-item pairs. Treating the pair as the object being compared allows information to generalize across both the user dimension and the item dimension. The authors also propose JRank, an online learning algorithm that generalizes perceptron learning for this formulation.

Experiments on the EachMovie dataset show significant improvements over standard approaches in the reported comparisons. These findings support the value of combining rating information with attributes through a shared similarity function. The contribution is both a representation for integrating the available information and a learning algorithm for using it, with empirical evidence from the movie recommendation setting.
summary.tldr: A similarity function over user-item pairs unifies ratings and attributes, with JRank showing improvements on EachMovie.

title: Unifying collaborative and content-based filtering

abstract: This paper is concerned with the problem of predicting relative performance of classification algorithms. It focusses on methods that use results on small samples and discusses the shortcomings of previous approaches. A new variant is proposed that exploits, as some previous approaches, metalearning. The method requires that experiments be conducted on few samples. The information gathered is used to identify the nearest learning curve for which the sampling procedure was carried out fully. This in turn permits to generate a prediction regards the relative performance of algorithms. Experimental evaluation shows that the method competes well with previous approaches and provides quite good and practical solution to this problem.

The method requires that experiments be conducted on few samples. The information gathered is used to identify the nearest learning curve for which the sampling procedure was carried out fully. paragraphs: Choosing a classification algorithm can involve estimating how competing methods will perform before carrying out extensive experiments. This paper studies predictions of relative performance using results from small data samples. It discusses weaknesses in earlier approaches and proposes a variant based on metalearning, using information from previously completed learning experiments.

The new method first runs experiments on a few samples. It uses the resulting observations to identify the nearest learning curve among curves whose sampling procedures have already been completed. That matched curve then supplies information for predicting the relative performance of the classification algorithms.

The approach matters because a limited set of observations is connected to a more complete record of how learning progressed elsewhere. It uses that connection to make a comparative prediction without requiring the full sampling procedure for the new case. The experimental evaluation finds that the method competes well with previous approaches and offers a practical solution. The stated result supports its usefulness for comparative algorithm assessment, without claiming that every predicted ranking will be correct.
summary.tldr: Matching a few sample-based results to previously completed learning curves helps predict which classification algorithms will perform better.

title: Predicting relative performance of classifiers from samples

abstract: We propose a method for the classiﬁcation of matrices. We use a linear classiﬁer with a novel regularization scheme based on the spectral ℓ₁ -norm of its coeﬃcient matrix. The spectral regularization not only provides a principled way of complexity control but also enables automatic determination of the rank of the coeﬃcient matrix. Using the Linear Matrix Inequality technique, we formulate the inference task as a single convex optimization problem. We apply our method to the motor-imagery EEG classiﬁcation problem. The method not only improves upon conventional methods in the classiﬁcation performance but also determines a subspace in the signal that concentrates discriminative information without any additional feature extraction step. The method can be easily generalized to regression problems by changing the loss function. Connections to other methods are also discussed.

Using the Linear Matrix Inequality technique, we formulate the inference task as a single convex optimization problem. We apply our method to the motor-imagery EEG classiﬁcation problem. The method not only improves upon conventional methods in the classiﬁcation performance but also determines a subspace in the signal that concentrates discriminative information without any additional feature extraction step. The method can be easily generalized to regression problems by changing the loss function. Connections to other methods are also discussed.

paragraphs: This paper develops a linear classifier for examples represented as matrices. Its main contribution is a regularization scheme based on the spectral ℓ₁ norm of the classifier's coefficient matrix. The regularizer controls model complexity while also allowing the rank of that coefficient matrix to be determined automatically, linking prediction with the discovery of a lower-dimensional structure.

The authors formulate the inference task as one convex optimization problem using linear matrix inequalities. This brings the classification objective and spectral regularization into a single optimization framework. The rank is therefore addressed as part of fitting the classifier rather than being treated only as a separate representation choice.

In an application to motor-imagery EEG classification, the method improves classification performance over conventional methods. It also identifies a signal subspace that concentrates information useful for discrimination, without requiring an additional feature-extraction step. The abstract further states that changing the loss function extends the approach to regression. The contribution thus combines matrix classification, complexity control, and discriminative subspace identification within one formulation.
summary.tldr: Spectral regularization lets a matrix classifier control complexity and determine coefficient rank while improving motor-imagery EEG classification.

title: Classifying matrices with a spectral regularization

abstract: We cast model-free reinforcement learning as the problem of maximizing the likelihood of a probabilistic mixture model via sampling, addressing both the infinite and finite horizon cases. We describe a Stochastic Approximation EM algorithm for likelihood maximization that, in the tabular case, is equivalent to a non-bootstrapping optimistic policy iteration algorithm like Sarsa(1) that can be applied both in MDPs and POMDPs. On the theoretical side, by relating the proposed stochastic EM algorithm to the family of optimistic policy iteration algorithms, we provide new tools that permit the design and analysis of algorithms in that family. On the practical side, preliminary experiments on a POMDP problem demonstrated encouraging results.

We describe a Stochastic Approximation EM algorithm for likelihood maximization that, in the tabular case, is equivalent to a non-bootstrapping optimistic policy iteration algorithm like Sarsa(1) that can be applied both in MDPs and POMDPs. On the theoretical side, by relating the proposed stochastic EM algorithm to the family of optimistic policy iteration algorithms, we provide new tools that permit the design and analysis of algorithms in that family. On the practical side, preliminary experiments on a POMDP problem demonstrated encouraging results.

paragraphs: This paper interprets model-free reinforcement learning as fitting a probabilistic mixture model. The learning objective becomes maximizing likelihood through sampling, with formulations covering both finite and infinite horizons. This creates a connection between a sequential decision-making problem and a familiar form of probabilistic learning.

The authors develop a stochastic approximation expectation-maximization algorithm for that likelihood objective. In the tabular setting, it is equivalent to a non-bootstrapping optimistic policy iteration algorithm of the kind represented by Sarsa(1). The algorithm can be applied in both Markov decision processes and partially observable Markov decision processes, covering the two settings identified in the abstract.

The theoretical value of the connection is that stochastic EM supplies additional tools for designing and analyzing optimistic policy iteration algorithms. Preliminary experiments on a partially observable problem give encouraging results. The strongest stated contribution is thus the formulation and algorithmic relationship; the practical evidence is presented as an initial demonstration, rather than a broad empirical conclusion about performance.
summary.tldr: Model-free reinforcement learning is reformulated as mixture-model likelihood maximization, linking stochastic EM to optimistic policy iteration.

title: Model-free reinforcement learning as mixture learning

abstract: We consider the problem of multi-task reinforcement learning where the learner is provided with a set of tasks, for which only a small number of samples can be generated for any given policy. As the number of samples may not be enough to learn an accurate evaluation of the policy, it would be necessary to identify classes of tasks with similar structure and to learn them jointly. We consider the case where the tasks share structure in their value functions, and model this by assuming that the value functions are all sampled from a common prior. We adopt the Gaussian process temporal-difference value function model and use a hierarchical Bayesian approach to model the distribution over the value functions. We study two cases, where all the value functions belong to the same class and where they belong to an undefined number of classes. For each case, we present a hierarchical Bayesian model, and derive inference algorithms for (i) joint learning of the value functions, and (ii) efficient transfer of the information gained in (i) to assist learning the value function of a newly observed task.

As the number of samples may not be enough to learn an accurate evaluation of the policy, it would be necessary to identify classes of tasks with similar structure and to learn them jointly. We consider the case where the tasks share structure in their value functions, and model this by assuming that the value functions are all sampled from a common prior. We adopt the Gaussian process temporal-difference value function model and use a hierarchical Bayesian approach to model the distribution over the value functions. We study two cases, where all the value functions belong to the same class and where they belong to an undefined number of classes. For each case, we present a hierarchical Bayesian model, and derive inference algorithms for (i) joint learning of the value functions, and (ii) efficient transfer of the information gained in (i) to assist learning the value function of a newly observed task.

paragraphs: This paper considers reinforcement learning across several tasks when only a small number of samples can be collected for any given policy. Those samples may be insufficient to evaluate a policy accurately within each task alone. The proposed response is to identify shared structure and use information from related tasks jointly.

The sharing assumption concerns value functions: the authors model them as draws from a common prior. They combine a Gaussian process temporal-difference model with a hierarchical Bayesian description of how the value functions are distributed. The hierarchy provides a way to model relationships among tasks while learning their individual value functions.

The paper treats two possibilities: all value functions belong to one class, or they belong to an unspecified number of classes. For each, it provides a model and inference algorithms for joint learning. It also derives a way to transfer the information learned across existing tasks to a newly encountered task. The contribution is a framework for evaluation and transfer under the stated shared-structure assumption.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical Bayesian models share value-function information across related reinforcement learning tasks and transfer it to new tasks.
